questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In which stage of meiosis is the primary oocyte arrested?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Diplotene

The primary oocyte is arrested in prophase I of meiosis during a specific substage called diplotene.

Primary oocytes initiate meiosis I, but are arrested in prophase I before birth.

The arrest persists until puberty, when hormonal signals trigger the resumption of meiosis in a selected number of oocytes during each menstrual cycle.

Meiosis I (Reduction Division): Homologous chromosomes separate.

• Prophase I: Chromosomes pair, cross over.
• Metaphase I: Homologous pairs align at the equator.
• Anaphase I: Homologous chromosomes separate.
• Telophase I: Two haploid cells form.

Meiosis II (Equational Division): Sister chromatids separate.

• Prophase II: Chromosomes condense.
• Metaphase II: Chromosomes align at the equator.
• Anaphase II: Sister chromatids separate.
• Telophase II: Four genetically unique haploid cells form.

Prophase I consists of several substages (leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene, and diakinesis). In primary oocytes:

• Leptotene: Chromosomes condense and become visible. (Option B)
• Zygotene: Homologous chromosomes pair up through synapsis. (Option C)
• Pachytene: Crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids. (Option D)
• Diplotene stage: The homologous chromosomes are connected at chiasmata (sites of crossing over), and the oocyte enters a prolonged resting phase. At ovulation, the primary oocyte completes meiosis I and becomes a secondary oocyte, which then gets arrested in metaphase II of meiosis until fertilization.
• Diakinesis: Chromosomes fully condense; nuclear envelope breaks down.
questions.learning: Diplotene — The primary oocyte is arrested in prophase I of meiosis during a specific substage called diplotene. Primary oocytes initiate meiosis I, but are arrested in prophase I before birth.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 23-year-old man with epilepsy presents with pain in the right shoulder. On examination, the right upper limb is found to be abducted and externally rotated, and active movements are not possible. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s limb position—abducted and externally rotated—is the classic presentation of an anterior shoulder dislocation. Subglenoid dislocation is a common subtype of anterior dislocation where the humeral head rests inferior to the glenoid fossa. Regarding the distractors, posterior dislocation (Option D) is classically associated with seizures (epilepsy) but presents with adduction and internal rotation. Luxatio erecta (Option B), or inferior dislocation, is rare and presents with the arm locked in hyper-abduction over the head. Intrathoracic dislocation (Option A) is an extreme rarity where the head enters the rib cage. While the history of epilepsy often points toward a posterior dislocation, the specific physical examination findings of external rotation and abduction in this case override the history and definitively confirm an anterior (subglenoid) dislocation
questions.learning: The patient’s limb position—abducted and externally rotated—is the classic presentation of an anterior shoulder dislocation. Subglenoid dislocation is a common subtype of anterior dislocation where the humeral head rests inferior to the glenoid fossa.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which one among the following essential amino acids is usually the “limiting” amino acid in most of the pulses?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Methionine

Pulses (legumes) are an excellent source of plant protein and are rich in lysine, but they are relatively deficient in the sulfur-containing essential amino acid methionine, making it the limiting amino acid. This is why combining pulses with cereals provides a balanced amino acid profile and improves the overall biological value of dietary protein.

• Limiting amino acid in pulses: Methionine ⭐
• Limiting amino acid in cereals: Lysine ⭐
• Pulse + cereal combination (e.g., dal + rice, khichdi, idli, dosa) provides mutual protein supplementation, resulting in a high-quality protein. ⭐
• Pulses are rich in:

• Lysine
• Leucine
• Isoleucine

• Pulses are poor in:

• Methionine
• Cysteine
questions.learning: Methionine Pulses (legumes) are an excellent source of plant protein and are rich in lysine, but they are relatively deficient in the sulfur-containing essential amino acid methionine, making it the limiting amino acid.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention the type of joint present at the marked region.
questions.explanation: The arrow in the X-ray identifies the first carpometacarpal (CMC) joint, which is the articulation between the trapezium and the base of the first metacarpal. This joint is functionally classified as a saddle (sellar) joint. Saddle joints feature reciprocal concave-convex surfaces that allow for a wide range of motion, including flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, and uniquely, opposition. Ellipsoid joints (Option A), such as the wrist (radiocarpal) joint, allow for biaxial movement but lack the axial rotation seen in saddle joints. Condylar joints (Option B), like the knee, allow primarily for flexion and extension with limited rotation. Plane joints (Option C), found between the other carpal bones, permit only limited gliding movements. The saddle configuration of the first CMC joint is what gives the human thumb its exceptional mobility and ability to grasp objects, making it a common site for osteoarthritis due to the high mechanical loads it bears during daily activities
questions.learning: The arrow in the X-ray identifies the first carpometacarpal (CMC) joint, which is the articulation between the trapezium and the base of the first metacarpal.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 45-year-old man is admitted to the hospital after experiencing disorientation and confusion. He describes when he looks in the mirror, he cannot see his own reflection. This phenomenon is best described as which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Negative autoscopy

Negative autoscopy is a perceptual disturbance in which a person looks in a mirror or reflective surface and fails to see their own reflection, despite intact vision and reality testing. It is a rare form of autoscopic phenomenon and may occur in neurologic or psychiatric conditions such as epilepsy, migraine, delirium, or psychosis.

Types of autoscopic phenomena:

• Negative autoscopy: inability to see one’s own reflection
• Internal autoscopy: perception of seeing internal organs within one’s body
• Autoscopic hallucination: seeing one’s double outside the body
• Heautoscopy: seeing a double and difficulty identifying the real self

Distinguishing terms:

C. Extracampine hallucination: perception outside normal sensory field (eg, seeing someone behind you)

D. Hypnagogic hallucination: occurs while falling asleep
questions.learning: Negative autoscopy Negative autoscopy is a perceptual disturbance in which a person looks in a mirror or reflective surface and fails to see their own reflection, despite intact vision and reality testing.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The relaxation of the intestinal segment distal to the segment with the bolus of food during peristalsis is because of
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. VIP

The relaxation of the intestinal segment distal to the segment of a bolus of food during peristalsis is due to Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP).

Peristaltic contractions in the small intestine are designed to propel the food towards the large intestine.

The food bolus in the small intestine is sensed by enterochromaffin cells of the intestinal mucosa, which release 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT)(serotonin). The 5-HT then binds to the receptors on intrinsic primary afferent neurons (IPANs), which when activated, initiate the peristaltic reflex in that segment of the small intestine. Behind the bolus, excitatory transmitters like acetylcholine, Substance P, neuropeptide Y are released in the circular muscle, while these pathways are inhibited in the longitudinal muscle; thus this segment of small intestine (behind the bolus) contracts and lengthens.

(Recall that contraction of circular muscle decreases the diameter of that small intestinal segment whereas contraction of the longitudinal muscle decreases the length of that segment. To prevent the conflict that would occur if circular and longitudinal are contracted at the same time, they are reciprocally innervated)

In front of the bolus, inhibitory pathways like vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) and nitric oxide (NO) are activated in the circular muscle, while excitatory pathways are activated in the longitudinal muscle;thereby relaxing and shortening this segment of small intestine.
questions.learning: VIP — The relaxation of the intestinal segment distal to the segment of a bolus of food during peristalsis is due to Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient developed atonic postpartum hemorrhage after a normal vaginal delivery. She was shifted to the OT and the obstetrician planned ligation of vessels to arrest the bleeding. What is the order of ligation of the blood vessels supplying the uterus?
options: Uterine artery - Ovarian artery - Internal iliac artery
Uterine artery - Ovarian artery- External iliac artery
Uterine artery - Ovarian artery - Vaginal artery
Uterine artery - pudendal artery - Vaginal artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Uterine artery - Ovarian artery - Internal iliac artery

The order of ligation of vessels to arrest bleeding in atonic postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is the uterine artery - ovarian artery - internal iliac artery.

The ascending branch of the uterine artery is ligated between the upper and lower segments of the uterus, at the lateral border. If the bleeding continues, the ovarian and uterine artery anastomosis is ligated just below the ovarian ligament. If the bleeding still persists, the anterior division of the internal iliac artery is ligated 5 cm distal to the common iliac bifurcation.

Unilateral or bilateral ligation of the internal iliac artery ligation causes a reduction in the pulse pressure in the arteries distal to the ligation. This increases the chances of hemostasis via pressure and clot formation.

Surgical methods to control PPH are outlined as stepwise uterine devascularization procedures:

• Compression sutures: B-Lynch suture
• Ligation of uterine arteries
• Ligation of ovarian and uterine anastomosis
• Ligation of internal iliac artery
• Angiographic embolization of the bleeding vessel

Pelvic packing (usually done prior to embolization) and hysterectomy are other surgical methods employed to control PPH.
questions.learning: Uterine artery - Ovarian artery - Internal iliac artery The order of ligation of vessels to arrest bleeding in atonic postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is the uterine artery - ovarian artery - internal iliac artery.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 45-year-old multiparous woman presents with a vaginal bulge that protrudes beyond the introitus, urinary leakage while coughing, and is able to void urine normally. She undergoes anterior colporrhaphy with mesh repair (colpopexy). Which condition is this surgery primarily performed to correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cystocele

A cystocele is the herniation of the urinary bladder through the weakened anterior vaginal wall due to defects in the pubocervical fascia. It commonly occurs in multiparous women as a result of pelvic floor weakness and presents with:

• Vaginal bulge or mass
• Stress urinary incontinence
• Pelvic pressure or heaviness
• Urinary frequency or incomplete bladder emptying

Anterior colporrhaphy is the standard surgical repair for cystocele. Mesh augmentation (colpopexy) may be used in selected patients with recurrent or severe pelvic organ prolapse to reinforce the anterior vaginal wall.

Why not the other options?

• A. Rectocele: Herniation of the rectum through the posterior vaginal wall, presenting with constipation, difficult defecation, or the need for digital pressure during defecation; treated with posterior colporrhaphy.
• C. Enterocele: Herniation of the pouch of Douglas containing small bowel through the vaginal apex, usually following hysterectomy.
• D. Vesicovaginal fistula: Presents with continuous leakage of urine through the vagina, not a vaginal bulge, and requires fistula repair.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The given graph shows the effect of PTH on blood calcium and phosphate levels in an experimental animal. How does PTH increase plasma calcium levels?
options: By decreasing renal excretion of calcium
By increasing osteoclastic activity and decreasing renal excretion of calcium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. By increasing osteoclastic activity and decreasing renal excretion of calcium

The parathyroid hormone increases the plasma calcium levels by increasing osteoclastic activity and decreasing renal excretion of calcium.

By regulating intestinal reabsorption, renal excretion, and the exchange of these ions between the extracellular fluid and bone, PTH offers a potent mechanism for controlling the concentrations of calcium and phosphate in extracellular fluid.

The parathormone (PTH) increases Ca+2 concentration by:

• Increased reabsorption of Ca+2 by renal tubules, decreasing the urinary Ca+2 excretion
• Increasing bone resorption, leading to Ca+2 release into the ECF
• Decreased phosphate reabsorption by the renal tubules, increasing the urinary excretion of phosphate
• Conversion of 25-hydroxycholecalciferol to 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol which increases intestinal Ca2+ absorption

Activation of the osteoclasts occurs due to activated osteoblasts and osteocytes that send secondary signals to the osteoclasts. Preosteoclast cells become mature osteoclasts when their receptors are activated by RANKL, a significant secondary signal. Activation of the osteoclastic system occurs in two stages: (1) immediate activation of the osteoclasts that are already formed and (2) formation of new osteoclasts.

PTH administration decreases proximal tubular reabsorption of phosphate ions, which results in a rapid loss of phosphate in the urine. At the same time that PTH reduces phosphate reabsorption, it also increases calcium reabsorption through renal tubules. This ultimately leads to a decrease in the renal excretion of calcium.

Furthermore, it increases the reabsorption of hydrogen and magnesium ions while decreasing the reabsorption of ions from amino acids, potassium, and sodium in a manner similar to how it affects phosphate. Distal tubules and the thick ascending loop of the Henle are the primary sites of the increased calcium reabsorption.
questions.learning: By increasing osteoclastic activity and decreasing renal excretion of calcium The parathyroid hormone increases the plasma calcium levels by increasing osteoclastic activity and decreasing renal excretion of calcium.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of Apixaban?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Factor Xa inhibitor

Apixaban, a novel oral anticoagulant (NOAC) is a factor Xa inhibitor that is used in the treatment of VTE (Venous Thrombo Embolism)/DVT and in its prophylaxis after major orthopedic surgery.

Direct factor Xa inhibitors:

* Rivaroxaban

* Apixaban

* Edoxaban

* Betrixaban

Parenteral direct thrombin inhibitors:

* Bivalirudin

* Argatroban

* Desirud

Oral direct thrombin inhibitor—Dabigatran is the only oral direct thrombin inhibitor available for clinical use.

The FDA recently approved the drug Apixaban for a new indication. The drug is now used to reduce the risk of stroke and systemic embolism in patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation.

Pearl PF0414: Classification of Anticoagulants

Classification of Anticoagulants

1) Vitamin K antagonist

Warfarin

2) Direct thrombin inhibitors (DTI)
Oral DTI

Dabigatran

Parenteral DTI

Monovalent DTI- Argatroban

Bivalent DTI- Lepirudin, Desirudin, Bivalirudin

3) Indirect thrombin inhibitors
Unfractionated heparin

Low molecular weight heparins

Enoxaparin, Dalteparin, Tinzaparin

Fondaparinux

4) Direct Oral Factor Xa Inhibitors
Rivaroxaban, Apixaban, Edoxaban, Betrixaban
questions.learning: Factor Xa inhibitor Apixaban, a novel oral anticoagulant (NOAC) is a factor Xa inhibitor that is used in the treatment of VTE (Venous Thrombo Embolism)/DVT and in its prophylaxis after major orthopedic surgery.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 40-year-old diabetic patient presented with the squint. On examination, the secondary deviation was found to be more than the primary deviation. Forced duction test is negative. Which of the following types of squint is most likely to be present in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Paralytic squint

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of paralytic squint. It is characterized by the presence of secondary deviation more than the primary deviation and a negative forced duction test.

The squint may be either comitant or incomitant.

• Comitant squint: The angle of squint measured is same in all gazes.
• Incomitant squint: The angle of squint measured is different in different gazes.

The differences between comitant and incomitant squint are shown in the table below:

Features
Comitant squint
Incomitant squint

Magnitude of squint
Same in all gazes
Varies with the gaze

Diplopia
Absent
Present

Ocular movements
Full
Restricted

False projection
Absent
Present

Abnormal head posture
Absent
Present

Secondary deviation
Equal to primary deviation
More than primary deviation

The incomitant squint is further divided into two main types: Paralytic and restrictive.

Paralytic squint occurs due to the paralysis of extraocular muscle while restrictive squint is due to the mechanical restriction caused by tight or fibrosed muscle.

Forced duction test(FDT) differentiates between these two types. In this test, the eye is moved mechanically with the help of a forceps.

• The test is negative if there is no resistance to the movement. It is seen in a paralytic squint.
• The test is positive if there is resistance to the movement. It is seen in a restrictive squint.
questions.learning: Paralytic squint — The above clinical scenario is suggestive of paralytic squint. It is characterized by the presence of secondary deviation more than the primary deviation and a negative forced duction test.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the investigation shown in the image:
questions.explanation: The image presents the two standard views used in breast cancer screening: the Mediolateral Oblique (MLO) view and the Craniocaudal (CC) view. This characterizes mammography, a diagnostic tool that uses low-dose X-rays and breast compression to achieve high-resolution images of breast tissue. The MLO view is critical as it captures the upper outer quadrant and the pectoralis muscle. While mammography is technically a form of X-ray (Option C), "Mammography" is the specific clinical term for this specialized breast imaging study. CT scans (Option B) and MRIs (Option D) use entirely different cross-sectional technologies and do not present the breast in these specific compressed CC/MLO views. Therefore, the architectural detail and standard positioning confirm that the investigation is a mammogram

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following methods cannot be used to precipitate proteins?
options: Moving pH away from isoelectric pH
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Moving pH away from isoelectric pH

Precipitation of proteins is maximum at isoelectric pH and decreases as pH moves away from it. Hence, moving pH away from isoelectric pH cannot be used for precipitating proteins.

The isoelectric point or isoelectric pH (pI) is the pH at which the molecule carries no net charge.

Significance of Iso-electric pH (pI):

• The number of anions and cations present on the protein molecule will be equal and the net charge is zero.
• The proteins will not migrate in an electrical field
• Buffering capacity is minimum (note: maximum buffering action of an amino acid is seen when pH=pKa, and not at isoelectric pH)
• Viscosity will be minimum
• Precipitability will be maximum and solubility is minimum

Various precipitation reactions of proteins are:

1. Salting out: higher the molecular weight of protein, the lesser the salt required. Globulins would require only half-saturated salt whereas albumin would need full saturation.
2. Isoelectric precipitation: proteins are least soluble at their isoelectric pH and get precipitated immediately.
3. Precipitation by organic solvents like alcohol and acetone.
4. Precipitation by heavy metal ions: positively charged metal ions precipitate the negatively charged proteins in an alkaline medium. Salts of heavy metals can precipitate normal proteins of the GI tract in poisoning.
5. Precipitation by alkaloidal reagents like tungstic acid, trichloroacetic acid, and picric acid.
6. Heat coagulation is an irreversible precipitation process.
questions.learning: Moving pH away from isoelectric pH Precipitation of proteins is maximum at isoelectric pH and decreases as pH moves away from it. Hence, moving pH away from isoelectric pH cannot be used for precipitating proteins.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 60-year-old male recovering from facial nerve palsy complains of food getting stuck between the cheek and teeth while eating. What is the muscle affected in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Buccinator

This patient, recovering from facial nerve palsy, getting food stuck between the cheek and teeth while eating, is because of the buccinator being affected.

The buccinator is a muscle of facial expression. It is innervated by the facial nerve. It is known as the whistling muscle.

The buccinator muscle is primarily responsible for keeping food between the teeth during mastication by pressing the cheek against the teeth (involved in flattening the cheeks against the gums and teeth).

In facial nerve palsy, paralysis of the buccinator muscle can lead to food accumulating in the cheek pouch, as the muscle is unable to contract properly.

Other options:

Option B: Levator Labii Superioris: This muscle elevates the upper lip and contributes to facial expressions like showing the upper teeth and dilates the nostrils. It is not involved in keeping food in place during chewing.

Option C : Zygomaticus Major: Responsible for pulling the corner of the mouth upward and outward, contributing to smiling. It does not influence food placement during mastication.

Option D : Orbicularis Oris: Encircles the mouth and helps in closing the lips. While it is involved in mastication and speech, its paralysis would not cause food to accumulate in the cheek.
questions.learning: Buccinator — This patient, recovering from facial nerve palsy, getting food stuck between the cheek and teeth while eating, is because of the buccinator being affected.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old lady, G3P2 with 10 weeks intrauterine gestation comes to OPD with an Intra Uterine Contraceptive Device(IUCD) and the tail of the IUCD is noted to be protruding from the cervical os. The most appropriate course of action is?
options: Keep the IUCD in place and continue prophylactic antibiotics
Keep the IUCD in place without any treatment
Remove the IUCD immediately and continue pregnancy
Terminate the pregnancy because of high risk of infection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Remove the IUCD immediately and continue pregnancy

The most appropriate course of action in this patient at 10 weeks intrauterine gestation is to Remove the IUCD immediately and continue pregnancy.

Intrauterine Devices in Pregnancy

• If IUD strings are visible and  the pregnancy is less than 13 weeks, the IUD should be removed as soon as possible to prevent later septic abortion, premature rupture of the membranes, and premature birth .
• When the strings of the IUD are not visible, an ultrasound examination should be performed to localize the IUD and determine whether expulsion has occurred. If the IUD is present, there are three options for management:

• Therapeutic abortion .
• Ultrasound-guided intrauterine removal of the IUD.
• Continuation of the pregnancy with the device left in place

Note :

If the patient wishes to continue the pregnancy, ultrasound evaluation of the location of the IUD should be considered .

• If the IUD is not in a fundal location, ultrasound-guided removal using small alligator forceps may be successful.
• If the location is fundal, the IUD should be left in place. When pregnancy continues with an IUD in place, the patient must be warned of the symptoms of intrauterine infection and should be cautioned to seek care promptly for fever or flulike symptoms, abdominal cramping, or bleeding. At the earliest sign of infection, high-dose intravenous antibiotic therapy should be given and the pregnancy evacuated promptly.
questions.learning: Remove the IUCD immediately and continue pregnancy — The most appropriate course of action in this patient at 10 weeks intrauterine gestation is to Remove the IUCD immediately and continue pregnancy.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the order of insertion of muscles on Annulus of Zinn? 1. Medial rectus 2. Inferior rectus 3. Lateral rectus 4. Superior rectus
questions.explanation: The Annulus of Zinn (or common tendinous ring) is a circular fibrous structure at the apex of the orbit that serves as the origin for the four rectus muscles. In standard anatomical descriptions and medical board questions, the order of insertion around the ring is often listed as: 1. Medial Rectus (A) 2. Inferior Rectus (B) 3. Lateral Rectus (C) 4. Superior Rectus (D) This follows a clockwise or counter-clockwise sequence around the optic foramen. This anatomical landmark is critical because it surrounds the optic nerve and the ophthalmic artery. Additionally, several cranial nerves (III, VI, and the nasociliary branch of V) pass through the ring to enter the orbit. Options B, C, and D provide incorrect sequences of these muscles. Understanding the relationships at the orbital apex is essential for diagnosing orbital apex syndrome and planning complex orbital surgeries. The annulus acts as a structural anchor, ensuring the coordinated movement of the eye by the extraocular muscles
questions.learning: The Annulus of Zinn (or common tendinous ring) is a circular fibrous structure at the apex of the orbit that serves as the origin for the four rectus muscles.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Based on the stool examination findings, what is the most likely cause of lower abdominal pain and diarrhea in a 6-year-old boy?
questions.explanation: The stool examination reveals a trophozoite containing an ingested red blood cell (erythrophagocytosis). This is the definitive diagnostic feature that distinguishes the pathogenic Entamoeba histolytica from the non-pathogenic Entamoeba dispar. E. histolytica causes amoebic dysentery, characterized by abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. Giardia lamblia (Option A) trophozoites have a characteristic "owl’s eye" appearance with flagella and cause watery, fatty stools, not dysentery. Shigella (Option B) and Campylobacter (Option D) are bacteria; while they cause bloody diarrhea, they would not appear as large amoebic trophozoites on a wet mount. The trophozoite of E. histolytica also shows a characteristic cartwheel-like nucleus. Ingested RBCs are pathognomonic for active, invasive amoebiasis. Treatment requires a nitroimidazole like metronidazole followed by a luminal amoebicide. Therefore, based on the microscopic evidence of erythrophagocytosis, Entamoeba histolytica is the most probable cause
questions.learning: The stool examination reveals a trophozoite containing an ingested red blood cell (erythrophagocytosis). This is the definitive diagnostic feature that distinguishes the pathogenic Entamoeba histolytica from the non-pathogenic Entamoeba dispar.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An 8-year-old child has difficulty walking and getting up from a squatting position. A muscle biopsy was done and is as shown in the image. Which of the following is true about this condition?
options: It is a mitochondrial storage disorder
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Death occurs in 3rd decade

The clinical scenario and the muscle biopsy showing fatty replacement of muscle fibers are suggestive of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). Death in DMD occurs in the late teens and 20s (3rd decade).

DMD is the most common hereditary neuromuscular disease. It is inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern. It is caused by a mutation in the dystrophin gene on chromosome Xp21.

Normally, the dystrophin gene codes for the large protein dystrophin. Dystrophin protein forms a rod that connects the actin filaments to the transmembrane protein dystroglycan in the muscle cell membrane. This dystrophin-glycoprotein complex thereby provides strength to the muscle and connects them to the extracellular environment.

The image given below shows the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex.

Clinical features of DMD:

• Progressive weakness, developmental delay, and intellectual impairment
• In toddlers- delayed walking, falling, toe walking, and trouble running or walking upstairs
• Calf muscular pseudohypertrophy

The image given below shows pseudohypertrophy of the calf muscles.

• Gower's sign: Patient has to use their hands and arms to walk up their own body from squatting position due to the lack of hip and thigh muscle strength due to the weakness of proximal muscles, especially of the lower limbs.

• Trendelenburg gait/hip waddle
• The patient is unable to walk by the age of 12 years and death occurs by late 20 years of age, mostly due to respiratory failure during sleep.

The complications of DMD include contractures, scoliosis, dilated cardiomyopathy, and malignant hyperthermia after anesthesia.

Diagnosis of DMD:

• Elevated serum creatine kinase levels
• Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analysis for the dystrophin gene
• If PCR is normal, but clinical suspicion is high, muscle biopsy (fatty replacement of muscle fibers) with dystrophin immunocytochemistry (absence of the normal sarcolemmal staining) is done.

Treatment of DMD includes glucocorticoids (prednisone or deflazacort), and multidisciplinary management. Eteplirsen and casimersen are the two new FDA-approved drugs for the treatment of DMD.

Note- The FDA has approved Vamorolone, a novel corticosteroid for the treatment of DMD. The drug offers enhanced anti-inflammatory properties and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism as well. It is potentially a safer and more effective alternative to glucocorticoids.
questions.learning: Death occurs in 3rd decade — The clinical scenario and the muscle biopsy showing fatty replacement of muscle fibers are suggestive of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A male patient who was diagnosed with tuberculosis has successfully completed the full course of treatment. Subsequent to finishing both the intensive and continuation phases, the initial sputum examination was conducted. The results of this examination were negative. What is the current condition of the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cured

Under the National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP), treatment outcomes are defined based on:

• Completion of therapy
• Sputum examination results

A patient is classified as “cured” when they have completed the full course of anti-tubercular treatment and have documented bacteriological negativity at the end of treatment.

| Outcome | Definition

| ------- | ----------

| Cured | Bacteriologically confirmed TB + completed treatment + negative sputum

| Treatment completed | Completed treatment but no sputum result available

| Treatment failed | Sputum positive at end of treatment

| Lost to follow-up | Treatment interrupted ≥ 1 month

In this case, the patient completed both the intensive and continuation phases, and the post-treatment sputum examination is negative, fulfilling the criteria for cure.

“Treatment completed” is used only when bacteriological confirmation is unavailable at the end of therapy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 51-year-old lady presents with complaints of a mass in the right breast. On examination, the mass was larger than 2cm and ipsilateral mobile axillary lymph nodes were present. What is the staging, considering the mass is malignant?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. cT4N1M0

The clinical scenario of a 51-year-old lady with a breast mass >2cm, lymph node involvement (N1), and the image showing an ulcerative mass near the nipple of the right breast (T4), is clinically suggestive of inflammatory breast carcinoma. Its likely staging is cT4N1M0

Inflammatory breast carcinoma (stage T4) is an aggressive form of locally advanced breast cancer (LABC) and is associated with the worst prognosis among all subtypes of breast cancer. It accounts for <3% of breast cancers. It is characterized by skin changes of brawny induration, erythema, and edema (peau d’orange). The term peau d’orange describes the orange-peel appearance of the skin resulting from edema and dimpling at sites of hair follicles.

In order to determine the best course of treatment for a patient with IBC, it is important to stage cancer. Staging is the process of determining the extent to which cancer has spread within the breast and to other parts of the body. Some prefixes and suffixes are used with the cTNM (clinical) and pTNM (pathologic) staging systems to designate special cases. These do not affect the stage group but indicate that they must be analyzed separately. The “y” prefix, denotes patients who have received systemic therapy before surgery. In this patient, since the staging is being done clinically, "c" is added as a prefix.

The diagnostic criteria for inflammatory breast cancer are -

*

Rapid onset of breast erythema, edema and/or peau d’orange, and/or warm breast (with or without an underlying palpable mass)

*

Duration of history no more than six months

*

Erythema occupies at least one-third of the breast

*

Pathologic confirmation of invasive carcinoma

The pathologic hallmark is the presence of tumor cells within dermal lymphatics in skin biopsy specimens, but it is not a prerequisite for diagnosis. Mammography may be normal or show skin thickening. A PET-CT scan should be considered at the time of diagnosis to rule out concurrent metastatic disease.

Axillary nodal metastases are common, and there is a significant risk for distant metastases.

Combined-modality treatment is used, which includes

* Neoadjuvant chemotherapy

* Modified radical mastectomy

* Radiation therapy

* Hormonal therapy (for ER-positive tumors)

* Trastuzumab (for HER-2-positive tumors)

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The mother of a newborn in your unit is extremely sick and is unable to feed her baby. The relatives have arranged a breast milk donor and wish to feed the baby using the device shown in the image. This method of primary feeding can be recommended in newborns with a gestational age of _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 32-34 weeks

The given image shows paladai. It can be used as a primary feeding method during routine feeding in neonates born at gestational age 32-34 weeks only. Sick mothers or mothers with contraindications to breastfeeding can feed their child using paladai. The milk can either be expressed breastmilk or they can resort to using undiluted cow milk or formula feeds.

Newborns with a gestational age of <32 weeks will not have the coordination between swallowing and breathing. So, paladai can only be used occasionally.

Newborns with a gestational age >34 weeks will have a completely mature sucking pattern when breastfeeding becomes more preferred.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly man underwent Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery for obesity. He now presents to his physician with complaints of dizziness, fatigue, and tremors 2 hours after the ingestion of a carbohydrate-rich meal. His symptoms occur mainly due to * Hypoglycemia * Small volume of food intake * High osmotic load of food * Increased release of insulin * Increased release of glucagon
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 and 4

The patient is presenting with features of late dumping syndrome following Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery. This occurs due to an increased release of insulin and hypoglycemia.

Dumping syndrome occurs due to rapid gastric emptying. It is commonly seen following gastric surgeries. It can be divided into

* Early dumping syndrome is a condition that develops after consuming foods high in osmotic load. Fluid is sequestered from the circulation into the gastrointestinal tract as a result of the increased osmotic load in the intestine. Patients will develop hypovolemia and hypotension.

* Late dumping syndrome develops after ingestion of a large volume of meals and meals which are rich in carbohydrates. Blood sugar levels rise quickly as a result of the intestines absorbing a lot of glucose. This ultimately leads to an increase in insulin release, which results in hypoglycemia.

The mainstay in the management of dumping syndrome is dietary manipulation. The patient is advised to have small volume, regular meals that are rich in protein, fat, and low in carbohydrates. Somatostatin analogue like octreotide is used in the management of intractable syndromes.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 27-year-old pregnant woman in her first trimester presents for a routine antenatal checkup. In her case, ABO incompatibility does not occur due to the presence of which antibody?
questions.explanation: In most pregnancies where the mother is Type O and the fetus is Type A or B, ABO incompatibility can occur because the mother produces anti-A and anti-B antibodies of the IgG class (Option B), which can cross the placenta. However, in mothers with other blood types (like Type A or B), the anti-A or anti-B antibodies they produce are predominantly of the IgM class. IgM antibodies are large pentamers that CANNOT cross the placenta. Therefore, ABO incompatibility does not occur (or is extremely rare) in these cases because the maternal IgM antibodies are physically blocked from reaching the fetal circulation. IgA (Option A) and IgD (Option C) are not involved in these hemolytic interactions. This biological barrier is why ABO incompatibility is much less common and generally much milder than Rh incompatibility, where the IgG anti-D antibodies easily cross the placenta and cause severe hemolysis. Understanding antibody transport across the placental membrane is a fundamental concept in neonatal hematology and fetal medicine
questions.learning: In most pregnancies where the mother is Type O and the fetus is Type A or B, ABO incompatibility can occur because the mother produces anti-A and anti-B antibodies of the IgG class (Option B), which can cross the placenta.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of these conditions will cause a large ‘a’ wave and P WAVE in JVP and ECG respectively?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tricuspid stenosis

The ‘a’ wave in JVP corresponds to right atrial contraction against the tricuspid valve.

In tricuspid stenosis, right atrial contraction faces increased resistance, producing a prominent ‘a’ wave. It occurs just before ventricular systole.

Sequence: ECG: P wave → Atrial contraction → JVP ‘a’ wave

Mitral valve lesions affect left-sided pressures and do not enlarge the JVP ‘a’ wave.

Aortic valve lesions primarily alter arterial pulse, not JVP waveform.

Clinical Causes of Giant ‘a’ Wave-

| Condition | Mechanism

| --------- | ---------

| Tricuspid stenosis | RA contracts against stenotic valve

| Pulmonary hypertension | RV pressure overload

| Pulmonary stenosis | Increased resistance

| Right ventricular hypertrophy | Reduced RV compliance
questions.learning: Tricuspid stenosis — The ‘a’ wave in JVP corresponds to right atrial contraction against the tricuspid valve. In tricuspid stenosis, right atrial contraction faces increased resistance, producing a prominent ‘a’ wave.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 65-year-old male presented with history of dysphagia, halitosis and aspiration pneumonia. A barium swallow was done and is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Zenker’s diverticulum

The given image shows the collection of contrast in a pouch-like structure, which favours the diagnosis of Zenker's diverticulum.

Zenker’s diverticulum is a pulsion-type pseudodiverticulum. It occurs due to the protrusion of mucosa and submucosa through Killian’s triangle. Killian’s triangle represents a weak muscular space located between two parts of the inferior constrictor muscle - the oblique fibres of the thyropharyngeus and the transverse fibres of the cricopharyngeus. This phenomenon may lead to the creation of a sac with a narrow neck that can trap liquid and food. The distended sac may compress the cervical oesophagus.

Clinical presentation:

The entrapment of liquid and/or food within the diverticulum may result in:

* Globus sensation

* Dysphagia

* Halitosis

* Regurgitation

* Aspiration pneumonia

Diagnosis is by Barium swallow studies and video laryngoscopy.

Pearl PF1662: Zenker’s Diverticulum

Zenker's diverticulum occurs due to herniation of mucosa and submucosa through the Killian's triangle, which is a weak area between two parts of the inferior constrictor - (thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus) in the posterior pharyngeal wall. It is usually seen in elderly patients (>60 years).

Characteristics of Zenker's diverticulum:

* Hypopharyngeal

* False diverticula - doesn't have a muscle coat

* Acquired

* Pulsion diverticulum

Pathophysiology: Impaired relaxation and spasm of the cricopharyngeus muscle after swallowing can result in increased pressure within the distal pharynx, and cause the diverticulum.Clinical features:

* Dysphagia

* Regurgitation

* Halitosis

* Aspiration

* Gurgling sound during swallowing

The investigation of choice is barium swallow (lateral X-ray).

It is treated with:

* Cricopharyngeal myotomy

* Surgical diverticulectomy

* Marsupialization

* Dohlman’s procedure
questions.learning: Zenker’s diverticulum — The given image shows the collection of contrast in a pouch-like structure, which favours the diagnosis of Zenker's diverticulum.

questions.text: Which of the following cardiac biomarkers is the earliest to rise after acute myocardial infarction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Myoglobin

Myoglobin is the earliest to rise in acute MI followed by CK-MB, troponin and then LDH.

Serum myoglobin and heart-type fatty acid-binding protein are smaller molecules that diffuse through interstitial ﬂuids more rapidly after cell death than do the larger CK and troponin molecules. They become abnormal as early as 30 minutes after myocardial injury. Neither molecule is specific to myocardial tissue

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is not a component of Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. ASD, left ventricular hypertrophy

Tetralogy of Fallot is a cyanotic congenital heart disease characterized by four structural abnormalities resulting in right-to-left shunting. Right ventricular outflow obstruction leads to right-to-left shunt and cyanosis

Severity of pulmonary stenosis determines clinical presentation

Components (remember: PROV):

• Pulmonary stenosis
• Right ventricular hypertrophy
• Overriding aorta
• Ventricular septal defect (VSD)

• ASD is not a component of TOF

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with abnormal vaginal bleeding and is diagnosed with stage IB carcinoma of the cervix. What type of hysterectomy is most commonly recommended for managing this condition?
questions.explanation: For stage IB carcinoma of the cervix, a Type 3 radical hysterectomy (Meigs' or Wertheim’s procedure) is the standard surgical management. This procedure involves the comprehensive removal of the uterus, cervix, upper vagina, and the entire parametria (parametrium and paracolpium) to ensure negative margins. In contrast, Type 1 hysterectomy (Option A) is a simple extrafascial hysterectomy indicated only for very early stage IA1 disease without lymphovascular space invasion. Type 2 hysterectomy (Option C), or modified radical hysterectomy, involves removing only the medial half of the parametria and is usually reserved for stage IA2 disease. Type 4 radical hysterectomy (Option D) is an extended procedure involving the removal of periureteral tissue and superior vesical arteries, typically utilized for more advanced or recurrent cases. Therefore, for a stage IB patient where the tumor is confined to the cervix but clinically visible, Type 3 radical hysterectomy provides the necessary oncological clearance

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old patient presents with abdominal pain and fever for 3 days duration. The chest X-ray in the erect position is given below. What will be the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hollow viscus perforation

The given clinical scenario of acute abdominal pain and fever with chest X-ray in an erect position showing air under the diaphragm (pneumoperitoneum) is a characteristic of hollow viscus perforation.

The most common cause of pneumoperitoneum is bowel perforation (>90% of the cases). Gastric and posterior duodenal perforations are seen in long-standing cases of peptic ulcers. Intestinal perforations are seen with ischemia, inflammation, diverticula, or obstruction (E.g:- colonic carcinoma). Other causes also include iatrogenic, penetrating injuries, prolonged mechanical ventilation, peritoneal dialysis, etc.

Perforation of a viscus is a life-threatening condition due to leakage of the enteric contents which can lead to acute bacterial peritonitis.

Clinical features of hollow viscous perforation are due to the developed peritonitis. They include abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. On examination, the patient has tachycardia, tenderness, rebound tenderness, decreased or absent bowel sounds, and guarding on palpation. Fever may be present.

The patient is initially investigated with an upright chest X-ray which typically shows air beneath the diaphragm. Various other signs for pneumoperitoneum in the supine abdominal X-rays are Rigler’s sign, Cupola sign, falciform ligament sign, football sign, and Doge’s cap sign. However, CECT is the most sensitive investigation to detect minimal/ suspected pneumoperitoneum along with the cause and site of perforation.

Other options:

Option A: Gastric volvulus is a twisting or axial rotation of the stomach along its longitudinal axis (organo-axial) or vertical axis (mesentero-axial). The sudden onset of constant and severe upper abdominal pain, recurrent retching with the production of little vomitus, and the inability to pass an NG tube constitute the Borchardt triad. Plain films of the abdomen reveal a gas-filled viscus in the chest or upper abdomen.

Option C: Liver abscess will mostly have the classic presenting symptoms of fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain, with a tenderness to palpation. Chest X-ray findings generally reflect subdiaphragmatic diseases, such as an elevated right hemidiaphragm, right pleural effusion, or atelectasis.

A chest radiograph shows an air-fluid level in the right upper abdomen (arrow) and multiple nodular opacities in the bilateral lungs (arrowheads)

Option D: Empyema thoracis is an infection of the pleural space. An empyema thoracis on a chest X-ray can mimic a pleural effusion or a lung abscess.The fluid is commonly drained completely with a chest tube or small-bore catheter.

The chest radiograph showing pleural empyema.
questions.learning: Hollow viscus perforation — The given clinical scenario of acute abdominal pain and fever with chest X-ray in an erect position showing air under the diaphragm (pneumoperitoneum) is a characteristic of hollow viscus perforation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A 55-year-old patient presents with shortness of breath. Arterial blood gas analysis reveals the following- pH: 7.22, PaCO₂: 66 mmHg PaO₂: 45 mmHg HCO₃⁻: 26 mEq/L. What is the most likely acid-base disorder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Respiratory acidosis

Low pH (7.22) with markedly elevated PaCO₂ (66 mmHg) indicates a primary respiratory acidosis.

Near-normal bicarbonate (26 mEq/L) suggests minimal or no metabolic compensation, consistent with an acute process.

Acidemia (↓ pH)

+

↑ PaCO₂ (primary abnormality)

+

Normal HCO₃⁻ (no compensation)

Severe hypoxemia further supports hypoventilation as the underlying cause.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 37-year-old woman from Bihar presents with fever and unexplained weight loss over the past 6 months. Examination reveals massive splenomegaly and blood investigations show anemia, thrombocytopenia, and hypergammaglobulinemia. What is the vector of the organism causing this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phlebotomus species

From the given clinical features, the most likely disease is visceral leishmaniasis or Kala azar caused by Leishmania donovani, and the vector is a female Phlebotomus sandfly. A patient from Bihar presenting with fever, weight loss, and hepatosplenomegaly with a smear examination showing anemia, thrombocytopenia, and hypergammaglobulinemia point towards the diagnosis.

Leishmaniasis is transmitted by the bite of an infected female Phlebotomus sandfly. In India, it is endemic to Bihar, West Bengal, Jharkhand, and Uttar Pradesh. Patients present with high fever, hepatosplenomegaly, weight loss, and emaciation. The skin becomes dry, rough, and darkly pigmented. There is anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia.

The parasite exists in 2 forms:

• Amstigote form (also called LD bodies)- It is seen within macrophages and contains a kinetoplast.
• Promastigote form- It is the infective form in the sandfly. The kinetoplast is seen at the anterior end.

Kinetoplast are non-nuclear DNA present in addition to nucleus. They consist of blepharoplast and parabasal body. Flagellum originates near the kinetoplast.

Diagnosis of kala-azar is mainly by demonstration of amastigotes within macrophages in tissue aspirates such as blood smears, bone marrow, splenic, or lymph node aspirate. It is the gold standard for diagnosis.

The image below shows amastigotes located intracellularly within macrophages.

Treatment is with a pentavalent antimonial compound. In Bihar, there is resistance to antimony so amphotericin-B-deoxycholate or miltefosine is preferred.

In human beings, different species of Leishmania can cause the following diseases:

• Visceral leishmaniasis, or kala-azar,
• Cutaneous leishmaniasis,
• Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis, and
• Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis.

The life cycle of Lesihmania is shown below.

Other options:

Option B: The Aedes mosquito is the vector for diseases such as dengue, chikungunya, and Zika virus, none of which fit the clinical profile of visceral leishmaniasis.

Option C: Mites are vectors for diseases such as scrub typhus, which typically presents with fever and an eschar, but it does not explain the massive splenomegaly or hematologic findings seen in this case.

Option D: Ixodid ticks are vectors for tick-borne diseases such as Lyme disease and babesiosis. These conditions do not present with the clinical features observed in this patient.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: On examination, a patient is found to have a lesion affecting Wernicke’s area of the brain. Which condition is most likely associated with this defect?
options: He can make the decision what he speaks
He is able to understand words and speak properly
He is understanding language but unable to speak
questions.explanation: Wernicke's area, located in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus, is critical for language comprehension. Damage to this area results in Wernicke’s (fluent) aphasia, characteristically described as senseless, continuous speaking (often called "word salad"). While the patient is fluent and can speak with normal rate and rhythm, the content is nonsensical, and they lack awareness of their deficit. Option D describes Broca's (non-fluent) aphasia, where language is understood but speaking is difficult. Option C describes normal language function. Option A is incorrect as comprehension and decision-making about language content are impaired. In Wernicke's aphasia, the patient cannot understand spoken or written language. This condition most commonly occurs after a stroke involving the posterior division of the middle cerebral artery. Management involves intensive speech therapy, though the prognosis for comprehension recovery is often guarded. Recognizing the "fluent but meaningless" pattern is the key to localizing the lesion during a neurological exam

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Beta blockers should be avoided in all except__
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glaucoma

Beta-blockers should be avoided in all except glaucoma. They are contraindicated in all other conditions.

In glaucoma, the mechanism involves reduced production of aqueous humor by the ciliary body, which is physiologically activated by cAMP and decreases the intraocular pressure. Timolol and related β antagonists are suitable for local use in the eye because they lack local anesthetic properties.

Other options:

In asthma, blockade of the β2 receptors in bronchial smooth muscle may lead to an increase in airway resistance and precipitate it. Beta1-receptor antagonists such as metoprolol and atenolol may have some advantage over nonselective β antagonists when the blockade of β1 receptors in the heart is desired and β2-receptor blockade is undesirable.

In bradycardia blockade of β1 receptors in the heart can further decrease the heart rate and can lead to fatal cardiac arrest.

In hypothyroidism, blockade of adrenoceptors and inhibition of the peripheral conversion of thyroxine to triiodothyronine increases the severity of hypothyroidism.
questions.learning: Glaucoma Beta-blockers should be avoided in all except glaucoma. They are contraindicated in all other conditions.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The resting membrane potential(RMP) of the nerve is -70mV. Increased permeability of which ion is responsible for the RMP?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Potassium

Increased permeability of potassium ions(K+) is responsible for the RMP of a nerve as there are more K+ channels open at rest, facilitating the flow of potassium ions across the membrane.

Resting membrane potential (RMP) is the difference in the electrical potentials between the cytoplasm of the cell and the extracellular space.

At rest, there are more open K+ channels compared to Na+ channels, thus the membrane permeability of K+ is greater. As a result of this, the intracellular and extracellular K+ concentrations are the major determinants of the RMP. Furthermore, the RMP is close to the equilibrium potential of K+ in general.

Clinical Significance: In hyperkalemia, the extracellular level of K+ is increased. Thus the RMP moves closer to the threshold to elicit an action potential leading to a more excitable nerve. The excitable nerve, stimulates the muscle repeatedly causing fasciculations, exhaustion of muscle, and weakness. In hypokalemia, the extracellular level of K+ is reduced. Thus the RMP is reduced and the neuron is hyperpolarized.
questions.learning: Potassium Increased permeability of potassium ions(K+) is responsible for the RMP of a nerve as there are more K+ channels open at rest, facilitating the flow of potassium ions across the membrane.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old patient with peptic ulcer disease presents with abdominal pain that is not responding despite treatment in multiple hospitals. He was found to have ulcers in the jejunum and ileum. Gastric pH < 2, and gastrin levels after adequate cessation of PPIs are 10 times the normal value. Identify the lesion present and the boundaries of the triangle containing it.
options: Gastrinoma; triangle formed by common bile duct, junction of D2-D3, neck and body of pancreas
Insulinoma; triangle formed by cystic duct, junction of D2-D3, neck and body of pancreas
Gastrinoma; triangle formed by cystic duct, junction of D2-D3, neck and body of pancreas
Insulinoma; triangle formed by common bile duct, junction of D2-D3, neck and body of pancreas
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gastrinoma; triangle formed by cystic duct, junction of D2-D3, neck and body of pancreas

The above clinical scenario of abdominal pain, ulcers in the jejunum and ileum, gastric pH < 2, and elevated gastrin levels are suggestive of gastrinoma. It is commonly located in a triangle formed by the cystic duct, junction of D2-D3, neck and body of pancreas.

Gastrinoma is a neuroendocrinal tumour characterized by gastrin hypersecretion, resulting in gastrointestinal tract ulcers. It occurs more commonly in a sporadic pattern but can be associated with MEN-1 (multiple endocrine neoplasia-1) syndromes in the familial pattern.

Gastrinoma is most commonly located in the gastrinoma triangle (Passaro's triangle) bounded by the lines connecting the:

• cystic duct
• the junction between the second and third parts of the duodenum
• the junction between the neck and the body of the pancreas

The most common presentations of gastrinoma are epigastric pain, diarrhoea, and peptic ulcers. The ulcers occur at typical locations (proximal duodenum) and atypical locations (distal duodenum, jejunum). Duodenal ulcers are the most common. Gastrinoma if associated with marked gastric acid production and recurrent peptic ulcer is called Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

Diagnosis:

The gastric pH <2, basal acid output >15 mEq/hr and serum gastrin concentration more than 1000 pg/ml (normal is <100 pg/ml) confirm the diagnosis of gastrinoma. When the diagnosis is in doubt (like gastrin levels 100-1000 pg/ml), then a secretin test is performed. A secretin test is considered positive when serum gastrin levels are more than 200 pg/ml on secretin administration and confirms the diagnosis of gastrinoma.

For localization of the tumour for surgical management, CT or MRI scans should be done first. If the tumour is not localized on these scans, then somatostatin receptor scintigraphy or endoscopic ultrasound is done for better localization.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient sustained blunt trauma to the eye 6 months ago and now presents with double vision. What is the most likely condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Iriododialysis

The given image shows iridodialysis.

Iridodialysis refers to detachment of the iris root from the ciliary body and is associated with a D-shaped pupil. A black biconvex area is seen at the periphery at the site of detachment.

The given image depicts iridodialysis and a D-shaped pupil.

Other Options:

Option A: Cycloiriditis is inflammation involving both the ciliary body and iris, leading to pain, photophobia, and decreased vision. It's characterized by cells and flare in the anterior chamber, keratic precipitates, and possible synechiae formation.

Option B: Vossius ring is a circular ring of faint or stippled opacity, seen on the anterior surface of the lens due to brown amorphous granules of pigment lying on the capsule of the lens. It is usually seen after blunt trauma to the eye and orbit.

Option D: Coloboma is a congenital anomaly, that develops due to a defect in the closure of the embryonic cleft. It is characterized by poorly developed uveal tissue. These colobomas may involve the optic nerve, choroid, retina, and iris.
questions.learning: Iriododialysis — The given image shows iridodialysis. Iridodialysis refers to detachment of the iris root from the ciliary body and is associated with a D-shaped pupil.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with lacy white lesions involving the oral cavity and genital region, along with an abnormal forward extension of the proximal nail fold onto the nail bed. Based on these clinical features, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Lichen planus (LP) is a chronic inflammatory condition that affects the skin, mucous membranes, and nails. The "lacy lesions" in the mouth are known as Wickham striae, a hallmark of oral LP. Genital involvement is also common. The "extension of the proximal nail fold onto the nail bed" describes a "dorsal pterygium," which is a classic and highly characteristic nail finding in lichen planus caused by scarring of the nail matrix. Psoriasis (Option B) typically presents with nail pitting, oil spots, and onycholysis, not pterygium. Pityriasis rosea (Option C) presents with a herald patch and a "Christmas tree" distribution of lesions, usually sparing the nails and mouth. Pityriasis rubra pilaris (Option A) involves follicular papules and orange-red plaques. The skin lesions of LP are classically described as the "6 Ps": planar (flat-topped), purple, polygonal, pruritic, papules, and plaques. Diagnosis is usually clinical but can be confirmed by biopsy showing a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate
questions.learning: Lichen planus (LP) is a chronic inflammatory condition that affects the skin, mucous membranes, and nails. The "lacy lesions" in the mouth are known as Wickham striae, a hallmark of oral LP.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: All the following tests are related to pasteurization of milk except
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Iodine test

All the above tests are related to the pasteurization of milk except the iodine test. It is done to test if milk is adulterated with starch or cereal flour.

The iodine test is done by adding 2 drops of iodine solution containing potassium iodide and iodine to 1ml of milk. The appearance of a blue color indicates that the milk is adulterated with starch. A control sample of milk that is not adulterated with starch will develop a slightly yellowish color.

Pasteurization can be done by the following methods,

• Holder/Vat method: 63-66 °C for 30 minutes and then quickly cooled to 5°C.
• HTST method (High-temperature short time): 72°C for at least 15 seconds, and then cooled rapidly to 4°C.
• UHT method (Ultra-high temp): Rapidly heated to 125 °C for a few seconds, then cooled and bottled as quickly as possible.

Tests in pasteurization:

• Phosphatase test: It is based on the fact that raw milk contains phosphatase enzyme which gets destroyed at temperatures corresponding to the standard time and temperature required for pasteurization.
• Standard plate count: It is used to determine the bacteriological quality of pasteurized milk.
• Coliform count: The presence of coliform organisms in pasteurized milk indicates either improper pasteurization or post-pasteurization contamination.
• Methylene blue reduction test is an indirect method for the detection of microorganisms in milk. This test is carried out on the milk accepted for pasteurization. Definite quantities of methylene blue are added to 10 ml of milk at a uniform temperature of 37°C. The milk is considered satisfactory if it fails to reduce the methylene blue dye in 30 minutes under standard conditions.
questions.learning: Iodine test All the above tests are related to the pasteurization of milk except the iodine test. It is done to test if milk is adulterated with starch or cereal flour.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Discrete probability distribution that expresses probability of a given number of events in a particular time frame is known as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Poissons distribution

Poissons distribution is the probability distribution that describes the chances of an event in a particular time frame.

For example, if you plot the number of patients visiting the OPD of your hospital for a week on a chart, you can conclude that on a particular day(say Monday) there are more number of patients. And if the pattern of patients is similar you can estimate the number of patients in OPD next week or so.

It is usually done for rare events and is depends on μ = λt (where μ defines the number of events in happening in time t)

Other options
Gaussian distribution is another name for Normal distribution

Binomial distribution examples consist of those events which can only have two possible results given as yes or no / success or failure. It is usually done for finite number of events unlike Poissons distribution.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What specific action is performed by the muscle highlighted in the given image?
questions.explanation: The highlighted muscle in the image is the supraspinatus, which lies in the supraspinous fossa of the scapula, above the spine. It is one of the four rotator cuff muscles and plays a crucial role in shoulder movement and stability. Its primary function is to initiate abduction of the shoulder joint, specifically the first 0–15 degrees of arm elevation. After this initial phase, the deltoid muscle becomes the main abductor. The supraspinatus also helps stabilize the head of the humerus within the glenoid cavity during movement. Other options are incorrect because they involve different muscles. Retraction of the scapula is performed mainly by the trapezius (middle fibers) and rhomboid muscles. Protraction of the scapula is carried out by the serratus anterior. Adduction of the shoulder joint is mainly done by muscles like latissimus dorsi and pectoralis major. Thus, based on anatomical location and function, the muscle shown is responsible for initiating shoulder abduction
