questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman presents with obstructed labor and is grossly dehydrated. Investigations reveal fetal demise. What will be the management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cesarean section

The best management in the given clinical scenario is cesarean section.

Obstructive labor management involves administering intravenous fluids to correct dehydration, providing antibiotics to prevent infection, and promptly performing a cesarean section to relieve the obstruction. If the fetus is alive, an immediate cesarean section is typically performed. Management of obstructed labor never involves a wait-and-watch approach or augmenting with oxytocin.

Clinical features of obstructed labor include maternal exhaustion, dehydration, tachycardia, tachypnea, genital sepsis, postpartum hemorrhage, and shock.
On P/A examination the upper uterine segment is tender and tonically contracted. The lower uterine segment is thin and stretched. A groove/depression is felt between the upper uterine segment and the lower uterine segment. This is called a Bandls ring.

Complications of obstructed labor include rupture of the uterus and vesicovaginal fistula.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Flask shaped ulcers in the colon are caused by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Entamoeba Histolytica

Flask shaped ulcers are classically seen in amoebiasis caused by Entamoeba histolytica.

In amoebiasis, amoeba attach themselves to the colonic epithelium, induces apoptosis, invade crypts, and burrow laterally into the lamina propria. This recruits neutrophils and causes tissue damage, resulting in flask-shaped ulcers with a narrow neck and broad base.

Clinical manifestations:

• Amebic Colitis

• Colicky abdominal pains and frequent bowel movements.
• Diarrhea associated with tenesmus and heme-positive stool.
• Trophozoites invade the intestinal mucosa, produce flask-shaped ulcers.

• Amebic Liver Abscess

• Fever is the hallmark of amebic liver abscess
• It is associated with abdominal pain, abdominal distention, and enlargement and tenderness of the liver.
• Changes at the base of the right lung, such as elevation of the diaphragm and atelectasis or effusion, may also occur.
• The most common finding is a single abscess in the right hepatic lobe, detected on ultrasonography,computed tomography, or magnetic resonance imaging.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following are components of the trabecular meshwork? 1. Cribriform meshwork 2. Corneoscleral meshwork 3. Juxtacanalicular meshwork 4. Schlemm’s canal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

The trabecular meshwork is the principal conventional aqueous humor outflow pathway located at the iridocorneal angle. It consists of three anatomical layers that progressively increase outflow resistance, with the juxtacanalicular (cribriform) meshwork providing the greatest resistance. Schlemm’s canal lies external to the trabecular meshwork and drains aqueous humor into the episcleral veins.

•

The trabecular meshwork is composed of:

•

Cribriform (Uveal) meshwork ✓

• Corneoscleral meshwork ✓
• Juxtacanalicular meshwork ✓

4. Schlemm’s canal ✗ is not a component of the trabecular meshwork; it receives aqueous humor after it passes through the meshwork.

questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A researcher engineers a cell line lacking functional signal recognition particle (SRP). Which immediate consequence on protein localization would be expected for proteins normally destined for secretion?
options: Proteins would be correctly translocated into the RER lumen via an SRP-independent backup pathway
Proteins would accumulate in the cytosol due to failure of ribosome-RER targeting
Proteins would be retained in the Golgi due to failure of COPII vesicle formation
Proteins would be degraded by lysosomal enzymes due to failure of mannose-6-phosphate tagging
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Proteins would accumulate in the cytosol due to failure of ribosome-RER targeting

SRP traffics the polypeptide-ribosome complex from cytosol to RER. Absent or dysfunctional SRP → ribosome-mRNA-polypeptide complex never reaches RER → translation either continues in cytosol (for proteins lacking proper insertion) or the protein accumulates untranslocated, mislocalized in the cytosol rather than entering the secretory pathway.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents with swelling of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and is found to have elevated serum uric acid levels. The physician initiates first-line therapy for this condition. What is the mechanism of action of the drug prescribed?
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation of joint swelling combined with high serum uric acid levels is diagnostic of gout. While NSAIDs or colchicine are used for the acute flare, the "initial" and most common first-line treatment for the long-term management of hyperuricemia is Allopurinol. The mechanism of action of Allopurinol is that of a xanthine oxidase inhibitor (Option D). It works by blocking the enzyme responsible for converting hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid, thereby lowering the systemic levels of urate. A pyrimidine antimetabolite (Option A) refers to drugs like 5-fluorouracil used in chemotherapy. Colchicine acts as an inhibitor of neutrophil recruitment (Option B) and is used for acute attacks, not primary urate-lowering. Uricosuric drugs (Option C), such as probenecid, increase the renal excretion of uric acid but are generally second-line. Thus, xanthine oxidase inhibition is the definitive standard

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 44-year-old woman presents with a palpable flank mass measuring 4 cm on CT imaging, and urine examination reveals malignant cells. What is the most appropriate management for this condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a flank mass and malignant cells in the urine is strongly suggestive of a Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC). For small renal masses (typically defined as those less than 4 cm, or T1a tumors), "partial nephrectomy" (nephron-sparing surgery) is the preferred standard of care. This procedure removes the tumor while preserving as much healthy kidney tissue as possible, which helps maintain long-term renal function and reduces the risk of chronic kidney disease without compromising oncological outcomes compared to radical nephrectomy. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (Option B) is not a standard treatment for localized RCC as these tumors are largely chemoresistant. Radical nephrectomy (Option C), the removal of the entire kidney, is reserved for larger, more complex, or centrally located tumors where a partial approach is not feasible. Postoperative radiotherapy (Option D) has a very limited role in RCC management. Therefore, given the small 4 cm size and the patient's relatively young age, partial nephrectomy is the most suitable and recommended intervention

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient who underwent gastrointestinal surgery has had a portion of her jejunum resected. Which of the following drugs should be added to her postoperative treatment?
questions.explanation: Large resections of the small intestine, such as the jejunum, can lead to "Short Bowel Syndrome," where the remaining gut cannot absorb enough nutrients and water to sustain the body. Teduglutide is a specialized medication that is an analog of Glucagon-Like Peptide-2 (GLP-2). GLP-2 is a natural hormone that promotes the growth and maintenance of the intestinal lining. By mimicking this hormone, Teduglutide increases the surface area of the remaining small intestine (specifically increasing the height of the villi), thereby improving nutrient and fluid absorption. This can significantly reduce the patient's dependence on intravenous parenteral nutrition. Liraglutide (Option A), Exenatide (Option C), and Semaglutide (Option D) are all GLP-1 analogs used for the treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity; they work by increasing insulin secretion and slowing gastric emptying, which would not address the malabsorption issues in short bowel syndrome. Teduglutide represents a targeted physiological approach to managing gut failure
questions.learning: Large resections of the small intestine, such as the jejunum, can lead to "Short Bowel Syndrome," where the remaining gut cannot absorb enough nutrients and water to sustain the body.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What are the potential effects of folic acid deficiency during pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Folic acid is a crucial B-vitamin required for DNA synthesis and rapid cell division during fetal development. A deficiency in maternal folic acid is strongly linked to the development of neural tube defects (NTDs), such as spina bifida and anencephaly, which occur when the neural tube fails to close properly within the first 28 days of gestation. While severe deficiency might contribute to general pregnancy complications, Option B (preterm labor) is not the primary direct outcome of folate lack. Pernicious anemia (Option C) is specifically caused by Vitamin B12 deficiency due to a lack of intrinsic factor, not folic acid. Iron deficiency anemia (Option D) results from inadequate iron levels and is a separate nutritional pathology. Due to its critical role, universal periconceptional folic acid supplementation is recommended for all women planning pregnancy to significantly reduce the risk of NTDs

questions.text: A patient has adult respiratory distress syndrome. Which of the following is the action of IL-8 in the pathogenesis in this patient?

IL-8 is a potent chemokine responsible for recruitment and activation of neutrophils.

In ARDS, IL-8–mediated neutrophil activation leads to release of proteases and reactive oxygen species. This contributes to alveolar–capillary membrane damage and increased vascular permeability.

Endothelial injury and fibrin deposition are downstream effects, not the primary action of IL-8.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman at 36 weeks of gestation with a prosthetic valve replacement for mitral stenosis is on warfarin therapy. Her INR is 3. What is the appropriate next step in management? LMWH- Low molecular weight heparin
options: Stop warfarin, start LMWH and asprin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Stop warfarin and start LMWH

The next appropriate step in the management of a pregnant woman with a prosthetic valve on warfarin therapy at 36 weeks of gestation is to stop warfarin and start LMWH.

Warfarin is safe and effective in preventing thromboembolism in people with prosthetic valve. However, it is teratogenic and can lead to miscarriage, stillbirths, and fetal embryopathy if used in the first trimester. LMWH is safe for the fetus as it does not cross the placenta but is less effective than warfarin.

Period of gestation
Anticoagulant

Till 12 completed weeks

LMWH or UFH

13 to 36 weeks
Warfarin

36 weeks to 6 hours before delivery
LMWH or UFH

6 hours after vaginal and 24 hours after cesarian section
LMWH or UFH (ACOG recommendation)

(LMWH- Low molecular weight heparin, UFH- Unfractionated heparin)

It is recommended that all women on warfarin switch to LMWH or IV UFH at weeks 34–36. Since giving IV UFH until delivery is difficult, LMWH would be the better option till UFH is started. UFH should be started approximately 24 hours prior to labour induction or caesarean. IV UFH should be stopped once in labour or 6 hours prior to caesarean. UFH should be restarted 4 to 6 hours post-vaginal delivery or 6–12 hours post-caesarean section. Warfarin should be restarted on day 1 postpartum (uncomplicated vaginal delivery) or on day 2-3 if caesarian or bleeding complications occur.

Heparin should be discontinued just before delivery. If delivery occurs before discontinuation and there is extensive bleeding, then iv protamine sulfate can be given.(Easy reversal of anticoagulation). Warfarin, LMWH, and UFH do not accumulate in breast milk and do not have an anticoagulant effect in the newborn. They are compatible with breastfeeding.

Other options:

Option B: Unfractionated heparin can also be given instead of LMWH. However, in this case, the better answer is to give LMWH; because, in clinical practice, LMWHs have a long half-life, once-daily dosing, and fewer side effects. If LMWH is unavailable or cost-prohibitive, or if anti-Xa levels cannot be monitored, continuous infusion of UFH can be used as an alternative to LMWH.

Option D: Aspirin 75-100 mg can be given daily during pregnancy. It can be continued in women with mechanical heart valves if needed for other indications.
questions.learning: Stop warfarin and start LMWH — The next appropriate step in the management of a pregnant woman with a prosthetic valve on warfarin therapy at 36 weeks of gestation is to stop warfarin and start LMWH.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Identify the drug used to treat the condition shown below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anti-tubercular therapy

The given image shows an annular plaque with central scarring points to lupus vulgaris, which is treated using anti-tubercular drugs.

It is the most common cutaneous tuberculosis in India. The characteristic lesions are annular, infiltrated plaques with serpiginous edges, central atrophy and scarring and are commonly seen on face, buttocks and extremities.

On diascopy, apple jelly nodules are seen.

Histologically, tubercles are seen in the superficial dermis showing scanty or absent central caseation with surrounding epithelioid histiocytes and giant cells.

Other differential diagnoses for annular plaque include:

• Tinea corporis shows central clearing, peripherally raised scaly margins and presents with an itch.

• Cutaneous leishmaniasis lesions have central crusting and are seen on the face in patients from areas of high leishmaniasis prevalence.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following regions is considered free from rabies and therefore does not require priority inclusion in immediate rabies vaccination programs?
questions.explanation: Rabies is endemic throughout most of India, but specific island territories have successfully maintained a rabies-free status. The Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep (Option C) are recognized as rabies-free areas in India. Consequently, these regions are lower priorities for mass post-exposure vaccination campaigns compared to the mainland. Sikkim (Option A), Kerala (Option B), and Jammu and Kashmir (Option D) are all located on the mainland where rabies remains a significant public health threat due to large stray dog populations. Maintaining rabies-free status in island territories requires strict animal quarantine and surveillance measures. For public health planning, recognizing these disease-free zones is essential for appropriate resource allocation and tailoring prevention strategies. While rabies-free, these areas still focus on surveillance to prevent the accidental introduction of the virus. Therefore, Lakshadweep stands out as the correct rabies-free territory among the choices provided
questions.learning: Rabies is endemic throughout most of India, but specific island territories have successfully maintained a rabies-free status. The Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep (Option C) are recognized as rabies-free areas in India.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with unilateral nasal obstruction associated with watery nasal discharge and episodes of bleeding. The diagnosis is inverted papilloma. Which statement correctly describes this condition?
questions.explanation: An inverted papilloma (Schneiderian papilloma) is a unique tumor of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses. Histologically, it is benign, but clinically it is highly locally invasive, frequently destroying surrounding bone as it grows. The term "inverted" refers to its characteristic growth pattern where the surface epithelium proliferates inward into the underlying stroma rather than outward. Key features include a high rate of local recurrence after surgery and a significant risk (approximately 10%) of synchronous or metachronous transformation into Squamous Cell Carcinoma. Options A, B, and D are incorrect characterizations of its behavior. Clinically, it presents in middle-aged adults with unilateral nasal obstruction and epistaxis. On examination, it often resembles a firm, opaque, vascularized nasal polyp. The standard treatment is wide surgical excision, typically via Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS) or a medial maxillectomy, to ensure complete removal of the tumor and its bony attachments to prevent recurrence
questions.learning: An inverted papilloma (Schneiderian papilloma) is a unique tumor of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses. Histologically, it is benign, but clinically it is highly locally invasive, frequently destroying surrounding bone as it grows.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient sustains an injury on the lateral aspect of the knee. After a few days, he develops difficulty in walking due to dragging of foot, along with numbness over the upper lateral side of the leg and dorsum of the foot. Which of the following nerves is most commonly injured in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Common peroneal nerve

The common peroneal nerve winds around the neck of the fibula on the lateral side of the knee, making it highly vulnerable to injury.

Damage causes foot drop due to loss of dorsiflexion (deep peroneal nerve) and sensory loss over the upper lateral leg and dorsum of the foot (superficial peroneal nerve).
questions.learning: Common peroneal nerve — The common peroneal nerve winds around the neck of the fibula on the lateral side of the knee, making it highly vulnerable to injury.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The normal placenta is - 1. Discoid 2. Hemochorial 3. Deciduate
questions.explanation: Human placental anatomy and physiology are described by several specific biological terms. First, it is discoid (1), meaning it is a flat, circular, disc-shaped organ. Second, it is deciduate (3), which means that upon delivery, a portion of the maternal uterine lining (the decidua) is shed along with the placenta. Third, it is classified as hemochorial (2), which is the most intimate type of placental barrier where the maternal blood comes into direct contact with the fetal chorionic villi. Because the human placenta possesses all three of these definitive characteristics, Option D (1, 2, and 3) is the correct and comprehensive answer. Understanding these terms is fundamental in embryology and obstetrics to describe the efficient exchange of nutrients and gases between the mother and the developing fetus. Options A, B, and C are incomplete as they omit one of these essential descriptors
questions.learning: Human placental anatomy and physiology are described by several specific biological terms. First, it is discoid (1), meaning it is a flat, circular, disc-shaped organ.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: If the lung is allowed to undergo elastic recoil without the chest wall, the resultant volume of the lung would be?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Minimum volume

If lung is allowed to undergo elastic recoil without the chest wall, the resultant volume of the lung would be minimum volume as the opposing force by the chest wall would be non existant.

The yellow line in the above graph denotes the compliance of lungs alone. According to the graph, when the pressure (x axis)  inside the lung is zero, there is some volume of air lesser than FRC still present (y axis) inside the lungs which is less than the functional residual capacity and residual volume which can be called as minimum volume.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: All of the following are correct differences between normal radiography and mammography, except:
options: Radiography uses tungsten as the target, while mammography uses molybdenum
Beryllium is used as the exit window in mammography
Mammography uses Bremsstrahlung radiation for better tissue contrast
Aluminum filter is used in radiography, while molybdenum is used in mammography
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mammography uses Bremsstrahlung radiation for better tissue contrast

Normal radiography (X-ray):

• Uses Tungsten target
• Uses Aluminum filter
• More Bremsstrahlung radiation
• Higher energy X-rays (Needs to penetrate bone, chest, abdomen etc.)
• Think of it like a “powerful beam” that has to go through thick structures.

Mammography:

• Uses Molybdenum (or Rhodium) target
• Uses Molybdenum filter (molybdenum produces X-rays at ideal energy (17–19 keV)

Lower energy X-rays (for soft tissue contrast)
• Breast is a soft tissue organ, so we need to see tiny differences (like microcalcifications)
• So we use low energy X-rays
• Uses more characteristic radiation, not mainly bremsstrahlung.
• Think of it like a “gentle, precise beam” made specially for soft tissue contrast.

Bremsstrahlung radiation?

• Bremsstrahlung = wide range of X-ray energies (mixed spectrum).
• Good for general X-rays, not for fine soft tissue contrast.

Characteristic radiation?

• Very specific energy peaks.
• In mammography, molybdenum produces X-rays at ideal energy
• This gives excellent breast tissue contrast.

Option-wise:

A) Radiography uses tungsten, mammography uses molybdenum

✔ Correct

B) Beryllium is used as exit window in mammography

✔ Correct (allows low-energy X-rays to pass)

C) Mammography uses Bremsstrahlung radiation for better tissue contrast

❌ Wrong. Mammography mainly uses characteristic radiation from molybdenum (17–19 keV) for better breast tissue contrast.

D) Aluminum filter in radiography, molybdenum filter in mammography

✔ Correct

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following features will not be manifested in an infection of the post-styloid compartment of the parapharyngeal space?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Trismus

Trismus is not a feature of infection of the post-styloid compartment of the parapharyngeal space. Trismus is seen in pre-styloid abscess due to the involvement of medial pterygoid muscle.

Parapharyngeal space is divided into two compartments by the styloid process and its attachments. Clinical features depend on the compartment involved.

In a post-styloid abscess, there is a bulge of the pharynx behind the posterior pillar, accompanied by paralysis of cranial nerves IX, X (resulting in vocal cord paralysis), XI, XII, and the sympathetic chain, which can manifest as Horner's syndrome. Swelling in the parotid region may also be present. Notably, trismus, the inability to fully open the mouth, is usually absent in this type of abscess.

A pre-styloid abscess exhibits distinct features including the prolapse of the tonsil and tonsillar fossa, along with trismus caused by the spasm of the medial pterygoid muscle. Marked odynophagia is common. Additionally, an external swelling can be observed behind the angle of the jaw.

Fever, sore throat, torticollis (caused by spasm of the prevertebral muscles), and signs of systemic toxicity are common features.

Diagnosis can be established using a contrast-enhanced CT scan (CECT). If there is suspicion of thrombosis of the internal jugular vein or an aneurysm of the internal carotid artery, magnetic resonance arteriography (MRA) can be useful.

Patients require intravenous antibiotic therapy with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, carbapenem antibiotics plus drugs that target anaerobic organisms, such as clindamycin or metronidazole. A parapharyngeal abscess is drained by an external horizontal incision made on the skin a few centimeters below the angle of the mandible.

questions.learning: Trismus Trismus is not a feature of infection of the post-styloid compartment of the parapharyngeal space. Trismus is seen in pre-styloid abscess due to the involvement of medial pterygoid muscle.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the site of drainage of the marked structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sphenoethmoidal recess

The marked structure in the given image is the sphenoid sinus and it drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess.

Paranasal sinuses are air-containing cavities that are present in the skull bones. These paranasal sinuses have been divided into two groups:

Anterior group: Their ostia drain into the middle meatus (Option B) through a common drainage pathway known as osteomeatal unit. This group includes:

• Maxillary sinus (antrum of Highmore)
• Frontal sinus
• Anterior ethmoidal sinus

Posterior group:

• Posterior ethmoidal sinuses: Opens in the superior meatus (Option A)
• Sphenoid sinus: Opens in sphenoethmoidal recess

The inferior meatus (Option C) has the Nasolacrimal duct draining into it with its terminal end being guarded by the Hasner's valve.

The images below show the location of paranasal sinuses:
questions.learning: Sphenoethmoidal recess — The marked structure in the given image is the sphenoid sinus and it drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess. Paranasal sinuses are air-containing cavities that are present in the skull bones.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What nutrient deficiency is commonly associated with delayed wound healing following minor surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitamin C

Delayed wound healing after minor surgery can be attributed to a deficiency in vitamin C.

Vitamin C, also known as ascorbic acid, plays a crucial role in collagen synthesis, a protein that is essential for wound healing and tissue repair. Collagen provides structural support to the skin, blood vessels, and other connective tissues. A deficiency in vitamin C can lead to impaired collagen formation, weakening of blood vessels, and delayed wound healing.

Factors influencing healing:

* Infection: one of the most important causes of delay in healing; prolongs inflammation; increases the local tissue injury

* Diabetes: most important systemic cause of abnormal wound healing

* Nutritional status: protein deficiency and vitamin C deficiency inhibit collagen synthesis and retard healing.

* Glucocorticoids (steroids): anti-inflammatory effects; results in weakness of the scar due to inhibition of TGF-β production and diminished fibrosis

* Mechanical factors: such as increased local pressure or torsion; may cause wounds to pull apart or dehisce

* Poor perfusion: due to arteriosclerosis, diabetes, or obstructed venous drainage; also impairs healing

* Foreign bodies: such as fragments of steel, glass, or even bone; impede healing

* Type and extent of tissue injury: affect subsequent repair;

* Location of the injury and the character of the injured tissue: also important

Even though zinc also causes poor wound healing, Vitamin C is more commonly implicated.
questions.learning: Vitamin C Delayed wound healing after minor surgery can be attributed to a deficiency in vitamin C. Vitamin C, also known as ascorbic acid, plays a crucial role in collagen synthesis, a protein that is essential for wound healing and tissue repair.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Injury to which part causes difficulty in dorsiflexion of the foot?
questions.explanation: In the provided image, point B identifies the common peroneal nerve as it courses superficially around the neck of the fibula. This nerve is highly susceptible to injury at this site. It branches into the deep and superficial peroneal nerves, with the deep peroneal nerve responsible for innervating the tibialis anterior muscle. This muscle is the primary driver of dorsiflexion (lifting the foot upward). An injury at point B results in "foot drop," where the patient cannot dorsiflex the foot. The sciatic nerve (Point A) would cause much more extensive leg weakness. The tibial nerve (Point C) innervates the posterior compartment, and its injury would cause difficulty in plantarflexion (pointing the foot down). While the deep peroneal nerve (Point D) also causes foot drop, the injury at the fibular head (B) is the more classic clinical site
questions.learning: In the provided image, point B identifies the common peroneal nerve as it courses superficially around the neck of the fibula. This nerve is highly susceptible to injury at this site.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: During autopsy, the doctor tied the bronchus and immersed the lung in water to check whether it floats or sinks. This test is identified as ______ .
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hydrostatic test

Hydrostatic test is done to determine whether the newborn has respired or not. It is also known as Floatation test/ Breslau’s first life test/ Raygat’s test.

It is based on the principle that the specific gravity of the unrespired lungs varies from 1.04 to 1.05 and that of  the respired lungs is 0.94, because of the increase in volume due to inhalation of air.

Procedure:

* Put each lung separately into a jar of water, see whether it sinks or floats.

* Cut each into 10 to 12 pieces observe the blood exuding.Test each of them for buoyancy.

* Pick up the floating pieces, and press firmly under water. Observe the nature of bubbles streaming up. Note whether they continue to float or not.

Interpretation:

* If the lung pieces float in water, it means that respiration has taken place, indicating a live birth.

* If the pieces sink, respiration has not taken place, which means it is a stillborn.

A respired lung (live birth) may sink in water in the following conditions :

* Lung edema

* Lung collapse

* Pneumonia

* Congenital syphilis

An unrespired lung (still birth) may float due to gases of decomposition, as seen in putrefaction, or due to artificial inhalation.

Hydrostatic test is not necessary when:

* The fetus is born before 180 days of gestation.

* The fetus is a monster and thereby incapable of leading a separate existence.

* The fetus shows signs of intra-uterine macerations.

* The umbilical cord has separated and the umbilicus has cicatrised.

* The stomach contains milk showing active digestive system.

Other options:

Gettler's test is done for drowning. It estimates the chloride content of blood from both sides of the heart.

* Normally, chloride content is equal in the right and left chambers of the heart (approx. 600 mg/100 ml).

* In freshwater drowning, due to hemodilution, the chloride content is decreased on the left side of the heart by 50%.

* In saltwater drowning due to hemoconcentration, the chloride content is increased in the left side of the heart by 30-40%.

Ploucquet’s test: Weight of lungs Before respiration: 1/70 of body weight, after respiration: 1/35 of body weight

Diatom's test: Diatoms are a class of microscopic unicellular algae found suspended in most natural waters. The presence of diatoms in the brain or bone marrow indicates antemortem inhalation of water/ antemortem drowning. Diatoms are not found in the brain or bone marrow in case of dry drowning and when a dead body is thrown into the water. At the present time, the diatom test should be used only as an indicative aid and not as legal proof of drowning.

Pearl PF1099: Hydrostatic Test/Floatation Test/Raygat's Test

It is based on the lung changes in a foetus after respiration.

Principle : Respired air remains in the lungs as residual air which cannot be removed after death. Hence lung floats in water.

False negative test in:

* Atelectasis

* Pulmonary edema

* Pneumonia

* Congenital syphilis

* Air absorbed from air passages if circulation continued for long time after cessation of respiration

* More air exhaled from the lungs compared to air entering during inspiration

* Obstruction by alveolar duct membrane

False positive test in:

* Putrefied foetus

* Artificial inflation

Hydrostatic test is not required when

* Fetus is monstrous

* Foetus is macerated or mummified.

* Foetus is born before 180 days of gestation.

* Stomach contains milk.

* Umbilical cord has separated and scar has been formed.
questions.learning: Hydrostatic test Hydrostatic test is done to determine whether the newborn has respired or not. It is also known as Floatation test/ Breslau’s first life test/ Raygat’s test.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which options are correctly matched? 1. Gefitinib: EGFR (HER-1) 2. Sunitinib: EGFR (HER-1) 3. Trastuzumab: HER-2 4. Nilotinib: BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3 and 4

1. Gefitinib: EGFR (HER-1) — Correct

• Targets: EGFR-mutated (L858R mutation) NSCLC

2. Sunitinib: EGFR (HER-1) — Incorrect

• Sunitinib mainly inhibits: Tyrosine kinases: VEGFR/PDGFR/c-KIT

3. Trastuzumab: HER-2 — Correct

• Monoclonal antibody against HER-2/neu breast cancer

4. Nilotinib: BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor — Correct

Second-generation:

• BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor
• Used in: CML

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the operative procedure shown in the image?
questions.explanation: The image illustrates a Resection and Anastomosis procedure. Specifically, it shows an end-to-end intestinal anastomosis where two sections of the bowel are being sewn together to restore gastrointestinal continuity after a diseased segment has been removed. Primary closure of a perforation (Option A) would involve sewing up a single hole rather than joining two distinct loops. An ileostomy (Option C) involves bringing a loop of the ileum out through the abdominal wall as a stoma. Resection alone (Option D) would leave the bowel as two "blind" ends, which is incomplete without an anastomosis or stoma. This surgical technique is fundamental in the treatment of various conditions like intestinal obstruction, malignancy, or gangrenous bowel. Surgeons can perform these using hand-sewn techniques (as shown) or with mechanical stapling devices. A successful anastomosis must be watertight and tension-free with an adequate blood supply to ensure proper healing
questions.learning: The image illustrates a Resection and Anastomosis procedure. Specifically, it shows an end-to-end intestinal anastomosis where two sections of the bowel are being sewn together to restore gastrointestinal continuity after a diseased segment has been removed.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: From which of the following substrates is cholesterol synthesized?
questions.explanation: Cholesterol is a vital structural component of cell membranes and a precursor for steroid hormones and bile acids. The entire 27-carbon structure of cholesterol is synthesized solely from Acetyl-CoA molecules. The pathway begins with the condensation of two Acetyl-CoA molecules to form acetoacetyl-CoA, eventually leading to the rate-limiting step catalyzed by HMG-CoA reductase. Malonyl-CoA (Option B) is the critical building block for fatty acid synthesis, not cholesterol. Phenylalanine (Option C) is an essential amino acid involved in protein synthesis and the tyrosine pathway. Oxaloacetate (Option D) is a key intermediate in the TCA cycle and gluconeogenesis. Because every single carbon atom in the cholesterol sterol ring is derived from the acetate units provided by Acetyl-CoA, it remains the definitive primary substrate for the entire biosynthetic pathway. This metabolic source is the target for statin therapy
questions.learning: Cholesterol is a vital structural component of cell membranes and a precursor for steroid hormones and bile acids. The entire 27-carbon structure of cholesterol is synthesized solely from Acetyl-CoA molecules.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which amongst the following can be used to treat kesari dal toxicity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vitamin C

Vitamin C in doses of 500-1000 mg can be used for the prevention and treatment of lathyrism (kesari dal toxicity).

Lathyrism is a paralyzing disease of humans and animals. It is due to the consumption of khesari dal or Lathyrus sativus. When the husk is removed, it looks similar to red gram or Bengal gram. It is mostly consumed by poor agricultural laborers because it is relatively cheap. Lathyrism is more prevalent in parts of Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Odisha, and Bihar. The Prevention of Food Adulteration Act in India has banned Lathyrus sativus in all forms (whole/ split/ flour).

In humans, it is referred to as neurolathyrism because it affects the nervous system. It is characterized by gradually developing spastic paralysis of the lower limbs. Beta-oxalyl amino alanine (BOAA) is the toxic compound causing this disease. It is water-soluble and can be removed by the following methods:

* Soaking pulses in hot water and discarding the water

* Overnight soaking in lime water, followed by boiling

* Parboiling - for large-scale detoxification
questions.learning: Vitamin C Vitamin C in doses of 500-1000 mg can be used for the prevention and treatment of lathyrism (kesari dal toxicity). Lathyrism is a paralyzing disease of humans and animals.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: 'Mount Fuji sign' is seen in _____________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tension pneumocephalus

'Mount Fuji sign' is seen in tension pneumocephalus.

Mount Fuji sign refers to the presence of air (pneumocephalus) between the tips of the frontal lobes giving the appearance of Mount Fuji.

Tension pneumocephalus occurs with subdural air causing a mass effect over the underlying brain parenchyma, often from a ball valve mechanism causing one-way entry of air into the subdural space.

The appearance of this sign often warrants immediate surgery to prevent permanent damage.

The CT image below shows the Mount Fuji sign.
questions.learning: Tension pneumocephalus 'Mount Fuji sign' is seen in tension pneumocephalus. Mount Fuji sign refers to the presence of air (pneumocephalus) between the tips of the frontal lobes giving the appearance of Mount Fuji.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Among the following parasites, which one directly invades the skin?
questions.explanation: Schistosoma mansoni is a blood fluke characterized by a life cycle involving direct skin penetration. Infection occurs when humans come into contact with fresh water containing the infectious larval stage, known as cercariae. These cercariae use specialized proteolytic enzymes and vigorous movement to bore through the intact human skin, often causing a transient rash known as "swimmer's itch." Once inside, they travel to the mesenteric veins. Clonorchis sinensis (Option B) is the Chinese liver fluke, acquired by ingesting undercooked infected fish. Wuchereria bancrofti (Option C) is a filarial worm transmitted through the bite of an infected mosquito, which deposits larvae on the skin that then enter through the bite wound. Diphyllobothrium latum (Option D) is the fish tapeworm, acquired by ingesting undercooked fish containing plerocercoid larvae. Understanding the specific portal of entry is vital for diagnosing parasitic infections; for Schistosoma, a history of exposure to snail-infested water is the critical epidemiological clue
questions.learning: Schistosoma mansoni is a blood fluke characterized by a life cycle involving direct skin penetration. Infection occurs when humans come into contact with fresh water containing the infectious larval stage, known as cercariae.

questions.text: Regarding Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) in children, which of the following statements is false?
options: Plasmapheresis is not effective in GBS
IV immunoglobulins are the first line of treatment

• Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (AIDP)

• Often follows:

↓

↓

Demyelination of peripheral nerves

↓

↓ Nerve conduction

↓

Ascending weakness + areflexia

A. Plasmapheresis is not effective in GBS

• Plasmapheresis IS effective
• Removes circulating antibodies
• Used in:

So, statement is FALSE

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A surgical procedure is performed on the great saphenous vein, approximately 2.5 cm anterior to the medial malleolus. Which structure is most likely to be injured during this procedure?
questions.explanation: The great saphenous vein (GSV) is consistently located approximately 2.5 cm anterior to the medial malleolus at the ankle. At this level, the saphenous nerve, a branch of the femoral nerve, runs in very close proximity to the vein. Surgical procedures such as venous cut-down or stripping of the GSV carry a high risk of injuring this nerve. Damage typically results in paresthesia or numbness along the medial aspect of the foot and leg. The sural nerve (Option B) runs with the small saphenous vein posterior to the lateral malleolus. The deep peroneal nerve (Option C) is found deep in the anterior compartment of the leg and supplies the first web space of the foot. The tibial nerve (Option D) passes posterior to the medial malleolus within the tarsal tunnel. Because of the intimate anatomical relationship between the GSV and the saphenous nerve at the ankle, it is the most vulnerable structure during distal venous interventions
questions.learning: The great saphenous vein (GSV) is consistently located approximately 2.5 cm anterior to the medial malleolus at the ankle. At this level, the saphenous nerve, a branch of the femoral nerve, runs in very close proximity to the vein.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old female presents to the clinic complaining of severe vaginal irritation and pruritus. On examination, you note a greenish- yellow, frothy discharge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical combination of severe irritation/itching and a characteristic greenish-yellow, frothy vaginal discharge is diagnostic for Trichomoniasis, a sexually transmitted infection caused by the protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis. On examination, the cervix may also show punctate hemorrhages, known as a "strawberry cervix." Bacterial vaginosis (Option A) has a fishy odor and a greyish-white, non-frothy discharge. Candidiasis (Option C) involves a thick, white discharge and intense itching but no frothiness. Gonorrhea (Option D) primarily affects the cervix and causes a purulent, yellow discharge rather than a frothy vaginal one. Diagnosis is confirmed by seeing motile, pear-shaped trichomonads on a saline wet mount. Unlike BV, Trichomoniasis is a true STI; therefore, treatment of the male partner is mandatory to prevent reinfection, even if he is asymptomatic. The drug of choice for both the patient and her partner is oral metronidazole or tinidazole
questions.learning: The clinical combination of severe irritation/itching and a characteristic greenish-yellow, frothy vaginal discharge is diagnostic for Trichomoniasis, a sexually transmitted infection caused by the protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with miosis, anhidrosis, mild ptosis, and a pupil that remains constricted even in dim light. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The classic triad of miosis (constricted pupil), anhidrosis (lack of sweating), and mild ptosis (due to Müller muscle weakness) defines Horner syndrome. This condition results from a disruption in the sympathetic nerve supply to the eye. The pupil remains small even in low light because the sympathetic dilator fibers are non-functional. Adie's tonic pupil (Option A) typically presents with a dilated (mydriatic) pupil that is sluggishly reactive to light. Marcus Gunn pupil (Option C), or a relative afferent pupillary defect, is characterized by paradoxical dilation when light is swung from the normal to the affected eye. Argyll Robertson pupil (Option D), associated with tertiary syphilis, features bilateral small pupils that accommodate but do not react to light. Because the patient’s symptoms specifically include ipsilateral ptosis and anhidrosis alongside the small pupil, Horner syndrome is the most accurate clinical diagnosis
questions.learning: The classic triad of miosis (constricted pupil), anhidrosis (lack of sweating), and mild ptosis (due to Müller muscle weakness) defines Horner syndrome.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A thin, 34-year-old male, presents with sharp pain and sudden onset dyspnea. Chest X-ray was performed and is shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pneumothorax

The given chest radiograph clearly depicts the presence of pneumothorax, which represents air in the pleural space.

• The right hemithorax shows blackening (depicts area of low density) due to the presence of air.
• The visceral pleural line has separated from the chest wall by a transradiant zone devoid of vessels.
• The collapsed lung can be seen with a clear border.
• There is a mediastinal shift to the left side (contralateral), which is typically seen with cases of tension pneumothorax.

All the above features are suggestive of pneumothorax.

Note: Pleural effusions signify the presence of fluid accumulation in the pleural space. The fluid may have varying degrees of mobility depending on the nature of effusion (free-flowing or loculated).

While a small amount of free fluid is usually hard to detect on an erect PA chest x-ray, a significant pleural effusion (200-500 mL) is represented by obscured lateral and posterior costophrenic angles and the hemidiaphragm affected. Subsequently, homogenous opacification of the lower lung field develops, associated with concave superior margin relative to the lung. This margin is higher laterally than medially.

A massive pleural effusion cause dense opacification usually associated with a contralteral mediastinal shift.

Here is an image of a left-sided pleural effusion representing the homogenous opacification of the left lower and middle lung fields. There is associated blunting of the left sided costophrenic angle. The superior border of the effusion is concave and is higher laterally than medially.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A female patient with a known case of bronchial asthma is on levosalbutamol and Ipratropium bromide metered-dose inhalers. She now reports frequent nocturnal symptoms, including wheezing and breathlessness that wake her up several times a week. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Add LABA and inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)

Frequent nocturnal symptoms indicate poorly controlled persistent asthma despite short-acting bronchodilators.

The appropriate step-up therapy is adding inhaled corticosteroid with a LABA, which addresses airway inflammation and provides sustained bronchodilation.

Increasing SABA or adding oral steroids is inappropriate for long-term control, and montelukast is less effective as monotherapy at this stage.

Intermittent asthma

↓

SABA as needed

↓ (symptoms worsen)

Mild persistent

↓

Low-dose ICS

↓ (nocturnal symptoms / frequent symptoms)

Moderate persistent

↓

ICS + LABA

↓

Severe asthma

↓

High-dose ICS + LABA ± oral steroids

Mechanism synergy:

• ICS → reduces airway inflammation
• LABA → bronchodilation (long acting)

Together → better symptom control + fewer exacerbations

| Severity | Symptoms | Treatment

| -------- | -------- | ---------

| Intermittent | <2/week | SABA

| Mild persistent | >2/week | Low-dose ICS

| Moderate persistent | Nocturnal symptoms |  ICS + LABA

| Severe | Continuous | High-dose ICS + LABA ± OCS
questions.learning: Add LABA and inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) Frequent nocturnal symptoms indicate poorly controlled persistent asthma despite short-acting bronchodilators.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A soldier posted in Siachen is brought to you in the ER. In order to rule out hypothermia, how do you best measure his temperature?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rectal

In the given clinical scenario rectal temperature would be the preferred site to measure the core body temperature.

During low or high temperatures like in Siachen, the axillary and the oral temperatures are highly misleading and should not be used to measure the core body temperatures

Infrared tympanic thermometer measures the temperature of the eardrum which is representative of core body temperature. However, more often the thermometer is not inserted adequately or for safety reasons, they are manufactured in such a way that they do not reach deep into the ear canal, or the ear canal contains cerumen which can disturb the measurement. Hence the infrared thermometer more commonly delivers the temperature of ear canal cerumen and hence not a reliable method of measuring the core body temperature.
questions.learning: Rectal — In the given clinical scenario rectal temperature would be the preferred site to measure the core body temperature. During low or high temperatures like in Siachen, the axillary and the oral temperatures are highly misleading and should not be…

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: From the X-ray given, pick out the probable diagnosis:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pneumoperitoneum

The above X-ray clearly shows the presence of subdiaphragmatic free gas in the right upper quadrant. This indicates pneumoperitoneum.

Pneumoperitoneum is the presence of free gas within the peritoneal cavity but outside the viscera. The most common cause of pneumoperitoneum is bowel perforation.

• Gastric and posterior duodenal perforations are seen in long-standing cases of peptic ulcers.
• Intestinal perforations are seen with ischemia, inflammation, diverticula, or obstruction.
• Other causes also include iatrogenic, penetrating injuries, prolonged mechanical ventilation, peritoneal dialysis, etc.

Signs of pneumoperitoneum:

• Bowel-related signs

• Double wall sign/Rigler's sign/gas-relief sign- Air is seen on both sides of the bowel wall.
• Telltale triangle sign/triangle sign - Triangle of gas formed between three loops of the bowel or between the abdominal wall and two loops of the bowel.

• Peritoneal ligament-related signs

• Football sign- Air outlines the confines of the peritoneal cavity
• Falciform ligament sign-  Air outlines the falciform ligament
• Lateral umbilical ligament sign/inverted "V" sign- Air outlines the lateral umbilical ligament
• Urachus sign - Air outlines the urachus

• Right upper quadrant signs

• Cupola sign- Air outlines the median subphrenic space
• Fissure for ligamentum teres sign- Air outlines the ligamentum teres
• Hepatic edge sign- Cigar-shaped free-air pocket in the subhepatic region. It tracks superomedial following the contours of the liver
• Lucent liver sign - Reduction of hepatic radiodensity due to accumulation of free gas anterior to the liver
• Morison's pouch sign / Doge cap sign - Triangular/ crescentic gas lucency bound by the 11th rib
• Periportal free gas sign.
questions.learning: Pneumoperitoneum — The above X-ray clearly shows the presence of subdiaphragmatic free gas in the right upper quadrant. Pneumoperitoneum is the presence of free gas within the peritoneal cavity but outside the viscera.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old female patient underwent thyroidectomy. Three days after the surgery, she developed perioral numbness. Which of the following investigations need to be done for her?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Calcium, phosphate and parathormone levels

Calcium, phosphate, and parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels should be done in this patient to evaluate hypoparathyroidism secondary to thyroidectomy.

Hypoparathyroidism is a common complication of thyroid surgery. It is temporary and usually lasts for 4-6 weeks. Hypoparathyroidism following thyroid surgery can be diagnosed when there are decreased serum calcium and/ or PTH levels, or if there is symptomatic hypocalcemia.

The features of hypocalcemia are circumoral paresthesia, and paresthesia of the neck, fingers, and toes. Muscle twitching, weakness of the forearm, hand, foot, and carpopedal spasms can be seen. A carpal spasm can be induced by inflating a blood pressure cuff to 20 mmHg above the systolic blood pressure for 3 minutes. This is known as Trousseau's sign. Chvostek sign wherein twitching of facial muscles is demonstrated by tapping above the angle of the jaw. It is due to the stimulation of the branches of the facial nerve.

ECG shows prolonged QT interval.

Management of acute and symptomatic hypocalcemia is by giving 10 mL of intravenous 10% calcium gluconate over 5 minutes.
questions.learning: Calcium, phosphate and parathormone levels Calcium, phosphate, and parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels should be done in this patient to evaluate hypoparathyroidism secondary to thyroidectomy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: On radiological evaluation of a pregnant woman, the pelvic inlet is noted to be oval in the anteroposterior direction. According to the Caldwell and Moloy classification, this pelvic inlet shape corresponds to which type of pelvis?
questions.explanation: The Caldwell-Moloy system classifies the female pelvis into four types based on the shape of the inlet. The "Anthropoid pelvis" (Option B) is characterized by an inlet that is oval-shaped, where the anteroposterior (AP) diameter is significantly larger than the transverse diameter. This pelvis is common in non-Caucasian populations. The "Gynecoid pelvis" (Option C) is the most common female type, featuring a rounded or slightly transverse-oval inlet. The "Android pelvis" (Option A) has a heart-shaped inlet with a narrow fore-pelvis, resembling a male pelvis. The "Platypelloid pelvis" (Option D) has a flattened, transverse-oval inlet where the transverse diameter is much larger than the AP diameter. In an anthropoid pelvis, the fetus is most likely to engage in the "occipito-posterior" position due to the elongated AP dimension. Understanding pelvic architecture is crucial for predicting the mechanism of labor and the likelihood of successful vaginal delivery versus cephalopelvic disproportion

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 20–30-year-old man presents with NS1 positivity and has with fever for 5 days. There are no bleeding manifestations. The Hb is 9 gm/dL, platelet count is 20,000, and ALT is 112 U/L. Which of the following should be used in the management of this patient? 1. Paracetamol 2. Platelet transfusion 3. PRBC transfusion 4. Steroids
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 only

• NS1 positive → early dengue infection
• Day 5 fever → entering critical phase
• Platelets = 20,000 (low but platelet transfusion indicated below 5000/symptoms of bleeding)
• Hb = 9 g/dL → mild anemia
• ALT = 112 → mild hepatic involvement (very common in dengue)

Key clinical clue: NO bleeding manifestations

Dengue virus → Bone marrow suppression + immune destruction

↓

Thrombocytopenia

↓

↑ Capillary permeability (plasma leakage)

↓

Hemoconcentration (↑ Hct, not ↓ Hb initially)

• Platelets fall due to marrow suppression + immune destruction
• Bleeding is NOT directly proportional to platelet count
• Plasma leakage matters more than platelet number

| Feature | Management

| ------- | ----------

| Fever | Paracetamol

| Thrombocytopenia (no bleed) | Observation

| Bleeding | Platelets ± PRBC

| Shock (DSS) | IV fluids (crystalloids first)

| NSAIDs | ❌ Contraindicated

| Steroids | ❌ No role

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A government plans to outline tobacco control laws. What is the level of prevention here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Primary prevention

Creating tobacco control laws is a method of primary prevention.

Making tobacco control laws targets smokers who are already exposed to risk of smoking, who have not yet developed any disease. This aims to reduce smoking which is essentially a reduction of risk factor which is a primary prevention stratergy.

Primary prevention is defined as an action taken prior to the onset of disease, whose aim is to prevent the disease from occuring. Its target population is healthy individuals. It commonly institutes activities that limit risk exposure or increase the immunity of individuals at risk to prevent a disease from progressing in a susceptible individual. They approaches can be as follows:

* Population (mass) strategy where the target group is the whole population

* A high-risk strategy where the target group is limited to the people who are most at risk of developing a particular disease.

Pearl PF0215: Levels of Prevention

Primordial

Primary

Secondary

Tertiary

Reduce the incidence of disease

Reduce number and impact of complications

Soften the impact of long-term disease and disability, minimize suffering

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A worried mother brought her 6-year-old unimmunized child to the ER with complaints of fever, cough, and shortness of breath. Examination reveals a bull-neck appearance and a pseudomembrane over the tonsils that bleeds when removed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Diphtheria

The given clinical scenario of a 6-year-old suffering from fever, cough, and shortness of breath with a pseudomembrane and bull neck appearance on examination is suggestive of diphtheria.

Diphtheria is caused by the bacteria Corynebacterium diphtheriae which spreads via droplets through the respiratory tract (most important), cutaneous lesions, and fomites.

Respiratory tract diphtheria is characterized by a thick, adherent pseudomembrane (grey or white) on one/both tonsils and adjacent pharynx. Underlying soft tissue oedema and enlarged lymph nodes can cause a bull-neck appearance.

Patients with laryngeal diphtheria are at risk for suffocation because of local soft-tissue oedema and airway obstruction by the diphtheritic membrane.

Management includes antitoxin therapy as a single empirical dose of 20,000-100,000 units and antibiotics. Penicillin G/ Benzylpenicillin is the drug of choice for diphtheria. However, in case of an allergy to the same, Erythromycin is used. Other antibiotics used are clindamycin, rifampin, and tetracycline.

A greyish-white membrane forms over the tonsils in the oropharynx and spreads to the soft palate and posterior pharyngeal wall. The membrane in diphtheria extends beyond the tonsils onto the soft palate and is dirty grey. It is adherent, and its removal leaves a bleeding surface. In the larynx, the diphtheritic membrane may cause airway obstruction.

Cervical lymph nodes, particularly the jugulodigastric, become enlarged and tender, sometimes presenting a bull-neck appearance. The patient is ill and toxaemic, but fever seldom rises above 38°C.

D/D for membrane over tonsil:

* Streptococcus & other pyogenic organisms

* Diphtheria

* Infectious mononucleosis

* Vincent’s angina

* Leukaemia

* Candida

* Agranulocytosis

* Malignancy

* Aphthous ulcer

* Traumatic ulcer

Other options :

Option A: Infectious mononucleosis most commonly presents in adolescents with initial symptoms of fever, sore throat, fatigue, myalgia, and malaise. Pharyngitis is often the most prominent sign, with the enlargement of the tonsils and an exudate resembling that of streptococcal pharyngitis. It can be associated with tender, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy.

Option B: In acute membranous tonsillitis, exudates from the crypts coalesce to form a membrane on the surface of the tonsil that is easily wiped away without any bleeding.

Option D: Oral candidiasis/Oral thrush associated with candida albicans presents as white plaque-like lesions with cheesy exudate on an erythematous mucosa. They are typically painful and can be easily brushed off.
questions.learning: Diphtheria — The given clinical scenario of a 6-year-old suffering from fever, cough, and shortness of breath with a pseudomembrane and bull neck appearance on examination is suggestive of diphtheria.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presented to the OPD with a temperature of 102°F, and a cough with foul-smelling sputum. On examination, clubbing is present. His chest X-ray is given below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lung abscess

The clinical scenario of the patient with fever, cough with foul-smelling sputum, clubbing and a chest X-ray showing air-fluid level is suggestive of a lung abscess.

A lung abscess is caused by microbial infection, leading to necrosis and cavitation of the lung. These could either occur following aspiration or secondary to bronchial obstruction by a foreign body or malignancies, often in the background of immunosuppression. The patients usually present with complaints of fever, cough with sputum, and chest pain. If the lung abscess is putrid, it may produce discoloured and foul-smelling sputum. Chronic cases may present with anaemia, night sweats and fatigue. Patients usually have poor dental hygiene and gingival disease. Examination findings include clubbing, absent gag reflex, and cavernous breath sounds.

Radiological features of lung abscess:

• A lung cavity with an air-fluid level
• The cavity wall is thick and irregular with a surrounding pulmonary infiltrate and acute angle to the chest wall.
• Computed tomography (CT) is more sensitive than chest radiography and is used to detect small cavities

The X-ray image given below shows thick-walled cavities with air-fluid levels on lateral view.

Other options:

Option A: In pneumothorax, the patient will present with a history of breathlessness, and chest X-ray will show deep costophrenic angle, hyperlucency (darker area without lung markings) with inward shifting of the visceral pleural line (sharp white line). In tension pneumothorax, there will be a mediastinal shift to the opposite side.

The image below shows a left pneumothorax with total left lung collapse and tracheal deviation to the right.

Option B: Pneumatoceles are thin-walled cavities in the lung parenchyma that are seen in respiratory tract infections, most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus in children and Pneumocystis jirovecii in immunocompromised adults. Given below is the chest X-ray showing pneumatocele.

Option C: Empyema is the collection of pus in the pleural cavity. It is usually associated with pneumonia but may also develop after thoracic surgery or thoracic trauma. At the margins of the empyema, the pleura can be seen dividing into parietal and visceral layers, the split pleura sign. It is the most sensitive and specific sign on CT and helps distinguish an empyema from a peripheral lung abscess.

The image given below shows a split pleura sign of empyema.
questions.learning: Lung abscess — The clinical scenario of the patient with fever, cough with foul-smelling sputum, clubbing and a chest X-ray showing air-fluid level is suggestive of a lung abscess.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with hypertension. He has a history of renal stones and has experienced a few episodes of renal colic. Which diuretic is the most appropriate to use?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hydrochlorothiazide

Hydrochlorothiazide reduces urinary calcium excretion by increasing distal tubular calcium reabsorption. This helps prevent recurrent calcium renal stones while effectively treating hypertension.

Thiazide

↓

↓ NaCl reabsorption (DCT)

↓

↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption (via Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger)

↓

↓ Urinary Ca²⁺ (hypocalciuria)

↓

↓ Calcium stone formation

Loop diuretics increase calcium excretion, and spironolactone has no role in stone prevention.

| Diuretic | Site | Effect on Ca²⁺ | Stone Risk

| -------- | ---- | -------------- | ----------

| Thiazide | DCT | ↓ urinary Ca²⁺ | ✅ Prevents stones

| Loop (Furosemide) | TAL | ↑ urinary Ca²⁺ | ❌ Promotes stones

| K⁺-sparing | Collecting duct | Neutral | No effect

| Problem | Drug Benefit

| ------- | ------------

| Hypertension | Thiazide lowers BP

| Recurrent Ca stones | ↓ urinary Ca²⁺
questions.learning: Hydrochlorothiazide Hydrochlorothiazide reduces urinary calcium excretion by increasing distal tubular calcium reabsorption. This helps prevent recurrent calcium renal stones while effectively treating hypertension.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not an indication of inducing labor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Placenta previa

Placenta previa is an indication for cesarean delivery, not to induce labor.

Induction of labor is the process of stimulating uterine contractions for vaginal delivery by medical or surgical methods. It is indicated when the benefit to the mother or fetus outweighs the benefit of continuing the pregnancy.

Indications of induction of labor:

*

Gestational hypertension

*

Chronic hypertension

* Pre-eclampsia

*

Post-term pregnancy

*

Abruption placentae

*

IUGR(intra-uterine growth restriction)

*

IUD(Intra-uterine death)

*

Oligohydramnios

Contraindications of induction of labor:

* Contracted pelvis & CPD

* Cord prolapse

* Abnormally implanted placentae

* Previous classical cesarean/ hysterotomy

* Active genital herpes

* Appreciable macrosomia

* Severe hydrocephalus

* Malpresentation

* Pelvic tumor & Ca cervix

* Overdistention or complete transection of the uterus

* Two or more previous low transverse cesarean sections
questions.learning: Placenta previa Placenta previa is an indication for cesarean delivery, not to induce labor. Induction of labor is the process of stimulating uterine contractions for vaginal delivery by medical or surgical methods.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A chronic alcoholic patient presented to the casualty with confusion, ataxia, and painful eye movements. What could be the vitamin deficiency seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin B deficiency

The above clinical history is suggestive of Wernicke encephalopathy, which is caused by vitamin B1 (Thiamine) deficiency.

Vitamin B1/thiamine deficiency leads to following conditions:

1. Wernicke encephalopathy:

• An acute, neuropsychiatric syndrome characterized by nystagmus and ophthalmoplegia, mental status changes (confusion), and unsteadiness of stance and gait.
• Wernicke’s encephalopathy is a medical emergency, and thiamine should be initiated immediately, either intravenously or intramuscularly.
• The current standard of treatment for patients with symptoms of Wernicke's encephalopathy is to give thiamine 100 mg intravenously before administering glucose-containing IV fluids.

2. Korsakoff psychosis:

• Korsakoff syndrome is characterized by a pronounced anterograde and retrograde amnesia along with potential impairment in visuospatial, abstract, and other types of learning.
• Symptoms are similar to that of Wernicke encephalopathy, but also include memory loss and confabulation.
• Permanent in at least a partial form in about 50% of the people affected.

3. Beriberi: It can present with:

• Dry beriberi: sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy, muscle weakness
• Wet beriberi: tachycardia, cardiomegaly, high-output cardiac failure

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 49-year-old man presents with flu-like symptoms and a palmoplantar rash as seen below. On examination, he has epitrochlear lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Secondary syphilis

This clinical scenario of maculopapular rash with flu-like symptoms and epitrochlear lymphadenopathy points to secondary syphilis.

* Secondary syphilis occurs within 6 weeks to 8 weeks of onset of primary chancre.

* It is characterized by the following:

* Onset of systemic manifestations includes symptoms such as malaise, headache, loss of appetite, sore throat

* Generalized symmetric, asymptomatic maculopapular rash on the palms and soles of the feet

* Generalized adenopathy in 50% cases

* Condyloma lata are the classic findings; these are highly contagious exophytic broad excrescences that ulcerate. These are commonly seen on the vulva, perianal area and upper thighs.

Pearl PF1554: Stages of syphilis

* Primary Syphilis:

Chancre- Painless, indurated, usually single

Lymphadenopathy- Painless, unilateral or bilateral, shotty and rubbery inguinal nodes

Dory flop sign- As the chancre is too hard to fold, it will flip over once the prepuce is retracted back.

The chancre self heals in 1-4 months.

Secondary Syphilis:

A & B: Generalized rash(non-itchy, no vesicles, and palm and sole involvement).

This is the most common lesion.

C & D: Condyloma lata.

E: Moth-eaten alopecia (Non-scarring)

F: Mucous patches(Flat erosions on the tongue which can coalesce and form snail track ulcers).These are the most infectious lesions.

G: Pigmentary plaques

H: Psoriasiform syphilitic lesions

Generalized diffuse non-tender lymphadenopathy

Tertiary Syphilis:

Gummatous syphilis(deep punched-out ulcers, with gum-like secretions on the floor)

Pseudo-chancre redux is a gumma occurring at the site of a previously healed ulcer

CVS-Aortitis and aneurysm of the ascending aorta

CNS-General paresis of the insane and tabes dorsalis

Latent Syphilis-Period between secondary and tertiary syphilis, when the patient is asymptomatic clinically, and only serological evidence of infection is present.

* Early latent- Within 1 year of infection

* Late latent- After 1 year of infection

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 34-year-old man presents with chronic pain along the medial side of the elbow that is aggravated by weightlifting. On examination, there is tenderness over the medial epicondyle and a positive reverse Cozen’s test. Which nerve is most likely involved in this condition?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with symptoms of medial epicondylitis, commonly known as "golfer's elbow," which involves inflammation of the common flexor origin. The "reverse Cozen's test" is a diagnostic maneuver used to confirm this condition by having the patient resist wrist flexion, which elicits pain at the medial epicondyle. The ulnar nerve is anatomically the most vulnerable nerve in this region, as it passes immediately posterior to the medial epicondyle within the cubital tunnel. Chronic inflammation or repetitive stress at the medial elbow can lead to ulnar nerve irritation or entrapment (cubital tunnel syndrome). The median nerve (Option A) passes anteriorly and is less likely to be directly involved at this bony prominence. The radial and axillary nerves (Options C and D) are located in the lateral and superior aspects of the limb, respectively. Thus, ulnar neuropathy is the most logical complication
questions.learning: The patient presents with symptoms of medial epicondylitis, commonly known as "golfer's elbow," which involves inflammation of the common flexor origin.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 24-year-old male is brought to the ER after he was hit by a motorbike while he was crossing the road. He sustained injuries over his abdomen with visible bruising. His blood pressure is 88/60 and IV fluids are immediately instituted. A FAST was done and it was positive. Which of the following is the next step in the management of this patient? FAST: (Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Exploratory laparatomy

The clinical vignette describes a case of blunt abdominal injury. In hemodynamically unstable patients with FAST positive, the next step of management is exploratory laparotomy.

Blunt abdominal injury:

Primary assessment (i.e the primary survey) follows the ABCDE pattern: Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability (neurologic status), and Exposure. It is crucial to realize that the absence of abdominal pain or tenderness does not rule out the presence of significant intra-abdominal injury.

The following signs strongly correlate with intraabdominal injury

* Seatbelt sign

* Rebound tenderness

* Hypotension

* Abdominal distension

* Abdominal guarding

* Concomitant femur fracture

The management is as detailed in the protocol given below:
