questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A schizophrenic patient was prescribed drug A after he did not respond to haloperidol and thioridazine. He now presents with excessive salivation, an increase in blood glucose, and hyperlipidemia. What is drug A?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Clozapine

Drug A is clozapine, an atypical antipsychotic used in the treatment of refractory schizophrenia. Excessive salivation, an increase in blood glucose, and hyperlipidemia are side effects of clozapine.

The side effects of clozapine are

• Agranulocytosis
• Weight gain
• Seizures
• Drooling
• Hyperthermia
• Hyperglycemia
• Hypertriglyceridemia

Clozapine causes the highest weight gain among all antipsychotics. Agranulocytosis is a dose-independent side effect and seizures are a dose-dependent side effect.

Other options:

Option A: Ziprasidone - Although it is an atypical antipsychotic, it does not typically cause excessive salivation, significant increases in blood glucose, or hyperlipidemia. The side effects of ziprasidone include orthostatic hypotension, QT prolongation, and minimal weight gain.

Option B: Risperidone - Risperidone is another atypical antipsychotic, but its side effect profile differs from the symptoms presented in the question. Risperidone is more likely to cause hyperprolactinemia, weight gain, sedation, dystonia, and parkinsonism features than the symptoms mentioned.

Option D: Aripiprazole - It is an atypical antipsychotic used to treat schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, but its side effects are typically less severe than those of clozapine. Aripiprazole is more likely to cause nausea, anxiety, and insomnia than the symptoms described.
questions.learning: Clozapine Drug — A is clozapine, an atypical antipsychotic used in the treatment of refractory schizophrenia. Excessive salivation, an increase in blood glucose, and hyperlipidemia are side effects of clozapine.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the nerve supply of the structure marked in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Median nerve

The median nerve supplies the 1st lumbrical which is marked.

There are four lumbrical muscles. They originate from the tendons of the flexor digitorum profundus. It passes to the radial side of the corresponding fingers and is inserted into the dorsal digital expansion of the extensor digitorum.

The action of lumbricals is flexion at the metacarpophalangeal joint and extension of interphalangeal joints.

Lumbricals can be tested only along with interosseous muscle. The examiner will hold the metacarpophalangeal joint of the index finger in hyperextension. Then the patient is asked to extend the proximal interphalangeal joint against resistance. The test is repeated on other fingers as well.

The median nerve innervates the first and second lumbricals. The deep terminal branch of the ulnar nerve innervates the third and the fourth.

The median nerve is formed by the union of the lateral root (C6, 7) from the lateral cord, and the medial root (C8, T1) from the medial cord.

On the hand, it is seen proximal to the flexor retinaculum and lateral to the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis. It also lies between the tendons of flexor carpi radialis and palmaris longus.

Its cutaneous supply in hand is as follows:

• Lateral 2/3rd of the palm by superficial cutaneous branch
• Lateral 3½ fingers (palmar aspect and dorsal aspect of nailbeds) by palmar digital nerves

The muscles supplied by the median nerve in the hand are flexor pollicis brevis, abductor pollicis brevis, and opponens pollicis

The median nerve sometimes gets compressed under the fibro-osseous tunnel beneath the flexor retinaculum leading to carpal tunnel syndrome.

Pen test is used to test the median nerve in the hand. It tests the abductor pollicis brevis muscle.  The hand must remain flat with the palm facing upwards. A pen is held above the palm and the patient is asked to touch the pen with his thumb.
questions.learning: Median nerve — The median nerve supplies the 1st lumbrical which is marked. They originate from the tendons of the flexor digitorum profundus.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: In a child with recurrent upper respiratory tract infections, nasal obstruction, hearing difficulties, and a high-arched palate, what is the most appropriate treatment approach?
questions.explanation: The child is displaying the classic signs of chronic adenoid hypertrophy, often referred to as "adenoid facies" (mouth breathing, high arched palate, nasal obstruction). The "hearing problems" suggest the concurrent development of Otitis Media with Effusion (OME), also known as "glue ear," which occurs due to adenoids blocking the Eustachian tube. The most comprehensive and standard treatment approach is an Adenoidectomy to remove the primary obstruction and Grommet insertion (myringotomy with ventilation tubes) to drain the middle ear fluid and restore hearing. Adenoidectomy alone (Option B) may not immediately resolve the established ear effusion. Tonsillectomy (Option A) is indicated for throat infections but does not address the nasal or ear issues. Myringotomy with grommets alone (Option D) treats the symptoms but fails to remove the underlying cause of Eustachian dysfunction. Therefore, the dual surgical approach is necessary to address both the airway and auditory components of the child's condition simultaneously
questions.learning: The child is displaying the classic signs of chronic adenoid hypertrophy, often referred to as "adenoid facies" (mouth breathing, high arched palate, nasal obstruction).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following provides valuable information about the reproductive behavior of couples within a population?
questions.explanation: The Total Fertility Rate (TFR) is defined as the average number of children a woman would have if she were to pass through her childbearing years (15–49) experiencing the age-specific fertility rates of a given year. It is considered the most comprehensive indicator of the reproductive behavior of couples and the ultimate completed family size in a population. The General Fertility Rate (GFR, Option C) is a simpler measure of the number of births per 1,000 women of reproductive age. The Gross Reproduction Rate (GRR, Option D) measures only the average number of daughters born, while the Net Reproduction Rate (NRR, Option B) also accounts for the mother's survival to reproductive age. TFR is a critical metric for demographic planning; a TFR of 2.1 is known as "replacement-level fertility," the rate at which a population exactly replaces itself from one generation to the next without migration. Most developed nations have a TFR below this level, while many developing nations are working toward this target to stabilize population growth
questions.learning: The Total Fertility Rate (TFR) is defined as the average number of children a woman would have if she were to pass through her childbearing years (15–49) experiencing the age-specific fertility rates of a given year.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: With regards to treatment of thyrotoxicosis of Graves’ disease, consider the following statements: 1. Propylthiouracil is suitable in breastfeeding patients. 2. Large goitre is an indication for thyroidectomy. 3. Radioiodine is recommended for management in pregnancy. 4. Agranulocytosis is a complication associated with carbimazole. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 and 4

Graves’ disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism, resulting from TSH receptor-stimulating autoantibodies. Treatment options include antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine (RAI), and thyroidectomy, with the choice depending on the patient’s age, pregnancy status, goiter size, and comorbidities.

Why is C correct?

• 1. Propylthiouracil is suitable in breastfeeding patients✅: PTU (and low-dose methimazole/carbimazole) can be used during breastfeeding, as only small amounts are secreted into breast milk.
• 2. Large goitre is an indication for thyroidectomy✅: Surgery is preferred in patients with large goiters, compressive symptoms, suspected malignancy, or those unsuitable for RAI.
• 4. Agranulocytosis is a complication associated with carbimazole✅: A rare but serious adverse effect of carbimazole and methimazole; patients should stop the drug and seek medical attention if they develop fever or sore throat.

Incorrect statement:

• 3. Radioiodine is recommended for management in pregnancy❌: Radioiodine is absolutely contraindicated during pregnancy and lactation, as it crosses the placenta and destroys the fetal thyroid gland.

* The proximal row is made up of the talus and calcaneum.

* The distal row from medial to lateral contains, the medial, intermediate, and lateral cuneiforms and the cuboid.

* Medially the navicular bone is interposed between the head of the talus and the cuneiforms.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In the case of drowning, following autopsy, an organism was isolated from the water present in the internal organs. Which of the following is true regarding the isolated organism?
options: Present only in the bone marrow
Dried outer wall contains silica and chlorophyll
It is a microscopic unicellular bacteria
It is not heat and acid resistant
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dried outer wall contains silica and chlorophyll

Diatoms enter pulmonary circulation on antemortem drowning. Diatoms are a class of microscopic unicellular algae (option C) found suspended in most natural waters. Their cell walls are impregnated with silica, chlorophyll, diatomic, and a brown pigment.

The drowning fluid and the particles in it, e.g., diatoms and plankton, pass from the ruptured alveolar wall into lymph channels and pulmonary veins and thus enter the left heart. Only a live body with circulation could transport diatoms from the lungs to the brain, bone marrow, liver and other viscera, and skeletal muscle. They are also found in bile and urine. Bone marrow is highly suitable and reliable.

Isolation of diatoms involves acid digestion of tissue - bone marrow, lung, blood, and kidneys with subsequent centrifugation and the final residue is aspirated and examined for diatoms, which are birefringent, using dark ground illumination. A water sample is collected at the time of body retrieval in a clean container and the similarity of different species of diatom is compared. Diatoms are both heat and acid-resistant (option D).

• The presence of diatoms in the lung, brain, liver, kidneys, and bone marrow (option A) of the femur (best site for analysis) or humerus is suggestive proof of antemortem drowning.
• Since diatoms resist putrefaction, the diatom test may have some value in the examination of decomposed bodies.
• The test is negative in postmortem submersion and in dry drowning.

Diatoms are ubiquitous in the environment and may enter circulation via the gastrointestinal tract (as contaminants of foods)or via the respiratory tract (which are present in the air). Still, the diatom test is considered the gold standard for the diagnosis of typical drowning.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the type of ulcer?
questions.explanation: The ulcer shown is located in the gaiter area (the medial aspect of the lower leg), which is the classic site for a venous ulcer. These ulcers result from chronic venous insufficiency and are typically shallow with irregular, sloping edges. Arterial ulcers (Option A) are usually found on the toes or heels, are very painful, and have "punched-out" edges. Diabetic and Neuropathic ulcers (Options C and D) typically occur on the weight-bearing pressure points of the foot, such as the metatarsal heads or the heel, and are often painless due to associated neuropathy. The location and appearance of the lesion in the image are pathognomonic for venous disease

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Chocolate agar is primarily used for the isolation of which of the following organisms?
questions.explanation: Haemophilus influenzae is a fastidious organism that requires specific growth factors: X (hemin) and V (NAD). These factors are readily available in chocolate agar, which is prepared by heating blood agar to lyse red blood cells and release these nutrients. This organism is a major cause of pediatric meningitis and epiglottitis, particularly strains with the type b capsular polysaccharide. Listeria monocytogenes (Option B) can grow on standard blood agar and does not require lysed cell factors. Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option C) grows best on regular blood agar and requires an enriched carbon dioxide environment rather than heated blood. Escherichia coli (Option D) is a robust gram-negative rod that is typically identified as a lactose fermenter on MacConkey agar rather than requiring specialized chocolate agar. Therefore, chocolate agar is the essential medium for the recovery and diagnosis of H. influenzae in clinical samples
questions.learning: Haemophilus influenzae is a fastidious organism that requires specific growth factors: X (hemin) and V (NAD). These factors are readily available in chocolate agar, which is prepared by heating blood agar to lyse red blood cells and release these nutrients.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug is preferred for management of diabetes in a patient with cardiac and renal failure?
questions.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors (such as empagliflozin and dapagliflozin) are the preferred drugs for managing diabetes in patients with both cardiac and renal failure because of their strong cardioprotective and renoprotective benefits, independent of glucose control. These drugs act on the proximal renal tubules to inhibit sodium–glucose cotransport, leading to glycosuria and natriuresis. This results in osmotic diuresis, reduced preload and afterload, improvement in heart failure outcomes, and slowing of chronic kidney disease progression. Pioglitazone (Option B) is contraindicated in heart failure due to fluid retention and weight gain, which can worsen cardiac function. Metformin (Option C), although first-line for type 2 diabetes, is contraindicated in advanced renal failure because of the risk of lactic acidosis. Sulfonylureas (Option D) increase the risk of prolonged hypoglycemia, especially in renal impairment due to reduced drug clearance. Thus, SGLT2 inhibitors provide the greatest overall benefit with the lowest risk in diabetic patients with concomitant heart failure and chronic kidney disease, making them the drug of choice in this scenario
questions.learning: SGLT2 inhibitors (such as empagliflozin and dapagliflozin) are the preferred drugs for managing diabetes in patients with both cardiac and renal failure because of their strong cardioprotective and renoprotective benefits, independent of glucose control.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following antidiabetic drugs is known to cause unexplained diarrhea?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Metformin

Metformin is known to cause unexplained diarrhoea as its adverse effect.

Metformin is a member of the biguanide class of oral hypoglycemic drugs. It acts by primarily by inhibiting hepatic gluconeogenesis. It activates AMP-dependent protein kinase, leading to stimulation of hepatic fatty acid oxidation, glucose uptake, and nonoxidative glucose metabolism and reduction of lipogenesis and gluconeogenesis. It also appears to act in the gut.

Metformin is accepted as the first-line treatment of type 2 diabetes and is the most commonly used oral agent for this condition. It has been used as a treatment of infertility in women with polycystic ovarian syndrome.

The most common side effects of metformin are gastrointestinal: nausea, indigestion, abdominal cramps, bloating, and diarrhea. The use of metformin is also associated with lower blood levels of vitamin B12.

Most adverse GI effects of metformin abate over time and can be minimized by starting at a low dose and gradually titrating to a target dose over several weeks, as well as by having patients take the drug with meals. Extended-release metformin has decreased GI side effects and can be substituted for immediate-release metformin. Lactic acidosis has been linked with the use of metformin.

Other options:

Option A - Sitagliptin is a dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor. Its use is associated with an increased risk of heart failure.

Option C - Glimepiride belongs to the class of sulfonylureas. It stimulates insulin release by inhibiting the activity of the β cell KATP channel complex. Its side effects include hypoglycemia, and weight gain.

Option D - Pioglitazone is an activator of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPARγ), which is involved in the regulation of genes related to glucose and lipid metabolism. Its adverse effects include increased incidence of heart failure, peripheral edema, weight gain, macular edema, and osteoporosis.
questions.learning: Metformin Metformin is known to cause unexplained diarrhoea as its adverse effect. Metformin is a member of the biguanide class of oral hypoglycemic drugs.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which term most accurately refers to the social conditions or factors that play a role in the development and causation of diseases?
questions.explanation: The term "social pathology" refers specifically to the study of social factors, such as poverty, poor housing, and lack of education, that act as determinants or contributors to the occurrence and spread of diseases in a population. It views these societal ills as "pathological" states that directly impact public health. Sociology (Option A) is the broad scientific study of human society and social behavior but is not limited to disease causation. Society (Option C) and Community (Option D) are general terms describing groups of individuals living together, which provide the context for health but do not define the specific causal factors themselves. In social medicine, identifying social pathology is crucial for implementing primordial and primary prevention strategies that target the root social causes of illness. By addressing these systemic factors, healthcare systems can reduce the overall disease burden beyond purely clinical interventions
questions.learning: The term "social pathology" refers specifically to the study of social factors, such as poverty, poor housing, and lack of education, that act as determinants or contributors to the occurrence and spread of diseases in a population.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following management techniques helps in standardising the methods of performing jobs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Work Sampling

Work sampling is a work measurement and management technique used to analyze how workers spend their time during a job. By making random observations of work activities, it helps identify inefficiencies and standardize the best method of performing a job, thereby improving productivity.

• A. Systems Analysis ✗

• Studies the functioning of an entire system and its components to improve overall efficiency.
• Does not standardize individual job methods.

• B. Decision Making ✗

• Refers to selecting the best course of action from available alternatives.
• It is a managerial function, not a method for standardizing work.

• C. Work Sampling ✓

• Uses random observations to determine how time is utilized.
• Helps establish standard methods, improve workflow, and increase efficiency.

• D. Personnel Management ✗

• Deals with recruitment, training, motivation, and appraisal of employees.
• It is not used to standardize job performance.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: All of the following are major diagnostic criteria for allergic fungal sinusitis except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Positive fungal culture

A positive fungal culture is a minor and not a major diagnostic criterion for allergic fungal rhinosinusitis (AFRS).

The Bent and Kuhn diagnostic criteria for allergic fungal rhinosinusitis include:

Major criteria:

1. Type I hypersensitivity
2. Nasal polyposis
3. Characteristic CT findings
4. Eosinophilic mucin without invasion
5. Positive fungal stain

Minor criteria:

1. Asthma
2. Unilateral disease
3. Bone erosion
4. Fungal cultures
5. Charcot-Leyden crystals
6. Serum eosinophilia

All the major criteria must be met by the patient while the minor criteria serve to support the diagnosis and describe individual patients.

Characteristic CT findings in AFRS include heterogeneous signal intensities within the paranasal sinuses filled with allergic mucin (double density sign), expansion of the paranasal sinuses/nasal cavity, unilateral or asymmetric disease load, and bony erosion.

The treatment of allergic fungal sinusitis includes avoidance of allergen exposure, antihistamines, corticosteroid nasal sprays, aggressive surgical intervention for mucin removal which improves sinus drainage, post-surgery oral corticosteroids, and immunotherapy against fungal and non-fungal allergens.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following should be avoided by a patient of fish odour syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Choline

A fishy odor is seen in trimethylaminuria. Consumption of food products with choline should be avoided in fish odor syndrome.

Fish odor syndrome (trimethylaminuria) is an autosomal recessive disease where TMA(trimethylamine) is not converted to the non-odorous TMAO (TMA-N-oxide) in the liver. This is due to the deficiency of flavin-containing mono oxygenase 3 (FMO3). TMA then builds up in the body and is released in sweat, urine, and breath, giving off a strong odor of rotting fish from the body.

Choline, lecithin, and TMAO are precursors of trimethylamine which are found in food products. These food products are eggs, liver, peanuts, meat, poultry, fish, dairy foods, pasta, and rice.
questions.learning: Choline — A fishy odor is seen in trimethylaminuria. Consumption of food products with choline should be avoided in fish odor syndrome.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with splenic trauma is being treated conservatively. Certain findings on contrast- enhanced CT may indicate the need for further intervention, such as angiography. Which of the following CT scan findings would not usually warrant angiography during conservative management of splenic injury?
questions.explanation: In the conservative (non-operative) management of splenic trauma, angiography and embolization are targeted toward signs of active bleeding or vascular instability. Findings such as a pseudoaneurysm (Option C) and active contrast extravasation (Option D) are high-risk indicators of impending or ongoing hemorrhage and almost always require angiography. Significant hemoperitoneum (Option B) can also be a marker for vascular injury requiring intervention. However, a subcapsular hematoma (Option A), even one covering 40% of the surface area (Class II injury), is a localized, contained collection of blood. As long as the patient remains hemodynamically stable, this finding is traditionally managed with strict bed rest and serial imaging rather than invasive angiography. Therefore, a contained subcapsular hematoma is the "least" concerning vascular finding among the choices provided and does not mandate an immediate angiographic procedure
questions.learning: In the conservative (non-operative) management of splenic trauma, angiography and embolization are targeted toward signs of active bleeding or vascular instability.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Testosterone production is mainly contributed by ______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Leydig cells

Testosterone production is mainly contributed by Leydig cells.

Testosterone is synthesized from cholesterol in the Leydig cells and also from androstenedione secreted by the adrenal cortex.

The diagnosis of testosterone deficiency should be made only on the basis of clinical signs and symptoms consistent with androgen deficiency, and consistently subnormal serum testosterone concentrations at 8 to 10 AM on three occasions.

Testosterone has been used to treat primary or secondary hypogonadism in adult men.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old male with a history of chronic alcoholism presents with high-grade fever and right upper quadrant pain for 5 days. He gives a history of diarrhoea one week ago. On examination, he is febrile and has tender hepatomegaly. Ultrasound abdomen reveals a solitary liver abscess measuring 25 cc in the right lobe. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Medical management

These findings suggest amoebic liver abscess.

Reason:

• Amoebiasis often follows intestinal infection → diarrhoea
• Infection spreads via portal vein to liver
• Right lobe involvement is most common.

The abscess is 25 cc, which is small.

| Abscess size | Treatment

| ------------ | ---------

| Small (<5 cm) | Medical therapy only

| Large (>5 cm) | Percutaneous drainage

| Risk of rupture / left lobe abscess | Drainage

So here → medical treatment first.

Drugs used

1. Metronidazole – kills tissue amoeba

2. Luminal agent (to clear intestinal cysts)

Diloxanide furoate

Paromomycin

❌ A) PAIR

PAIR = Puncture–Aspiration–Injection–Reaspiration

Used for hydatid cyst, not amoebic abscess.

❌ B) Surgery

Rarely required;  Only if rupture or complications.

❌D) Percutaneous drainage

Indicated when:

• Abscess >5 cm
• Left lobe abscess
• Risk of rupture
• No response to drugs

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which artery is most commonly affected in bleeding from the nose?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sphenopalatine artery

The most commonly affected artery in bleeding from the nose is the sphenopalatine artery. It is called the artery of epistaxis because of the same

Arterial supply of lateral wall of nose is given

Sites of epistaxis

* Little’s area: It is the site in 90% of the patients with epistaxis. Four arteries form a vascular plexus called “Kiesselbach’s plexus” in the antero-inferior part of the nasal septum just above the vestibule. It is more prone to finger nail trauma and the drying effect of air.

* Above the level of middle turbinate: The bleeding usually occurs from the anterior and posterior ethmoidalvessels (internal carotid system).

* Below the level of middle turbinate: The bleeding is from the branches of sphenopalatine artery.

* Posterior part of the nasal cavity or the nasopharynx: The blood flows into the pharynx.

* Woodruff’s venous plexus: It is the site of posterior epistaxis in adults and is situated inferior to the posterior end of inferior turbinate.

* Diffuse: It is often indicative of general systemic disorders and blood dyscrasias.

The stepwise management of epistaxis:

* Pinching of the nose with thumb and index finger for about 5 minutes compresses the vessels of the Little’s area.

* Cauterization of the bleeding point with silver nitrate or electrocautery. This is done under topical anesthesia.

* Anterior nasal packing.

* Posterior nasal packing for which patients should be hospitalized.

* Endoscopic cauterization of the bleeding point.

* Elevation of the mucoperichondrial flap and submucosal resection operation- for persistent and recurrent bleeds from the septum.

* Ligation of vessels.

The recommended hierarchy of ligation of vessels in a patient of epistaxis is Sphenopalatine artery → Internal maxillary artery→ External carotid artery → Anterior /posterior ethmoidal artery.

* Transnasal endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation (TESPAL) is done under topical anesthesia with sedation or under general anesthesia. It is effective in controlling refractory posterior bleeds.

* Embolization of the internal maxillary artery by an interventional radiologist, via femoral artery catheterization.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study was conducted on two different samples for comparing variation between DBP and Vitamin D. The mean diastolic blood pressure is 110 with standard deviation 11 and the mean vitamin D level is 18 with standard deviation 3. Which of the following statement is true regarding the coefficient of variation (CV)?
options: CV of DBP is more than Vitamin D
CV of Vitamin D is more than DBP
Both DBP and Vitamin D have equal variability
It cannot be ascertained from information provided
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CV of Vitamin D is more than DBP

The coefficient of variation of vitamin D is more than that of diastolic blood pressure.

The coefficient of variation (CV) is given by the formula:

CV = 100(s/x̅)

where,

CV = Coefficient of variation

s = standard deviation

x̅ = mean

Substituting the data given in the question, in the above formula,

The CV of diastolic blood pressure is:

CV(DBP)= 100(11/110)

= 100(1/10)

= 10%

The CV of vitamin D is

CV(Vitamin D)= 100(3/18)

= 100(1/6)

= 16.67%

Therefore, the CV of vitamin D is more than the CV of DBP.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The number of live births occurring in a year per 1,000 women of reproductive age refers to which demographic indicator?
questions.explanation: The General Fertility Rate (GFR) is a refined measure of fertility that relates the number of live births in a year to the population of women who are biologically capable of bearing children (typically ages 15-44 or 15-49). It is expressed as live births per 1,000 women in the reproductive age group. Gross Reproduction Rate (Option A) measures the number of daughters a woman would have. Total Fertility Rate (Option B) represents the average number of children a woman would have if she completed her reproductive years at current rates. Net Reproduction Rate (Option C) adjusts for maternal mortality. GFR is a more accurate indicator of fertility than the Crude Birth Rate because it uses the specific sub-population at risk of childbearing as the denominator. This makes it a useful tool for comparing fertility levels across different regions or time periods with varying demographic structures
questions.learning: The General Fertility Rate (GFR) is a refined measure of fertility that relates the number of live births in a year to the population of women who are biologically capable of bearing children (typically ages 15-44 or 15-49).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy presents with a small nodule on the sclera as shown in the image below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Dermoid

A dermoid is a likely diagnosis based on the ocular finding and the given image.

An orbital dermoid is a choristoma (a mass of histologically normal tissue in an abnormal location) formed due to subcutaneous displacement of the ectoderm.

It is lined by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium and contains dermal appendages like sweat glands, sebaceous glands, and hair follicles. It can be located anteriorly (superficial) or posteriorly (deep) to the orbital septum.

Clinical features: Superficial dermoid presents in infancy as a painless nodule in the superotemporal part of the orbit whereas deep dermoid presents in adulthood as a gradually protruding eye or acutely as an inflamed orbit. CT imaging would show a well-circumscribed cystic lesion.

Treatment is by excision in toto.

Other options:

Option A: Pterygium is a triangular fibrovascular ingrowth of degenerative bulbar conjunctival tissue on the limbus as a result of chronic exposure to UV rays.

Option B: Pinguecula is an asymptomatic yellow-white mound of degenerated conjunctival stroma seen adjacent to the limbus. It is more common on the nasal limbus.

Option C: Dermolipoma presents in adulthood as a subconjunctival yellowish mass near the outer canthus of the eye. It contains dermal appendages and fatty tissue.
questions.learning: Dermoid — A dermoid is a likely diagnosis based on the ocular finding and the given image. An orbital dermoid is a choristoma (a mass of histologically normal tissue in an abnormal location) formed due to subcutaneous displacement of the ectoderm.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which radioisotope is most commonly used in PET scans?
questions.explanation: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is a functional imaging technique that detects pairs of gamma rays emitted indirectly by a positron-emitting radioisotope. The most "commonly used radioisotope" in PET scans is "Fluorine-18" (18F). It is standardly incorporated into a glucose analogue called "Fludeoxyglucose" (-FDG). Because cancer cells have a high metabolic rate, they take up more FDG than normal cells, making -FDG an excellent tracer for oncology imaging. Carbon-13 (, Option A) is a stable isotope and not used for PET. Carbon-14 (, Option B) is a radioisotope used in carbon dating but not in clinical PET imaging due to its extremely long half-life and low-energy beta emission. is preferred because it has an ideal half-life of 110 minutes, providing enough time for imaging after tracer administration while minimizing the long-term radiation dose to the patient. PET is often combined with CT (PET-CT) to provide both metabolic and anatomical information
questions.learning: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is a functional imaging technique that detects pairs of gamma rays emitted indirectly by a positron-emitting radioisotope.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An 8-year-old boy presented with dark-colored urine as shown below, oliguria, hypertension, and facial puffiness for 3 days. The urine test is positive for albumin. He had a history of throat infection 2 weeks back. On microscopic examination, enlarged, pale glomeruli and epithelial humps are seen. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

The clinical scenario given in the question is suggestive of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN).

Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis(PSGN) is characterized by the sudden onset of gross hematuria, oedema, hypertension, and renal insufficiency. It usually occurs following a throat infection by nephritogenic strains of group A β-hemolytic streptococci. It can also occur after streptococcal skin infection or pyoderma.

The typical patient develops an acute nephritic syndrome following 1 to 2 weeks after antecedent streptococcal pharyngitis or 3 to 6 weeks after streptococcal pyoderma. The pathogenesis involves circulating antibodies elicited by streptococcal antigens reacting with normal glomerular antigens, and complement activation by directly deposited streptococcal antigens causing the immunologic injury.

In this immune complex-mediated APSGN, we see a decrease in the serum complement (C3) level (levels normalise in 6 to 8 weeks), and ASO titer is increased (the titers decrease to low levels within 4 to 6 weeks).

Microscopic Findings in PSGN include

* Light microscopy: Enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli with diffuse mesangial proliferation and leukocyte infiltration.

* Immunofluorescence: Granular deposits of IgG and complement C3 along the glomerular basement membrane(GBM)and in the mesangium.

* Electron microscopy: Electron-dense deposits, or humps, are observed on the epithelial side of the GBM.

Below is the image showing light microscopy findings of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

Other options:

Option A: Post-staphylococcal glomerulonephritis is a kidney condition that occurs after a Staphylococcus infection, leading to immune complex deposition in the glomeruli. It presents with hematuria, proteinuria, oedema, and hypertension, often seen in adults with underlying health conditions.

Option C: Nephrotic syndrome is a kidney disorder characterized by massive proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), hypoalbuminemia, oedema, and hyperlipidemia. It results from increased glomerular permeability, leading to fluid retention and other systemic complications.

Option D: IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease) is the most common type of glomerulonephritis worldwide. It is characterized by recurrent hematuria/ nephritic syndrome and the presence of prominent IgA deposits in the mesangium. Clinically, children and young adults present with gross or microscopic hematuria within 1-2 days of onset of an upper respiratory (synpharyngitic presentation) or gastrointestinal infection.

The below image is an immunofluorescence study of IgA nephropathy showing the characteristic IgA deposition in the mesangial regions.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 68-year-old man suffers severe hypoxic brain injury following a prolonged cardiac arrest and is diagnosed with a persistent vegetative state (PVS). He has no advance directive (living will) and is unable to express his wishes. He remains dependent on mechanical ventilation and artificial life support. After extensive discussions, the treating team and the legally authorized family members decide to withdraw life-sustaining treatment. This scenario is best classified as which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Non-voluntary passive euthanasia

The patient is incapable of making or communicating a decision regarding continuation or withdrawal of treatment because he is in a persistent vegetative state and has no living will.

The decision to withdraw life support is therefore made by the legally authorized surrogate/family (and, depending on jurisdiction, the treating team and court), making it non-voluntary.

Since the intervention involves withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining treatment, it is passive euthanasia.

Thus, the scenario represents: ✅ Non-voluntary passive euthanasia

Classification of euthanasia

1. Voluntary euthanasia

• Patient competently requests euthanasia.
• Decision is made by the patient.

2. Non-voluntary euthanasia

• Patient cannot express a choice (e.g., coma, PVS, severe dementia, neonates).
• Decision is made by surrogates or legal authorities.

3. Involuntary euthanasia

• Performed against the patient's expressed wishes.
• Ethically and legally unacceptable.
questions.learning: Non-voluntary passive euthanasia — The patient is incapable of making or communicating a decision regarding continuation or withdrawal of treatment because he is in a persistent vegetative state and has no living will.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Caspases are involved in which of the following types of programmed cell death?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pyroptosis and Apoptosis

Caspases = cysteine proteases

• Exist as inactive precursors
• Get activated during programmed cell death

Caspases are central mediators of apoptosis, with initiator and executioner caspases driving programmed cell death.

Pyroptosis is a caspase-dependent inflammatory cell death mediated mainly by caspase-1.

Necroptosis and ferroptosis are caspase-independent forms of regulated cell death.

Hence, caspases are involved in apoptosis and pyroptosis.
questions.learning: Pyroptosis and Apoptosis Caspases = cysteine proteases • Exist as inactive precursors • Get activated during programmed cell death Caspases are central mediators of apoptosis, with initiator and executioner caspases driving programmed cell death.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which one of the following drugs can be used for the treatment of cryptorchidism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pulsatile GnRH

The pulsatile dose of GnRH agonist is used in the treatment of cryptorchidism, especially if bilateral.

Pulsatile administration of GnRH agonist increases FSH and LH secretion and is used to treat male and female infertility associated with cryptorchidism.

A non-pulsatile or a continuous dose of GnRH agonist results in suppression and decreased concentrations of gonadotropins (LH and FSH). Hence, it cannot be used in the treatment of male infertility.

Orchidopexy is the treatment of choice for cryptorchidism but medical treatment using GnRH and HCG can be used along with it to increase fertility rates as well.

GnRH is preferred over hCG due to decreased side effects such as increased penile or testicular size and scrotal erythema.

Studies show that the efficacy of GnRH is around 20 % for undescended testis. However, it is useful in the treatment of infertility associated with cryptorchidism.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with muffled heart sounds, hypotension, and elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP). Which specific feature of the JVP waveform is most likely to be observed in this scenario?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of muffled heart sounds, hypotension, and elevated JVP is known as Beck’s triad, which is diagnostic for cardiac tamponade. In tamponade, the heart is compressed by high-pressure pericardial fluid, which severely restricts ventricular filling. On the JVP waveform, the y-descent represents the rapid emptying of the right atrium into the right ventricle during early diastole. Because the high intrapericardial pressure prevents rapid filling, the y-descent is characteristically blunted or absent. The x-descent (Option A) is typically preserved or even accentuated in tamponade. Enlarged C waves (Option C) and absent A waves (Option D) are not characteristic of tamponade; absent A waves are seen in atrial fibrillation. Recognizing these specific waveform nuances is essential for differentiating tamponade from other causes of high JVP like constrictive pericarditis, where a sharp, steep y-descent (Friedreich's sign) is seen. Immediate management of tamponade requires emergency pericardiocentesis to relieve the life-threatening cardiac compression

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 25-year-old male presents with complaints of urethral discharge and dysuria for the past 1 week. The discharge was scant and mucoid for a few days but he reports profuse and yellowish discharge since 2 days. Gram staining of the urethral discharge reveals gram-negative intracellular monocoсci and diplococci. On further questioning, he gives a history of unprotected sexual intercourse 15 days ago. Which one of the following conditions will be your most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gonorrhea

The most likely diagnosis is gonococcal urethritis caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

• Profuse, thick, yellowish/purulent urethral discharge
• Dysuria
• Gram stain shows gram-negative intracellular diplococci (GNID)
• History of unprotected sexual intercourse

The initial scant mucoid discharge can occur before the typical purulent gonococcal discharge becomes prominent.

Why not other options?

• A. Gonorrhea: Correct. N. gonorrhoeae appears as gram-negative intracellular diplococci and causes profuse purulent urethral discharge.
• B. Chancroid: Caused by Haemophilus ducreyi; presents with a painful genital ulcer and tender inguinal lymphadenopathy.
• C. Syphilis: Caused by Treponema pallidum; classically presents with a painless chancre in primary syphilis.
• D. Lymphogranuloma venereum: Caused by Chlamydia trachomatis L1–L3; typically causes a transient painless genital lesion followed by painful inguinal lymphadenopathy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
Which of the following statements is true regarding the instrument shown below?

A. It is used in women not on thromboprophylaxis and planned for caesarean section.
B. It is used in women on thromboprophylaxis and planned for caesarean section.
C. It is removed once the patient starts ambulating.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. A and C

The given image shows a pneumatic compression device. It is used in women who are not on any thromboprophylaxis and planned for cesarean section (statement A) and it is discontinued once the patient starts ambulating post-surgery (statement C).

The device is used because pregnancy and surgery increase the risk of thromboembolism.

According to recent guidelines, patients with no additional risk factors and not placed on any pharmacological thromboprophylaxis are placed on pneumatic compression devices before cesarean delivery. Patients undergoing cesarean delivery with additional risk factors are put on both pneumatic compression devices and pharmacological therapy (UFH or LMWH). UFH-unfractionated heparin, LMWH-lower molecular weight heparin.

Indications of pharmacological thromboprophylaxis:

• Inherited coagulation disorder
• Overweight or obese patient

• Heart failure
• Family history of deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism
questions.learning: A and C — The given image shows a pneumatic compression device. It is used in women who are not on any thromboprophylaxis and planned for cesarean section (statement A) and it is discontinued once the patient starts ambulating post-surgery (statement C).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The following cells seen in the lymph node are indicative of
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Measles

The given slide is pathognomonic for measles. This is a slide of a lymph node biopsy showing a Warthin–Finkeldey giant cell with large grapelike clusters of inclusion bodies.

The lymphoid organs typically have marked follicular hyperplasia, large germinal centers, and randomly distributed multinucleate giant cells (Warthin-Finkeldey cells) which have eosinophilic nuclear and cytoplasmic inclusion bodies.

These are pathognomonic of measles and are also found in the lung and sputum.
questions.learning: Measles — The given slide is pathognomonic for measles. This is a slide of a lymph node biopsy showing a Warthin–Finkeldey giant cell with large grapelike clusters of inclusion bodies.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A girl presents with microcephaly accompanied by a characteristic high-pitched cry. Which chromosomal abnormality is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation: Microcephaly combined with a characteristic high-pitched, "cat-like" cry is the clinical hallmark of Cri-du-chat syndrome. This condition is caused by a congenital chromosomal deletion on the short arm of chromosome 5 (designated as 5p−). Other associated features include hypotonia, moderate to severe intellectual disability, and facial dysmorphisms like epicanthal folds. An isochromosome (Option B) results from the duplication of one chromosome arm and the loss of another, commonly seen in Turner syndrome variants. Trisomy (Option C) refers to an extra chromosome (e.g., Trisomy 21 or 18); while these can cause microcephaly, they do not present with the unique cat-like cry. Mosaicism (Option D) involves a mixture of cell lines and leads to a broad spectrum of phenotypes but is not the primary mechanism of Cri-du-chat. Therefore, the specific combination of small head size and a distinctive cry strongly points to a chromosomal deletion
questions.learning: Microcephaly combined with a characteristic high-pitched, "cat-like" cry is the clinical hallmark of Cri-du-chat syndrome. This condition is caused by a congenital chromosomal deletion on the short arm of chromosome 5 (designated as 5p−).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is seen in MEN 2B syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Medullary thyroid carcinoma

Medullary thyroid carcinoma is seen in multiple endocrine neoplasia 2B (MEN 2B) syndrome.

Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) describes conditions with tumors involving two or more endocrine glands. There are four types - MEN 1-4. They have an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance and can also be sporadic.

MEN type 2 comprises groups of disorders caused by gain-of-function mutations of the RET proto-oncogene at chromosomal locus 10q11.2. There are three variants:

• MEN 2A, also known as MEN 2 (most common type)
• MEN 2B, also known as MEN 3
• MTC only

MEN 2A is also known as Sipple's syndrome. It is characterized by medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), pheochromocytomas, and parathyroid tumors.

In MEN 2B along with MTC and pheochromocytoma, it is associated with other abnormalities such as mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus, medullated corneal nerve fibers, and megacolon. Parathyroid tumors are generally not seen here, in contrast to the MEN 2A type.

MTC presents early and is usually aggressive. MTC is the most common feature, presents as a palpable mass in the neck, and can be associated with pressure symptoms. Ectopic adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) secreted by the tumor can cause Cushing's syndrome.

Pheochromocytoma is frequently bilateral. Palpitations, sweating, and headaches are the features of pheochromocytoma.

Mucosal neuromas can present with bumpy and enlarged lips, tongue, and eyelids. Intestinal autonomic ganglion dysfunction can lead to megacolon and diverticula. Medullated corneal fibers and delayed puberty can also be seen. Marfanoid habitus marked by tall stature, long limbs, arachnodactyly, and joint hypermobility is an associated feature.

Other options:

Cafe au lait spots and optic nerve gliomas are seen in neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1).
questions.learning: Medullary thyroid carcinoma Medullary thyroid carcinoma is seen in multiple endocrine neoplasia 2B (MEN 2B) syndrome. Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) describes conditions with tumors involving two or more endocrine glands.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following IV induction agents is associated with the highest risk of histamine release and cardiovascular depression?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thiopental

• Thiopental → causes histamine release → vasodilation → hypotension
• Effect is exaggerated in hypovolemic or shock patients
• Thiopental, a barbiturate, is most strongly associated with histamine release, leading to vasodilation, hypotension, and myocardial depression.
• It directly depresses cardiac contractility and reduces systemic vascular resistance, making cardiovascular collapse more likely, especially in hypovolemic or cardiac-compromised patients.
• Histamine-mediated effects can also cause bronchospasm and flushing.

Why others are incorrect:

• Option A: Propofol causes hypotension via vasodilation but has minimal histamine release.
• Option C: Ketamine is sympathomimetic, typically increasing heart rate and blood pressure.
• Option D: Etomidate is hemodynamically stable with negligible histamine release.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 22 year old female presents within 8 hours of having sexual intercourse and asking for emergency contraception.She says she doesn't want multiple pills and wants just one pill. What will be your advice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg

The patient asks for emergency contraception and the drug used is Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg.

Levonorgestrel (LNG):

Prostinar tablet contains 0.75 mg LNG. One tablet should be taken within 72 h of unprotected intercourse and another 12 h later. Alternately, two tablets can be taken as a single dose. The failure rate is 1.1%. The tablets can be offered up to 120 h but their efficacy decreases with the longer coital-drug interval. LNG prevents ovulation and causes desynchronization of endometrium through its receptors (luteal phase deficiency). The period may come earlier or be delayed.

Side effects are those of progestogens. The hormone is not teratogenic in case pregnancy does occur but the risk of ectopic pregnancy remains.

Advantages:

* It has no estrogen and its associated side effects

* It can be offered to hypertensive, cardiac, and diabetic women

* It can be offered to a lactating woman

* It can be given as late as 120 hours after the unprotected intercourse

* Single-dose therapy is an advantage

Contraindicated in liver disease, contains lactate, and with an allergy to galactose. The drug is also contraindicated in a woman with a history of thrombophlebitis and migraine.

Pearl PF1657: Hormonal contraceptives

Oral pills:

* Combined oral contraceptive pills (COC)

* Mala D - Levonorgestrel 0.15 mg + Ethinyl estradiol  0.03 mg + Ferrous fumarate

* Mala N - Levonorgestrel 0.15 mg + Ethinyl estradiol  0.03 mg + Ferrous fumarate (Govt. supply, free of cost)

* Progesterone only pills (POP) - suitable for lactating women

* Norethisterone 350 μg

* Norgestrel 75 μg

* Levonorgestrel (LNG) 30 μg

* Once a month or long-acting pills - highly disappointing results

* Quinestrol (long-acting estrogen) + short-acting progesterone

* Gossypol - male pill : Cottonseed derivative and causes azoospermia and severe oligospermia

* Post-coital pills or interceptive

* Levonorgestrel 0.75 mg, 2 doses, 12 hours apart

* Mifepristone 10-600 mg

* Ulipristal 30 mg, within 5 days of intercourse

* Centchroman 60 mg, 2 tablets, within 24 hrs of intercourse

* GnRH agonists

* CuT IUCD, inserted within 5 days

Injectable contraceptives

* Progesterone only injectables

* DMPA 150 mg IM every 3 months

* NET-EN 200 mg IM every 2 months

* Combined injectables

* Cyclofem - DMPA 25 mg + Estradiol cypionate 5 mg

* Mesigyna - NET-EN 50 mg  + Estradiol valerate 5 mg

Subdermal implants

* Norplant I - Levonorgestrel 35 mg

* Norplant II or Jadelle - 2 rods with levonorgestrel 70 mg in each and released at a rate of 50 μg/day

Others

* Hormonal IUCD - Mirena which contains LNG 52 mg with release rate of 20 μg/day

* Orthoevra patch - Norelgestomin + Ethinyl estradiol weekly for 3 weeks, then patch free for 1 week

* Vaginal ring or Nuvaring - Etonogestrel + ethinyl estradiol daily release, use for 3 weeks with withdrawal for 1 week

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child with fused carpal bones comes to your clinic, diagnosed with hand-foot syndrome. What is the gene associated with hand-foot syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. HOXA13

In the given clinical scenario, a child with fused carpal bones is diagnosed with hand-foot syndrome, and the associated gene is HOXA13.

The HOXA13 gene is part of the HOX gene family, which is crucial for the regulation of embryonic development, particularly in the formation of limbs and genital organs. Mutations in the HOXA13 gene can lead to congenital conditions such as hand-foot-genital syndrome (HFGS), which is characterized by abnormalities in the hands, feet, and reproductive organs.

Hand-foot-genital syndrome (HFGS) is a rare congenital disorder caused by mutations in the HOXA13 gene, which is responsible for the development of limbs and genitalia. The condition is characterized by abnormalities in the hands and feet, such as fused or extra fingers and toes, as well as malformations in the genital organs, including underdeveloped or absent structures.

Other symptoms may include urinary tract anomalies and, in some cases, growth retardation. HFGS is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, meaning that a single copy of the mutated gene is sufficient to cause the condition. Early diagnosis and management are essential to address the physical and developmental challenges associated with the syndrome.

Other options:

Option B: The BCL6 gene encodes a protein that acts as a transcriptional repressor, playing a key role in regulating immune system function, particularly in B cells. Mutations in BCL6 are associated with various lymphomas, including diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL).

Option C: FGFR (Fibroblast Growth Factor Receptor) is a family of cell surface receptors involved in regulating cell growth, differentiation, and development. Mutations in FGFR genes are linked to various congenital disorders, including craniosynostosis syndromes and certain cancers.

Option D: COLA1 (Collagen Type I Alpha 1) gene encodes the alpha-1 chain of type I collagen, a major component of connective tissues such as skin, tendons, and bones. Mutations in COLA1 are associated with connective tissue disorders like osteogenesis imperfecta, leading to brittle bones and other skeletal issues.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: All of the following statements regarding Toxoplasma gondii are true, except:
options: Transmitted more in third trimester than first
Releases cysts in stool that are immediately infective
Can be grown in peritoneum of mice
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Releases cysts in stool that are immediately infective

Understanding transmission and life cycle of Toxoplasma gondii is essential.

Correct concepts:

• Transmission risk to fetus increases in the third trimester, but severity is higher when infection occurs in the first trimester
• It can be grown in the peritoneum of mice (used in laboratory diagnosis)
• It infects a wide range of mammals and birds (definitive host: cat)

Incorrect statement:

• Oocysts passed in cat feces are not immediately infective; they require 1–5 days in the environment to sporulate and become infective

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A contact lens user presents with the following clinical picture. He had watering, redness, and foreign body sensation in the eye for the past 2 months. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Giant papillary conjunctivitis

The clinical history of watering, redness, foreign body sensation in a contact lens user, along with the image showing giant papillae in the conjunctiva suggests a probable diagnosis of giant papillary conjunctivitis.

Giant papillary conjunctivitis is a severe form of mechanically induced papillary conjunctivitis. It is most commonly associated with contact lens wear. It can also be associated with ocular prostheses, exposed sutures, and scleral buckles.

The patients usually present with redness, foreign body sensation, increased mucus production, itching, blurring, and loss of contact lens tolerance. On examination, giant papillae are seen on the upper tarsal conjunctiva with hyperemia. Focal apical ulceration and whitish scarring may develop on larger papillae.

Papillae are reddish, flat-topped raised areas that give a red and velvety appearance to the tarsal conjunctiva These are the hyperplasia of the normal vascular system with glomerulus-like bunches of capillaries growing into the epithelium.

The image below shows papillae in the tarsal conjunctiva.

Treatment includes removing the offending cause. Mast cell stabilizers such as sodium cromoglycate, and drugs like azelastine and olopatadine which have combined antihistamine and mast cell stabilizing effects are effective. Steroids can be used for resistant cases.

Other options:

Option A - Trachoma is caused by chlamydia trachomatis. In acute trachoma, sago grain follicles are characteristically seen as shown below.

Option B - Follicular conjunctivitis has follicles which are greyish-white raised areas seen on fornices and palpebral conjunctiva. These are formed due to localized aggregations of lymphocytes in the sub-epithelial adenoid layer. It is most commonly caused by herpes and adenoviruses. The image is shown below.

Option D - In spring catarrh (vernal catarrh), cobblestone appearance is a papillary reaction in the palpebral conjunctiva, ropy discharge, and Maxwell–Lyon sign are present. Horner-Tranta’s spots which are discrete whitish raised dots along the limbus can also be seen. It is more common during summer.

Image showing Horner-Tranta’s spots.

Pearl PF1374: WHO Programme to Control Trachoma: SAFE Strategy

* S—Surgery: Trichiasis and entropion correction surgery → 3° prevention.

* A—Antibiotics: Oral azithromycin, topical 1% tetracycline, topical 1% azithromycin → 2° prevention

* F—Facial hygiene → 1° prevention.

* E—Environmental cleanliness → primordial prevention

Strategy depends on the prevalence of trachoma follicle in children (1–9 yrs)

* Prevalence >10% → SAFE

* 5 to 10% → FE

* < 5% → NO intervention

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Prolactin level is highest during :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 24 hours after delivery

Among the given options, the prolactin level is highest 24 hours after delivery.

The maximum level of prolactin is seen during pregnancy and in the immediate postpartum period. During pregnancy, the secretion is increased reaching a peak at the time of delivery. After delivery, the plasma concentration falls to nonpregnant levels in a few weeks. Suckling produces surges of prolactin release.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 40-year-old man with a history of poor dental hygiene undergoes tooth extraction and develops low-grade fever with a new-onset heart murmur two weeks later. Blood cultures show alpha-hemolytic gram-positive cocci arranged in chains. Which organism is most likely responsible for his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Streptococcus viridans

Streptococcus viridans is a group of gram-positive cocci arranged in chains, often a common cause of infective endocarditis, particularly in cases of subacute bacterial endocarditis.

Streptococcus viridans is a part of the normal flora of the human mouth, throat, and upper respiratory tract. They are alpha-hemolytic, meaning they cause partial hemolysis on blood agar, resulting in a greenish colouration of the agar, hence the name "viridans," which means "green" in Latin.

Although Viridans streptococci are typically susceptible to penicillin, certain strains may exhibit resistance. Therefore, it is crucial that when dealing with endocarditis, the specific strain responsible is identified, and its sensitivity to antibiotics is assessed. This ensures the selection of suitable antibiotics at effective bactericidal levels for treatment.

Other options:

Option A) Staphylococcus aureus is  Beta-hemolytic, and appears in grape-like clusters, not chains. It causes acute endocarditiswith rapid valve destruction, usually in IV drug users.

Option B) Streptococcus pyogenes is also beta-hemolytic, not alpha. It is the Group A Streptococcus causing pharyngitis, impetigo, and rheumatic fever.

Option C) Streptococcus pneumoniae is Alpha-hemolytic but appears as lancet-shaped diplococci, not chains. It is optochin sensitive and causes pneumonia, meningitis, and otitis media.

Pearl PF1994: Modified Duke's criteria for diagnosis of infective endocarditis

Diagnosis of Infective endocarditis is by Duke's Criteria, which requires either:

* Pathologic criteria

* Clinical criteria

If clinical criteria are used, definitive endocarditis is defined by the presence of 2 major or 1 major + 3 minor or 5 minor criteria.

The presence of single pathological criteria is definitive of infective endocarditis.

Note: The diagnosis of endocarditis is rejected if an alternative diagnosis is established either when:

* Symptoms resolve and do not recur with <4 days of antibiotic therapy OR

* If surgery or autopsy yields no pathologic or macroscopic evidence of endocarditis in <4 days of antimicrobial therapy.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Arrange the following bands in the sarcomere from the periphery to the center.

1. Z line
2. M line
3. A band
4. H zone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1,3,4,2

The correct sequence of bands in the sarcomere from the periphery to the centre is: Z line→ A band→ H zone→ M line.

The sarcomere is the contractile unit of the skeletal muscle fibre.

• Z line provides attachment to actin filaments. The area between two adjacent Z lines is called the sarcomere. It is composed of thick and thin filaments:

• Thick filament: Myosin
• Thin filaments: Actin, tropomyosin and troponin

• I band is isotropic to light. It contains only actin filaments.
• A band is anisotropic to light. It contains myosin plus overlapped actin.
• H bands are the lighter areas in the centre of the A band. These are the areas where the the thick filaments do not overlap the thin filaments, when the muscle is relaxed.
• M line is present in the centre of H band. There are slender cross-connections that hold the thick filaments in proper array.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An 11-month-old boy with had a recent urinary tract infection that resolved with antibiotics. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows reveal an empty scrotum on the right side with normal left testis. But a mass was palpable on the right inguinal canal. The USG revealed the right testicle under the subcutaneous fat near the right inguinal canal as shown in the image below. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Orchidopexy

The given clinical vignette is suggestive of cryptorchidism and the next best step is to perform an orchidopexy.

Orchidopexy is the treatment of choice for incompletely palpable unilateral undescended testis. Orchidopexy is usually performed before the boy reaches 12 months of age.

About 4% of boys are born with one or both testes incompletely descended. About two-thirds of these reach the scrotum during the first 3 months of life, but full descent after that is uncommon.

Cryptorchidism is the failure of the descent of the intra-abdominal testes into the scrotal sac.  It is the most common congenital abnormality of the genitourinary tract. The testes can arrest anywhere during descent, and the most common site is the inguinal region.

Phases of testicular descent:

* Transabdominal phase: Testes come to lie in the lower abdomen or pelvis, and this descent is regulated by Mullerian-inhibiting substances.

* Inguinoscrotal phase: Testes descend along the inguinal canal and reach the scrotal sac, and this phase of the descent is regulated by androgen-induced calcitonin gene-related peptide from the genitofemoral nerve.

The exact pathogenesis remains unknown; however, deficiency in gonadotropins and Mullerian-inhibiting substance (MIS) and increased expression of estradiol in the placenta are thought to play a role.

Cryptorchidism is histopathologically characterized by the following:

* Testicular atrophy: thickening of the basement membrane, arrested germ cell development, marked hyalinization

* Tubules showing Sertoli cells but no spermatogenesis

* Increase in the interstitial Leydig cells

It is associated with testicular atrophy and dysfunction, which result in sterility. Cryptorchid testes carry a 3–5-fold higher risk for testicular cancer (usually seminoma). Thus, observation is never the policy. (Option -A)

When the testis is impalpable, ultrasound may be helpful in identifying the intracanalicular testis, while laparoscopy may be needed to differentiate between the abdominal testis and a truly absent testis. Since here testis is made out in the inguinal region, laparoscopy is not the next best line of management(Option-C)

Hence, orchidopexy is usually performed before the boy reaches 12 months of age to avoid the following complications remembered by the mnemonic TESTIS:

*

T- Torsion

*

E- Epididymorchitis

*

S- Sterility

*

T- Trauma (Increased risk)

*

I- Increased risk of inguinal hernia (Most commonly occurring complication)

*

S- Seminoma (Increased risk)

The given flowchart summarizes the treatment protocol for undescended testis.
questions.learning: Orchidopexy — The given clinical vignette is suggestive of cryptorchidism and the next best step is to perform an orchidopexy. Orchidopexy is the treatment of choice for incompletely palpable unilateral undescended testis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a normally distributed dataset with a mean of 82 and a standard deviation of 1.5, what is the range covered by two standard deviations from the mean?
questions.explanation: In a normal distribution, approximately 95.4% of the data falls within two standard deviations (±2 SD) of the mean. To find this range, you must calculate both the upper and lower limits from the mean value provided. Lower Limit = Mean − (2 × SD) = 82 − (2 × 1.5) = 82 − 3 = 79. Upper Limit = Mean + (2 × SD) = 82 + (2 × 1.5) = 82 + 3 = 85. Therefore, the range representing two standard deviations is 79–85. Option B, C, and D are numerically incorrect and do not follow the standard deviation formula for this data set. This statistical principle is fundamental in epidemiology and public health for determining normal reference ranges for clinical data
questions.learning: In a normal distribution, approximately 95.4% of the data falls within two standard deviations (±2 SD) of the mean. To find this range, you must calculate both the upper and lower limits from the mean value provided.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A diabetic patient presented with rhinitis and facial swelling. An intranasal biopsy revealed the presence of broad-based aseptate hyphae with branching at right angle. Evidence of vascular invasion was present. What will be the drug of choice for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Amphotericin B

The above scenario and biopsy findings showing broad-based aseptate hyphae with branching at right angles are suggestive of mucormycosis. The drug of choice for mucormycosis is amphotericin B.

Mucormycosis is an opportunistic mycosis. It is typically seen in patients with diabetes mellitus and/or diabetic ketoacidosis and invades blood vessels.

The rhino-orbital-cerebral is the most common form of mucormycosis. Patients present with rhinitis, eye or facial pain, and facial numbness followed by the onset of conjunctival suffusion and swelling along with blurry vision.

Diagnosis is made by biopsy with histopathologic examination. The biopsy shows characteristic wide, ribbon-like aseptate hyphal elements that branch at right angles.

The below image shows biopsy findings seen in mucormycosis.

Treatment of the infection includes 4 steps:

1. Initiation of therapy (amphotericin B) as early as possible.
2. Surgical debridement.
3. Reversal of underlying conditions and risk factors.
4. Treatment of underlying malignancy if present.

Amphotericin B binds to ergosterol in the fungal membrane and forms pores or channels in the fungal cell membrane. This allows the leakage of cytosolic molecules and ions, leading to a loss of membrane integrity.

It is a broad-spectrum antifungal that can be used against Candida albicans, Cryptococcus neoformans, Blastomyces dermatitidis, Histoplasma capsulatum, Sporothrix schenckii, Coccidioides immitis, Aspergillus.

Amphotericin B also has antiprotozoal action along with antifungal properties and is effective against Leishmania.

Adverse effects of amphotericin B:

• Infusion-related fever and chills
• Azotemia/nephrotoxicity- all lipid formulations of amphotericin B are less nephrotoxic than conventional amphotericin B
• Renal tubular acidosis
• Renal wasting of potassium and magnesium
• Hypochromic normocytic anemia- due to decreased erythropoietin production from the kidney

Note: Mucormycosis recently emerged as an important superinfection in COVID-19 patients, especially in India. The surge in cases is most likely due to diabetes mellitus and steroid use.

Other options:

Option A: Fluconazole is used for the treatment of candidiasis and cryptococcosis.

Option C: Ketoconazole is used for both dermatophytosis and deep mycosis, but it has been replaced by itraconazole.

Option D: Griseofulvin is used for dermatophytosis. It is effective against the mycotic disease of the skin, hair, and nails due to Microsporum, Trichophyton, and Epidermophyton.
questions.learning: Amphotericin B — The above scenario and biopsy findings showing broad-based aseptate hyphae with branching at right angles are suggestive of mucormycosis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following indicators stand consolidated in Physical Quality of Life Index (PQLI)? 1. Infant mortality 2. Life expectancy at age one 3. Per capita income 4. Literacy Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 and 4

The Physical Quality of Life Index (PQLI) was developed by Morris D. Morris (1979) to measure the physical well-being of a population, independent of economic indicators. It is calculated using three indicators:

• Infant Mortality Rate (IMR)
• Life Expectancy at Age One
• Basic Literacy Rate

Per capita income is NOT included in PQLI.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The three most important enzymes regulating the Citric Acid Cycle include all of the following, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Aconitase

The three rate-limiting enzymes/steps in the TCA cycle are specifically listed as:

1) Citrate synthase,

2) α-KG DH (alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase), and

3) Isocitrate Dehydrogenase. Aconitase catalyzes the conversion of citrate to isocitrate but is not mentioned among the key regulatory enzymes of the cycle.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A postmenopausal woman with a long-standing history of uterine fibroids presents with lower abdominal pain for the past four months. Radiological evaluation shows characteristic degenerative changes within the fibroids. Based on these findings, which type of degeneration is most likely present?
questions.explanation: Uterine leiomyomas (fibroids) can undergo several types of degeneration depending on changes in blood supply or the patient’s physiological state. "Calcific degeneration" is the most common form of degeneration seen in postmenopausal women. As the fibroid becomes ischemic due to postmenopausal circulatory changes, calcium carbonate and phosphate are deposited within the tumor tissue. On radiological imaging, this appears as characteristic "popcorn calcifications" within the pelvis, as seen in the provided X-ray. Hyaline degeneration (Option B) is the most common type overall but typically occurs during the reproductive years. Fatty degeneration (Option A) and cystic degeneration (Option D) are less common and present with different radiographic textures. Calcific degeneration is usually asymptomatic, although it can occasionally cause localized pain if the fibroid is large or if there is torsion. Identifying these distinct calcification patterns on imaging allows for the correct diagnosis of fibroids in the postmenopausal period, avoiding confusion with other pelvic masses or malignancies
questions.learning: Uterine leiomyomas (fibroids) can undergo several types of degeneration depending on changes in blood supply or the patient’s physiological state. "Calcific degeneration" is the most common form of degeneration seen in postmenopausal women.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A two-month-old infant presents with difficulty feeding, vomiting, and lethargy. Laboratory tests reveal hyperammonemia and high levels of orotic acid in the urine. Which of the following is the most probable enzyme deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency

The clinical scenario of a child with recurrent vomiting and failure to thrive, hyperammonemia and increased urinary excretion of orotic acid is indicative of Type 2 Hyperammonemia or ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency (OTC deficiency).

Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency leads to lethargy progressing to coma, protein aversion, intellectual disability, and hyperammonemia.

Type II hyperammonemia results from a deficiency of ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC). In the urea cycle, the enzyme ornithine transcarbamoylase catalyses the condensation of carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine to form citrulline. The deficiency of this enzyme leads to the accumulation of carbamoyl phosphate, which is channelled to pyrimidine synthesis, leading to increased excretion of orotic acid.

Clinical symptoms include vomiting, irritability and severe mental retardation. Mild forms show episodes of hyperammonemia, manifested by vomiting and neurologic abnormalities (e.g., ataxia, mental confusion, agitation). These episodes usually occur after ingestion of a high-protein diet or as a result of a catabolic state such as infection.

The laboratory findings during the acute attack are hyperammonemia accompanied by marked elevations of plasma concentrations of glutamine and alanine with low levels of citrulline and arginine. The blood level of urea is usually low. There is a marked increase in the urinary excretion of orotic acid. Diagnosis is confirmed by gene analysis.

Management includes treatment of acute hyperammonemia attacks. For enteral use, citrulline is used in place of arginine in patients with OTC deficiency. Liver transplantation is a successful treatment for patients with severe OTC deficiency. Long-term treatment consists of a protein-restricted diet.

Other options:

Option A: In Type 1 Hyperammonemia (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency), the symptoms appear during the first few days or even hours of life, and the baby presents with the signs and symptoms of hyperammonemia (refusal to eat, vomiting, lethargy, convulsion, and coma). Increased intracranial pressure is frequent. The child will show low levels of citrulline and orotic acid in the blood.

Option C: Argininosuccinate lyase enzyme splits argininosuccinate into arginine and fumarate. When deficient, argininosuccinate accumulates, leading to argininosuccinic aciduria, often presenting with brittle hair (trichorrhexis nodosa).

Option D: Orotic aciduria is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in uridine monophosphate (UMP) synthase. This enzyme contains two activities, orotate phosphoribosyltransferase and orotidine decarboxylase. The lack of pyrimidines impairs nucleic acid synthesis needed for haematopoiesis, would result in megaloblastic anaemia.
questions.learning: Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency — The clinical scenario of a child with recurrent vomiting and failure to thrive, hyperammonemia and increased urinary excretion of orotic acid is indicative of Type 2 Hyperammonemia or ornithine transcarbamylase…

questions.text: A patient is scheduled for laparoscopic surgery under general anaesthesia in a day care setting. Which of the following factors makes him unsuitable for day care surgery?
options: Home is 45 minutes drive away from the hospital
The surgical procedure is expected to last slightly over 1 hour
No attendant is available at home to care for the patient postoperatively
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. No attendant is available at home to care for the patient postoperatively

A mandatory requirement for day-care surgery is the presence of a responsible adult caregiver at home after discharge. Lack of an attendant is an absolute contraindication, making option C the correct factor that makes this patient unsuitable for ambulatory surgery.
