questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with sudden-onset right-sided hemiparesis. His blood pressure is 200/100 mmHg, and NCCT of the head shows intracerebral hemorrhage. Which of the following interventions should NOT be performed in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation: In any patient presenting with sudden hemiparesis where a Non-Contrast CT (NCCT) has confirmed a brain bleed (intracerebral hemorrhage), Thrombolysis is absolutely contraindicated. Thrombolytic agents like alteplase are only used for ischemic strokes; administering them during a hemorrhage would catastrophically worsen the bleeding. Blood pressure control (Option B) is essential to prevent hematoma expansion, typically targeting a systolic pressure around 140 mmHg. Edema management (Option C), using osmotic agents like mannitol, is necessary if there are signs of increased intracranial pressure. Elective hyperventilation (Option D) may be used briefly as a temporary measure to lower intracranial pressure by causing cerebral vasoconstriction if the patient deteriorates. The management of hemorrhagic stroke focuses on stabilization, neurosurgical consultation if indicated, and intensive monitoring to prevent secondary brain injury. Differentiating between ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke via imaging is the most critical first step in the entire stroke management algorithm
questions.learning: In any patient presenting with sudden hemiparesis where a Non-Contrast CT (NCCT) has confirmed a brain bleed (intracerebral hemorrhage), Thrombolysis is absolutely contraindicated.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which structures are most commonly affected in Takayasu arteritis?
questions.explanation: Takayasu arteritis, also known as "pulseless disease," is a chronic, large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis that primarily involves the aorta and its major branches. It most commonly affects the arch of the aorta and the vessels arising from it, such as the subclavian and carotid arteries. This leads to the characteristic clinical finding of absent or diminished peripheral pulses. While the abdominal aorta (Option C) and pulmonary arteries (Option A) can be involved, they are less common primary sites compared to the aortic arch. Coronary artery involvement (Option B) can occur as a late complication but is not the most frequent site of initial pathology. The disease typically affects young women under age 40. Management involves systemic corticosteroids and immunosuppressants to control inflammation and prevent further arterial narrowing or aneurysm formation
questions.learning: Takayasu arteritis, also known as "pulseless disease," is a chronic, large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis that primarily involves the aorta and its major branches.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is not a heme breakdown product?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ALA

Aminolevulinic acid (ALA) is not a product of heme breakdown; rather it is an intermediate in the synthesis of heme molecules.

The process of heme breakdown occurs over a series of reactions. In the reticuloendothelial system of the liver, spleen and bone marrow, heme is degraded by microsomal heme oxygenase. It requires NADPH and cytochrome c. In this process, the alpha methenyl bridge of the heme molecule is liberated as carbon monoxide. The Fe+ liberated is oxidized to Fe3+++ and taken up by transferrin.

The linear tetrapyrrole formed is biliverdin (green pigment), which is further reduced to bilirubin (red-yellow pigment) by an NADPH-dependent biliverdin reductase. The bilirubin is transported in the plasma bound to albumin and is taken up by the liver, where it is conjugated with glucuronic acid to make it water-soluble, which is finally excreted in the bile.

The intestinal bacteria deconjugate the bilirubin, which is reduced to urobilinogen. It is further reduced to stercobilinogen, which is excreted through feces.
questions.learning: ALA Aminolevulinic acid (ALA) is not a product of heme breakdown; rather it is an intermediate in the synthesis of heme molecules. The process of heme breakdown occurs over a series of reactions.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following has autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cystic fibrosis

Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, which encodes a chloride channel involved in fluid and electrolyte transport across epithelial cells.

Defective CFTR leads to thick, viscous secretions in multiple organs, resulting in:

• Chronic lung infections
• Pancreatic insufficiency and malabsorption
• Meconium ileus in newborns

Why other options are incorrect:

• Achondroplasia: Autosomal dominant (FGFR3 mutation).
• Huntington’s disease: Autosomal dominant (trinucleotide repeat disorder).
• Familial hypercholesterolemia: Typically autosomal dominant (LDL receptor defect).
questions.learning: Cystic fibrosis Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, which encodes a chloride channel involved in fluid and electrolyte transport across epithelial cells.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The most common cause of Cushing's disease in a 60-year-old male is ______ ACTH - Adrenocorticotropic hormone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pitutary microadenoma

The most common cause of Cushing's disease in a 60-year-old male is pituitary microadenoma.

Cortisol production is increased by adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) released from the pituitary gland in the brain. Hypercortisolemia (cortisol overproduction) causes Cushing syndrome, most often when a pituitary adenoma (a benign tumor) produces an excess of ACTH, resulting in Cushing's disease. The increased ACTH causes increased cortisol production, about three times more than the normal level.

The illustration given below shows the clinical features of Cushing syndrome.

Administration of large doses of dexamethasone can be used to differentiate between ACTH-dependent and ACTH-independent Cushing’s syndrome.

The illustration given below shows the diagnostic algorithm to determine the cause of Cushing syndrome.

In normal physiologic states, the ACTH levels are higher in the early morning as compared to the rest of the day. However, they are not as high as those in Cushing's disease.

Pearl PF0133: Causes of Cushing's Syndrome

Iatrogenic (Most common cause)

* Exogenous administration of glucocorticoids

Endogenous Causes

* ACTH Dependent – (90 % of endogenous causes)

* Cushing’s disease – ACTH-producing pituitary adenoma

* Ectopic ACTH syndrome – Due to ACTH secretion by

* Bronchial or pancreatic carcinoid tumors

* Small-cell lung cancer

* Medullary thyroid carcinoma

* Pheochromocytoma

* ACTH Independent – (10% )

* Adrenocortical adenoma

* Adrenocortical carcinoma

Rare causes

* Macronodular adrenal hyperplasia

* Primary pigmented nodular adrenal disease

* McCune – Albright syndrome

Pearl PF0134: Screening/Confirmatory Test for Diagnosing Cushing's Syndrome

* 24-h urinary free cortisol excretion increased above normal (3x)

* Dexamethasone overnight test

* Plasma cortisol >50 nmol/L at 8–9 a.m. after 1 mg dexamethasone at 11 p.m.

* Midnight plasma cortisol >130 nmol/L

* Midnight salivary cortisol >5 nmol/L

* Low dose Dexamethasone test – Best initial test

* Plasma cortisol >50 nmol/L after 0.5 mg dexamethasone q6h for 2 days

If a number of these tests are positive then a diagnosis of Cushing’s syndrome is confirmed.
questions.learning: Pitutary microadenoma — The most common cause of Cushing's disease in a 60-year-old male is pituitary microadenoma. Cortisol production is increased by adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) released from the pituitary gland in the brain.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A posterior staphyloma was noted on indirect ophthalmoscopy. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pathological myopia

Posterior staphyloma is a hallmark of pathological myopia.

Pathological/degenerative myopia is characterized by progressive anteroposterior elongation of the scleral envelope associated with secondary ocular changes due to the mechanical stretching of the involved tissues. The following changes are seen:

* A pale tessellated (tigroid) appearance of the fundus is seen as the choroid becomes visible due to diffuse attenuation of the RPE

* Temporal myopic crescent

* Focal chorioretinal atrophy

* Anomalous optic nerve head with tilted conformation

* Acquired optic disc pit formation

* Lattice degeneration

* Cystoid degeneration

* Lacquer cracks are fine, irregular yellow lines crisscrossing at the posterior pole due to ruptures in the Bruch membrane.

* Subretinal coin hemorrhages develop from lacquer cracks.

* Fuchs spot: It is a raised, circular, pigmented scar at the macula that develops after absorption of subretinal hemorrhage.

* Posterior staphyloma occurs due to progressive thinning and outpouching of the posterior sclera, visible on indirect ophthalmoscopy.

Staphyloma is an abnormal protrusion of the uveal tissue through a weak and thin portion of the cornea or sclera. Posterior staphyloma presents as a scleral and choroidal bulge behind the equator. Ophthalmoscopy reveals an excavated area with dipping retinal vessels. It is lined internally by uveal tissue and externally by weak cornea or sclera.

Types of Staphyloma:

* Anterior staphyloma: It is characterized by ectasia of the pseudo-cornea, which occurs after the total sloughing of the cornea. It is lined internally by the iris and externally by the newly formed epithelium.

* Intercalary staphyloma: This is located at the limbus and is lined by the root of the iris and the anterior-most part of the ciliary body

* Ciliary staphyloma: It is characterized by ectasia of weak sclera lined by the ciliary body. This affects the ciliary zone, which includes the region up to 8 mm behind the limbus.

* Equatorial staphyloma: This occurs at the equatorial region up to 14 mm behind the limbus of the eye.

* Posterior staphyloma: This affects the posterior pole of the eye.

Note :
The most common cause of anterior staphyloma is a sloughing corneal ulcer.
The most common cause of posterior staphyloma is degenerative high axial myopia.

Other options:

Option B: Hypermetropia is a refractive error of the eye in which parallel rays of light from infinity focus behind the retina when accommodation is at rest. Fundoscopy findings in hypermetropia include shot silk appearance (retina may shine due to the greater brilliance of light reflections) and pseudopapillitis.

Option C: Scleritis refers to an inflammation of the sclera proper. It usually occurs in females more than males. It is frequently associated with an underlying systemic inflammatory condition. The patient presents with moderate to severe pain, redness, lacrimation, photophobia, and diminution of vision.

Option D: Corneal ulcer is an anterior segment lesion of the cornea, while posterior staphyloma is a fundus finding due to pathological myopia.
questions.learning: Pathological myopia Posterior staphyloma is a hallmark of pathological myopia. Pathological/degenerative myopia is characterized by progressive anteroposterior elongation of the scleral envelope associated with secondary ocular changes due to the…

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following lobes of the prostate forms the uvula vesicae?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Median

The median lobe of the prostate forms the uvula vesicae.

Uvula vesicae is an elevation in the mucous membrane of the urinary bladder, behind the internal urethral orifice. It is often enlarged in benign prostatic hypertrophy.
questions.learning: Median — The median lobe of the prostate forms the uvula vesicae. Uvula vesicae is an elevation in the mucous membrane of the urinary bladder, behind the internal urethral orifice.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following techniques is used to detect DNA-protein interaction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. DNA footprinting

The technique used to detect DNA-protein interaction is DNA footprinting.

The parts of DNA that are protein-bound (Eg: RNA polymerase bound to the promoter region of DNA) are resistant to digestion by nuclease enzymes. Since the nucleases are unable to cleave the protein-bound regions of DNA, when the cleaved DNA fragments are run on polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis, there are missing bands indicating, protected sites of protein-bound DNA. These missing areas represent the footprint of the protected DNA-protein complexes. Hence DNA footprinting technique helps to identify the specific binding site of protein on a DNA sequence.

The image below illustrates the DNA footprinting technique.

Other options:

Option B: DNA fingerprinting uses RFLPs (restriction fragment length polymorphism) or repeat sequence DNA to identify a person's unique pattern of DNA. Polymorphisms are inherited differences found among individuals. with this technique, individuals can be differentiated by variations in their DNA sequence, using restriction endonucleases followed by gel electrophoresis, to visualize RFLPs. DNA fingerprinting is used for forensic analysis of crime scenes, and for paternity testing.

Option C: ELISA uses antibodies linked to certain enzymes to detect certain antigens present in the sample.

Option D: Northern blotting technique can be used to detect RNA. Here, the mixture of mRNA molecules is separated by electrophoresis and then transferred to a nitrocellulose membrane and hybridized with radiolabeled probes.
questions.learning: DNA footprinting — The technique used to detect DNA-protein interaction is DNA footprinting. The parts of DNA that are protein-bound (Eg: RNA polymerase bound to the promoter region of DNA) are resistant to digestion by nuclease enzymes.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: You are a doctor in a village. A 1 yr old child who is not taking feeds, presents with fever and cough for 2 days. On examination, he is calm, with a respiratory rate of 51 breaths/min, and stridor is present. According to IMNCI (Integrated management of neonatal and childhood illnesses), how is he classified?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Severe Pneumonia

This child is classified as having a very severe disease/severe pneumonia.

Signs of very severe disease are:

* Stridor in a calm child

* Not able to drink

* Convulsions

* Abnormally sleepy or difficult to wake

* Severe malnutrition.

In any of these cases, an urgent referral is very important.
questions.learning: Severe Pneumonia — This child is classified as having a very severe disease/severe pneumonia. Signs of very severe disease are: * Stridor in a calm child * Not able to drink * Convulsions * Abnormally sleepy or difficult to wake * Severe malnutrition.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following statements best describes the Fincham’s test result in a patient with lenticular halo?
options: Halos remain intact but brightness is reduced
Halos are broken and revolve as the slit moves
No halos are visible through the stenopaic slit
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Halos are broken and revolve as the slit moves

In lenticular halo (e.g., early cataract), Fincham’s test with a stenopaic slit breaks the halo into segments that move with the slit, confirming a lenticular origin.

A fits corneal edema where halos persist.

B is incorrect—lenticular halos don’t disappear.

D suggests absence of halos, not diagnostic.
questions.learning: Halos are broken and revolve as the slit moves — In lenticular halo (e.g., early cataract), Fincham’s test with a stenopaic slit breaks the halo into segments that move with the slit, confirming a lenticular origin.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An elderly patient presents with knee pain, and X-ray findings reveal arthritic changes. Synovial fluid analysis shows rhomboid-shaped crystals that are positively birefringent under polarized light. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pseudo gout

Rhomboid-shaped crystals with positive birefringence on polarized microscopy are diagnostic of pseudogout, caused by calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) deposition. It commonly affects elderly patients, especially the knee, and may mimic osteoarthritis or acute gout flares.

X-ray may show chondrocalcinosis, a hallmark of CPPD crystal deposition.

| Feature | Gout | Pseudogout

| ------- | ---- | ----------

| Crystal | Monosodium urate | Calcium pyrophosphate

| Shape | Needle-shaped | Rhomboid-shaped

| Birefringence | Negative | Positive

| Color under polarized light | Yellow when parallel | Blue when parallel

| Common joint | 1st MTP (podagra) | Knee

Deposition of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals in cartilage

Leads to:

• Cartilage calcification → chondrocalcinosis
• Inflammatory response → acute arthritis

| Feature | Pseudogout | Gout | Septic Arthritis | RA

| ------- | ---------- | ---- | ---------------- | ---

| Age | Elderly | Middle-aged | Any | Middle-aged

| Joint | Knee | 1st MTP | Any | Small joints

| Crystals | CPPD | Urate | None | None

| Shape | Rhomboid | Needle | — | —

| Birefringence | Positive | Negative | — | —

| X-ray | Chondrocalcinosis | Erosions | Joint destruction | Joint space narrowing
questions.learning: Pseudo gout Rhomboid-shaped crystals with positive birefringence on polarized microscopy are diagnostic of pseudogout, caused by calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) deposition.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The given image is of a patient in whom mastoidectomy is done. Identify the lateral semi-circular canal:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. B

The structure marked as ‘B’ in the given image represents the lateral (horizontal) semi-circular canal. The tympanic (horizontal) segment of the facial nerve lies below the lateral horizontal semicircular canal.

Other markings represent:

A: Superior semicircular canal (SSC)

C: Posterior semicircular canal (PSC)

D: Incus

The semicircular canals are positioned in the superior part of the mastoid region. These canals are situated adjacent to the middle ear, with the lateral semicircular canal being the nearest to the middle ear. The superior and posterior canals share a common crescent-shaped space in between. The one that lies in close proximity to the lateral semicircular canal is the posterior semicircular canal.

The semicircular canals are part of the bony labyrinth. They house the semicircular ducts which are the end organs for angular momentum. They are 3 semicircular canals, lateral (horizontal), superior (anterior), and posterior. They lie in planes at right angles to one another.

Stimulation of semicircular canals produces nystagmus. The nystagmus is rotatory from the superior canal, horizontal from the horizontal canal, and vertical from the posterior canal.
questions.learning: B The structure marked as ‘B’ in the given image represents the lateral (horizontal) semi-circular canal. The tympanic (horizontal) segment of the facial nerve lies below the lateral horizontal semicircular canal.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following are correct regarding puerperal blues? I. Its incidence is around 50%. II. There is no specific metabolic or endocrine derangement. III. Treatment is reassurance and psychological support. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. I, II and III

Puerperal blues (postpartum blues or “baby blues”) is the most common postpartum mood disorder, affecting approximately 50–80% of women after delivery. It is a self-limiting, transient emotional disturbance that usually begins 2–3 days postpartum, peaks around day 5, and resolves spontaneously within 10–14 days without specific medical treatment. All the given statements are correct:

• I. Its incidence is around 50%: Puerperal blues affect 50–80% of postpartum women, making it the most common postpartum psychiatric condition.
• II. There is no specific metabolic or endocrine derangement: Although rapid hormonal changes after delivery are thought to contribute, no specific metabolic or endocrine abnormality has been identified.
• III. Treatment is reassurance and psychological support: Puerperal blues are self-limiting and usually require only:

• Reassurance
• Emotional support
• Adequate rest
• Family support
• Follow-up to ensure symptoms do not progress
questions.learning: I, II and III Puerperal blues (postpartum blues or “baby blues”) is the most common postpartum mood disorder, affecting approximately 50–80% of women after delivery.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient is brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. On examination, the patient is in shock with hypotension. An extended focused assessment with sonography for trauma (eFAST) is negative, the chest X-ray is normal, and the ECG shows no abnormalities. Oxygen saturation is 93%, with hypotension and tachycardia noted on vital signs. Based on these findings, what type of shock is most likely?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation following a road traffic accident reveals a classic diagnostic triad: hypotension ( mmHg), bradycardia (pulse rate ), and a lack of significant findings on e-FAST, X-ray, or ECG. In trauma, the combination of hypotension with bradycardia is pathognomonic for neurogenic shock, which results from a sudden loss of sympathetic vasomotor tone, typically following a high-level spinal cord injury. Hemorrhagic shock (Option B) is the most common type in trauma but characteristically presents with tachycardia as a compensatory response to volume loss. Septic shock (Option A) usually involves fever, a source of infection, and tachycardia. Cardiogenic shock (Option C) would typically show abnormalities on ECG or bedside ultrasound (e.g., poor contractility or tamponade), which are absent here. The relative bradycardia distinguishes neurogenic shock from other forms of distributive or hypovolemic shock where heart rate typically rises to maintain cardiac output
questions.learning: The clinical presentation following a road traffic accident reveals a classic diagnostic triad: hypotension ( mmHg), bradycardia (pulse rate ), and a lack of significant findings on e-FAST, X-ray, or ECG.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements about Lafutidine is incorrect? 1. Increases gastric mucosal blood flow 2. Acts as an H₂ receptor antagonist 3. Decreases nitric oxide production 4. Increases somatostatin secretion+
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3 only

Lafutidine is a second-generation H₂ receptor antagonist used for:

• Peptic ulcer disease
• GERD
• Gastritis
• Stress ulcer prophylaxis

What makes it special is that it has both acid-suppressing and mucosal-protective actions.

Correct answer is C because lafutidine is an H₂ receptor antagonist that enhances mucosal defense by increasing gastric mucosal blood flow and stimulating protective mediators. It is known to promote nitric oxide–mediated mucosal protection rather than decrease nitric oxide production. Protective effects include:

| Effect | Mechanism

| ------ | ---------

| ↑ Gastric mucosal blood flow | via nitric oxide

| ↑ Prostaglandin synthesis | mucosal protection

| ↑ Somatostatin secretion | inhibits gastrin

| ↑ Mucus secretion | barrier protection

Thus it protects gastric mucosa beyond acid suppression.
questions.learning: 3 only Lafutidine is a second-generation H₂ receptor antagonist used for: • Peptic ulcer disease • GERD • Gastritis • Stress ulcer prophylaxis What makes it special is that it has both acid-suppressing and mucosal-protective actions.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act in India, what is the minimum age at which a woman can undergo MTP?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 16 years

Under the MTP Act, India, a woman aged 18 years or above can give valid consent for medical termination of pregnancy on her own.

For women below 18 years, guardian consent is mandatory.

Min age for MTP: There is no min age of MTP as long as consent is obtained from legal guardian in females below 18 years.
questions.learning: 16 years Under the MTP Act, India, a woman aged 18 years or above can give valid consent for medical termination of pregnancy on her own. For women below 18 years, guardian consent is mandatory.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: During an autopsy of a 65-year-old man who died from myocardial infarction, which staining methods are commonly employed to demonstrate infarcted areas of the heart muscle?
questions.explanation: During a forensic or clinical autopsy, detecting an early myocardial infarction (typically 2-12 hours old) can be challenging through gross examination alone. Triphenyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC) is the macroscopic staining technique used to highlight areas of infarction. TTC reacts with lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) in viable myocardium to produce a deep red color. In infarcted tissue, where enzymes have leaked out, the area remains pale or unstained, allowing for clear visualization of the damaged region. Oil red O (Option A) and Sudan black B (Option C) are used to stain lipids and are not specific for myocardial ischemia. Masson trichrome (Option D) is a histological stain used to highlight collagen (fibrosis) in old, healed infarctions, rather than the acute phase. Using TTC allows pathologists to accurately locate and measure the extent of the ischemic injury shortly after death. This is essential for confirming the cause of death in cases of sudden cardiac arrest where traditional histological changes might not have had sufficient time to develop
questions.learning: During a forensic or clinical autopsy, detecting an early myocardial infarction (typically 2-12 hours old) can be challenging through gross examination alone.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A couple presented to OPD with complaint of inability to conceive for last 3 years. Husband was advised semen analysis. What is the WHO criterion for minimum sperm count per ml in normal semen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 15 million

According to the WHO semen analysis reference values (2010 and retained in WHO 2021 lower reference limits), the lower reference limit for sperm concentration is 15 million sperm/mL.

Why not the other options?

• A. 10 million/mL: Below the WHO lower reference limit.
• C. 30 million/mL: Older reference values; not the current WHO criterion.
• D. 40 million/mL: Not a WHO lower reference limit.
questions.learning: 15 million According to the WHO semen analysis reference values (2010 and retained in WHO 2021 lower reference limits), the lower reference limit for sperm concentration is 15 million sperm/mL.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: An 18-year-old female was sexually assaulted by a 20-year-old male.Barberio's test was performed on the stains and showed yellow needle-shaped rhombic crystals.Which of the following is detected by this test?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Spermine

Barberio's test which detects the presence of spermine ,present in prostatic secretions and thus helps in the identification of seminal fluid.

In Barberio's test, a saturated aqueous or alcoholic solution of picric acid is added to the spermatic fluid. This produces yellow needle-shaped rhombic crystals of spermine picrate.

Option B: Acid phosphatase test is a quantitative test for the presence of acid phosphatase enzyme. High levels of acid phosphatase from prostatic secretions are present in seminal stains (The normal vaginal secretions have low levels of acid phosphatase). Positive reactions are found till 36 hours after which the enzyme levels fall and disappear within 72 hours. In the absence of demonstrable sperms or aspermia, this test can be considered conclusive.

Option C: Florence test detects choline which is secreted by seminal vesicles. The suspected seminal stain is extracted with 10% hydrochloric acid and a drop of it is placed over a slide. A coverslip is placed over it and a drop of Florence solution (potassium iodide, iodine, and water) is made to run under the coverslip. If semen is present, dark brown rhombic or needle-shaped crystals of choline iodide appear immediately. The test is not confirmatory for the presence of semen, however, a negative reaction rules out the presence of semen.

Option D: Fructose acts as an energy source for sperm. Its presence in seminal fluid indicates a patent efferent ductal system, as fructose will be absent in its obstruction.

The absolute proof of semen is finding at least one unbroken spermatozoon or electrophoretic LDH isoenzyme detection of sperms.
questions.learning: Spermine Barberio's test which detects the presence of spermine ,present in prostatic secretions and thus helps in the identification of seminal fluid.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A newborn is brought with severe respiratory distress soon after birth. A chest X-ray was done and is shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia

The most probable diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario and the X-ray showing herniation of the bowel loops into the chest is suggestive of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH).

CDH is a structural diaphragmatic defect with or without abdominal contents in the thorax. It allows the abdominal organs to push into the chest cavity resulting in pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension. The most common type of CDH is a bochdalek hernia involving the left side. They may also have a scaphoid abdomen.

Babies with CDH present with respiratory distress immediately after birth characterized by tachypnea, grunting, use of accessory muscles, and cyanosis. Auscultation of the chest may reveal bowel sounds with reduced breath sounds.

Diagnosis is done by a chest radiograph showing herniated bowel loops hemithorax, displacement of the mediastinum to the contralateral side, and reduced lung space. Prenatal diagnosis can be made using ultrasonography between 16 to 24 weeks of gestation.

The immediate step in the management is to place a naso- or orogastric tube for decompression. The airway is to be secured with endotracheal intubation. Bag and mask ventilation should be avoided. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) and high-frequency oscillatory ventilation have been used as a part of the ventilation strategy.

Bag and mask ventilation should be avoided. Surgical repair of the defect is to be considered at least 48 hours after stabilization and resolution of pulmonary hypertension.
questions.learning: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia — The most probable diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario and the X-ray showing herniation of the bowel loops into the chest is suggestive of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text:
A patient presented with nasal congestion and upon examination, nasal polyps were observed. A coronal CT scan of the patient was taken and is as shown below. Which of the following sinus drainage pathways is likely to be affected?

CT - Computed Tomography
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Maxillary

In this patient with rhinosinusitis and nasal polyps, the CT scan indicates that the maxillary sinus is likely affected, as evidenced by the presence of a polyp in this sinus.

Antrochoanal polyp is a type of non-neoplastic nasal polypoidal masses of edematous nasal or sinus mucosa. It arises from the mucosa of the maxillary antrum near its accessory ostium, comes out of it, and grows in the choana and nasal cavity. It is usually single and unilateral which are more commonly seen in children and young adults.

It has 3 parts namely

• Thin antral stalk,
• Round and globular choanal part, and
• Flat nasal part.

The clinical features include unilateral nasal obstruction, mucoid nasal discharge, and a hyponasal voice.

Anterior rhinoscopy may miss the antrochoanal polyp when it starts to grow posteriorly. A large polyp may protrude from the nasal cavity and may appear pink and congested. It is soft and can be moved with a probe. Posterior rhinoscopy may reveal a globular mass filling the choana and hanging down behind the soft palate.

X-ray (lateral view) of soft tissue nasopharynx, reveals a globular swelling in the postnasal space, it is differentiated from angiofibroma by the presence of a column of air behind the polyp known as Dodd sign or crescent sign.

Diagnosis is made by radiograph of the paranasal sinuses reveals opacity of the involved antrum. Non-contrast CT scan reveals the extent of the polyp. Endoscopic examination reveals the antrochoanal polyp hidden posteriorly in the nasal cavity.

Endoscopic sinus surgery is the treatment of choice. Recurrence is uncommon after the complete removal of the polyp.
questions.learning: Maxillary — In this patient with rhinosinusitis and nasal polyps, the CT scan indicates that the maxillary sinus is likely affected, as evidenced by the presence of a polyp in this sinus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 20-year-old woman with a known history of sickle cell anemia presents to the emergency department with severe pain in her legs and fingers for the past 4 hours. Examination reveals tenderness in the right upper quadrant, and investigations show sickle cells on peripheral smear along with elevated indirect bilirubin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient is presenting with a classic Vaso-occlusive (Pain) Crisis, the most common type of Sickle cell crisis. The extreme pain in the extremities (dactylitis) results from sickled RBCs blocking small capillaries, leading to tissue ischemia. Right upper quadrant pain and high indirect bilirubin indicate a superimposed hemolytic crisis and potential pigment gallstones, which are common in sickle cell disease. IDA (Option A) and Thalassemia (Option B) would not present with this acute pain/sickle cell smear. Anemia of chronic disease (Option C) is a different pathology. Management of a vaso-occlusive crisis involves aggressive hydration, oxygenation, and potent analgesia (often opioids). Triggers such as infection, dehydration, or cold exposure should be identified and managed. This clinical scenario is a hallmark of sickle cell management in emergency medicine, emphasizing the need for rapid pain control and fluid resuscitation to improve microvascular flow
questions.learning: The patient is presenting with a classic Vaso-occlusive (Pain) Crisis, the most common type of Sickle cell crisis. The extreme pain in the extremities (dactylitis) results from sickled RBCs blocking small capillaries, leading to tissue ischemia.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient reports the belief that his thoughts and feelings are being controlled or influenced by an external agency. What is this psychopathological phenomenon called?
questions.explanation: The belief that one's feelings, thoughts, or movements are being controlled or influenced by an external agency is known as a Passivity phenomenon (or delusion of control). This is one of Schneider’s First-Rank Symptoms of schizophrenia. Delusion of nihilism (Option A, Cotard’s syndrome) involves the belief that one is dead or that the world doesn't exist. Delusion of reference (Option B) is the belief that neutral events (like news broadcasts) have a special, personal meaning meant only for the patient. Othello syndrome (Option C) is a delusion of morbid jealousy, where the patient is convinced of a partner's infidelity without cause. Passivity phenomena are highly diagnostic for psychotic disorders. The patient may feel like a "puppet," with their will being overridden by outside forces. Identifying these core psychotic features is essential for differentiating schizophrenia from other mental health conditions and starting appropriate antipsychotic management
questions.learning: The belief that one's feelings, thoughts, or movements are being controlled or influenced by an external agency is known as a Passivity phenomenon (or delusion of control).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A man presents with a slowly progressive swelling over the past 1 and 1/2 years. On examination, it has a variable consistency and appears as shown in the image. What is the probable cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pleomorphic adenoma

A slowly progressive swelling, with a variable consistency, lifting the ear lobe, is suggestive of pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid gland.

Pleomorphic adenoma, the most common benign salivary gland tumor, primarily affects the parotid gland, particularly its superficial lobe. It is also referred to as a mixed tumor due to its combination of epithelial and mesenchymal components. This tumor most commonly occurs in females around the age of 40.

Clinical features:

• Painless, slow-growing swelling
• Lobulated, firm, variable in consistency
• Lifts the earlobe
• No facial nerve involvement
• Curtain sign positive - cannot be moved above the zygomatic bone.
• In case of deep lobe involvement, tonsils, and faucial pillars will be pushed medially.
• Features of malignancy - a sudden increase in size, ulceration of the overlying skin, facial nerve palsy (involvement of facial nerve), painful swelling, and restriction of jaw movements.

Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is the investigation of choice in diagnosing pleomorphic adenoma. Open biopsy is contraindicated due to the chances of injury to the facial nerve.

All tumors of the superficial lobe of the parotid gland should be managed by superficial parotidectomy. Radical parotidectomy is performed for malignant pleomorphic adenoma.

Other options:

Option A: Adamantinoma is a low-grade malignant tumor that usually presents with pre-tibial pain and swelling since it most commonly affects the tibial diaphysis.

Option B:  Dermoid cysts present as firm painless subcutaneous nodules and are of 4 types:

1. Sequestration dermoid - sequestration of epithelium during embryological development.
2. Tubulodermoid - accumulation of secretions from ectodermal tube/duct
3. Implantation dermoid - implantation of the epidermis due to trauma
4. Teratomatous dermoid - having all 3 germ layers (ecto, meso, and endoderm)

Option D: Sebaceous cysts are retention cysts of the sebaceous glands that present as smooth, non-tender, non-transillumination swelling with a punctum (in 70% of the patients).
questions.learning: Pleomorphic adenoma — A slowly progressive swelling, with a variable consistency, lifting the ear lobe, is suggestive of pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid gland.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 45-year-old male patient presents to the OPD with complaints of increasing pain in his right hand over the past few months. On examination, there is a palpable lump, and an x-ray was done which is given below. Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Chondrosarcoma

The clinical presentation at this age and the radiograph showing popcorn calcification are suggestive of chondrosarcoma.

Chondrosarcoma is the second most common nonhematological primary malignancy of the bone(Osteosarcoma is the commonest). It can be primary or secondary. Secondary chondrosarcomas develop at the site of a previously existing benign cartilage lesion.

Primary chondrosarcomas are commonly seen at 40-60 years of age whereas the age group for secondary chondrosarcoma is 25-45 years.

Clinical features:

* Pelvis, proximal femur, and proximal humerus are the common locations.

* The hand is a rare location. However, it is the most common primary bone malignancy in the hand.

* Primary chondrosarcoma usually presents with increasing pain and a palpable lump.

* Asymptomatic radiological abnormality is a common presentation in enchondromas but is not seen in chondrosarcomas.

Radiological findings:

* It arises from the medullary cavity and shows irregular matrix calcification.

* Characteristic calcification pattern is described as "popcorn", "punctate", or "comma-shaped"

* Bone destruction, cortical erosion, and periosteal reaction may be seen.

* CT or MRI is used to identify the presence of secondary chondrosarcomas.

* Secondary chondrosarcoma is suspected of the cartilage cap of the lesion is more than 2 cm in a skeletally mature patient.

Treatment:

* Extended curettage with intraoperative adjuvant treatments is considered for low-grade lesions confined to the medullary canal.

* Low-grade lesions with soft tissue extensions should be treated as high-grade lesions.

* High-grade lesions are managed with wide or radical resection or amputation.

* Chemotherapy is not indicated for conventional chondrosarcoma but is used for mesenchymal or dedifferentiated variants.

* Radiotherapy is only used as a palliative measure for surgically inaccessible tumors.

Other options:

Option A: Osteosarcoma is the most common non-hematologic primary malignancy of bone. It occurs most commonly in the second decade of life. It is typically metaphyseal. The distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus are the common sites.

Radiographic findings: The periosteal reaction is the typical finding and it may take the form of a "Codman's triangle" or it may have a "sunburst (sunray) appearance" on X-ray.

Option B: Ewing's sarcoma is a primary malignant tumor of the bone commonly involving the age group of 4-25 years. It commonly involves the diaphysis of the long bones like the femur, tibia, fibula, and humerus.

Radiographic findings: Onion-peel appearance due to deposition of periosteal reaction in layers is the typical finding.

Option C: Osteoclastoma or Giant cell tumor: The commonly affected age group is 20-40 years with a slight female preponderance. The distal end of the femur is the most common location followed by the proximal tibia and distal radius.

Radiographic findings:

* Eccentrically located solitary lytic lesion in the epiphysis

* Soap bubble appearance

* Periosteal new bone formation is absent.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a population with 4,050 total births, there are 50 stillbirths, 50 deaths within the first 7 days of life, and 150 deaths between 8 and 28 days of life. What is the Neonatal Mortality Rate (NMR) for this population?
questions.explanation: The Neonatal Mortality Rate (NMR) is defined as the number of deaths among live-born infants within the first 28 days of life per 1,000 live births. Let us calculate step by step: 1. Total births = 4050 This includes 50 stillbirths, which must be excluded. Why other options are incorrect: 1. Option A (12.5): Represents only early neonatal mortality rate (50/4000 × 1000). 2. Option C (49.4): Incorrectly uses total births (4050) instead of live births as the denominator. 3. Option D (62.5): Not derived from the given data. Thus, the Neonatal Mortality Rate is 50 per 1,000 live births, making Option (B) correct
questions.learning: The Neonatal Mortality Rate (NMR) is defined as the number of deaths among live-born infants within the first 28 days of life per 1,000 live births. Total births = 4050 This includes 50 stillbirths, which must be excluded.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following structures given below is related to the structure highlighted (red) in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pudendal nerve

The structure marked in red is the ischial spine and the pudendal nerve is related to it.

The pudendal nerve originates from the sacral plexus S2-S4. It exits out of the pelvis by passing through the greater sciatic foramen. It then enters the perineum below the pelvic floor by passing around the ischial spine. The ischial spine is used as a landmark for pudendal nerve block.
questions.learning: Pudendal nerve — The structure marked in red is the ischial spine and the pudendal nerve is related to it. The pudendal nerve originates from the sacral plexus S2-S4.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with paresthesia of the hands and feet, generalized weakness, easy fatigability, pallor, and ataxia. Which vitamin deficiency best explains this combination of symptoms?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation combines hematological and neurological symptoms. Pallor and fatigue suggest anemia, while tingling (paresthesia), weakness, and ataxia (loss of coordination) indicate subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord. This specific combination is the classic manifestation of Vitamin B12 deficiency. Vitamin B12 is essential for both red blood cell production and the maintenance of the myelin sheath in the nervous system. Vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency (Option A) causes beriberi, which involves peripheral neuropathy or heart failure but typically not ataxia and pallor together. Vitamin B2 (riboflavin) deficiency (Option C) presents with cheilosis and glossitis. Vitamin B3 (niacin) deficiency (Option D) causes pellagra, characterized by dermatitis and diarrhea. Because B12 deficiency is unique in causing both macrocytic anemia and progressive dorsal column neurological deficits, it is the most likely diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation combines hematological and neurological symptoms. Pallor and fatigue suggest anemia, while tingling (paresthesia), weakness, and ataxia (loss of coordination) indicate subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A surgically resected specimen of an ovarian mass is is shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mature cystic teratoma

The specimen showing an ovarian mass with a tuft of hair in a cystic space is a mature cystic teratoma.

Teratomas are germ cell tumors. They contain embryonic tissues leading to the differentiation of cells along these pathways. There are three classes of teratomas:

• Mature (benign) teratomas (e.g.: dermoid cyst)
• Immature (essentially malignant) teratomas (e.g.: solid teratoma)
• Monodermal (highly specialized) tumors (e.g.: struma ovarii)

Mature cystic teratomas, also known as dermoid cysts are unilocular, containing sebaceous material and hair. They have a smooth surface and are lined by squamous epithelium. Other structures like teeth, bone, cartilage, thyroid tissue, and neural tissues can also be found.

Most patients are asymptomatic. Common presentations include abdominal mass, acute pain due to torsion of the ovary, and rarely due to rupture of the cyst with spillage of contents into the abdomen.

Treatment of mature teratomas involves excision in order to prevent complications.

Option A - Immature teratomas of the ovary are solid and trabeculated. They also contain cartilage, bone, hair, and sebaceous material. There is no structural order. They are generally malignant. Grossly, they have a smooth external surface and are solid on sectioning. There may be areas of necrosis or hemorrhage.

The following image shows both mature (left) and immature teratomas (right).

Option C- Mucinous cystadenoma is a benign tumor showing multicystic appearance, delicate septa, and the presence of glistening mucin within the cyst.

Option D- Serous cystadenoma have multicystic lesion in which papillary epithelium is contained within fibrous walled cysts or as a mass projecting from the ovarian surface.
questions.learning: Mature cystic teratoma — The specimen showing an ovarian mass with a tuft of hair in a cystic space is a mature cystic teratoma. They contain embryonic tissues leading to the differentiation of cells along these pathways.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify pancreas, liver, and spleen?
questions.explanation: On a standard axial CT scan of the upper abdomen, the organs are identified by their characteristic positions: 1. A (Liver): The largest solid organ, occupying the right upper quadrant. 2. B (Pancreas): A lobulated, retroperitoneal organ that lies transversely across the midline, posterior to the stomach. 3. C (Spleen): A smaller, solid organ located in the left upper quadrant, lateral to the tail of the pancreas. Options B, C, and D provide incorrect assignments for these anatomical landmarks. Accurately identifying these organs is the first step in abdominal CT interpretation. The liver is typically on the left side of the image (the patient's right). The pancreas is often identified by its proximity to the splenic vein and the superior mesenteric artery. The spleen's location in the far left is a reliable marker. This anatomical spatial reasoning is a fundamental skill for medical board exams and clinical radiology practice
questions.learning: On a standard axial CT scan of the upper abdomen, the organs are identified by their characteristic positions: 1. A (Liver): The largest solid organ, occupying the right upper quadrant.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which hypersensitivity reaction mediates blood transfusion reactions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Type II

Type II hypersensitivity reactions mediate blood transfusion reactions.

There are 3 mechanisms involved in type 2 hypersensitivity reactions—

* Antibody-mediated cellular dysfunction—antibodies react with antigens present on cell surfaces or in the extracellular matrix cause disease by destroying these cells, triggering inflammation, or interfering with normal functions

* Myasthenia gravis (against acetylcholine receptor)

* Graves’ disease (against TSH receptor)

* Pemphigus Vulgaris (against epidermal cadherin)

* Pernicious anemia (against intrinsic factor)

* Insulin-resistant diabetes (against insulin receptor)

* Antibody-mediated opsonization and phagocytosis – antibodies may deposit in tissues or blood vessels, and elicit an acute inflammatory reaction by activating complement and recruiting phagocytes

* Transfusion reactions

* Erythroblastosis fetalis

* Autoimmune hemolytic anemia

* Autoimmune thrombocytopenic purpura

* Complement and Fc receptor-mediated inflammation – antibodies may deposit in tissues or blood vessels, and elicit an acute inflammatory reaction by activating complement

* Goodpasture syndrome

* Vasculitis due to ANCA

* Acute rheumatic fever

* Vascular rejection in organ graft

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following statements is/are True? 1. The basement membrane remains intact in dysplasia. 2. Dysplasia is an adaptive response to stress or injury. 3. Pleomorphism is observed in metaplasia. 4. Myositis ossificans is an example of dysplasia.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 only

Dysplasia is disordered growth and maturation of epithelial cells, characterized by cellular atypia, pleomorphism, hyperchromatic nuclei, and loss of normal tissue architecture. It is considered premalignant, but the basement membrane remains intact. When cells breach the basement membrane, it becomes invasive carcinoma.

1. The basement membrane remains intact in dysplasia. True. Basement membrane is intact in dysplasia.

2. Dysplasia is an adaptive response to stress or injury. False. Dysplasia is not an adaptive response (metaplasia is adaptive).

3. Pleomorphism is observed in metaplasia. False. Pleomorphism occurs in dysplasia, not in metaplasia.

4. Myositis ossificans is an example of dysplasia. False. Myositis ossificans is an example of metaplasia (bone formation in muscle), not dysplasia.

| Feature | Metaplasia | Dysplasia | Anaplasia

| ------- | ---------- | --------- | ---------

| Definition | Differentiated cell type (epithelial or mesenchymal) is replaced by another cell type | Disordered growth and loss of architectural orientation of cells | Lack of cellular differentiation and organisation

| Nature | Adaptive response to stress or injury | Preneoplastic | Associated with malignant transformation

| Reversibility | Reversible | Reversible in early stages (irreversible if whole epithelium is involved) | Irreversible

| Pleomorphism | Absent | Present in low-grade | Present in high-grade

| Nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio | Normal (1:4 to 1:6) | Increased (↑) | Increased (↑↑↑)

| Mitotic figures | Absent/minimal at normal places | Typical mitotic figures present at abnormal places | Atypical, bizarre mitotic figures present at abnormal places

| Basement membrane integrity | Intact | Intact | Breached

| Example | Barrett’s oesophagus, myositis ossificans | Cervical dysplasia of squamous cells | Carcinoma of the cervix, carcinoma oesophagus
questions.learning: 1 only Dysplasia is disordered growth and maturation of epithelial cells, characterized by cellular atypia, pleomorphism, hyperchromatic nuclei, and loss of normal tissue architecture.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old male patient with enteric fever presents to the emergency with sudden onset of generalised abdominal pain, abdominal distension, nausea, vomiting and constipation for last 48 hours. On examination, patient is dehydrated with PR = 110/min and BP = 100/60 mmHg. There is generalised tenderness, rebound tenderness present and board like rigidity on per abdomen examination. The most likely complication of enteric fever in this patient is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Small bowel perforation

Enteric (typhoid) perforation is a life-threatening complication of typhoid fever, usually occurring in the third week due to necrosis of Peyer’s patches in the terminal ileum. It presents as acute generalized peritonitis. Features include sudden severe abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, constipation, dehydration, guarding, rebound tenderness, and board-like rigidity.

Why not the other options?

• A. Small bowel enteritis: Does not cause generalized peritonitis with board-like rigidity.
• C. Small bowel obstruction: Causes distension and vomiting but not generalized peritonitis unless perforation occurs.
• D. Cholecystitis: Causes right upper quadrant pain, not diffuse peritonitis.
questions.learning: Small bowel perforation Enteric (typhoid) perforation is a life-threatening complication of typhoid fever, usually occurring in the third week due to necrosis of Peyer’s patches in the terminal ileum.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not true about Barrett's esophagus?
options: It is the intestinal metaplasia of esophagus
Mucus secreting foveolar cells are characteristic
Alician blue is used in the staining of biopsy specimen
It is a reversible cell adaptation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mucus secreting foveolar cells are characteristic

Mucus-secreting goblet cells (not foveolar cells) are characteristic of Barrett's esophagus, as there is intestinal metaplasia of the esophagus. Foveolar cells are the mucus-secreting cells in the stomach.

Barrett's esophagus is a complication of chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), and it is estimated to occur in about 10% of individuals with symptomatic GERD. Symptoms include heartburn, regurgitation and sometimes dysphagia. Obese white men over the age of 60 years represent the highest-risk group.

Intestinal metaplasia in the esophagus occurs due to chronic irritation of the esophagus in GERD (option A) since intestinal epithelium is better suited to handling gastric acid exposure. Hence, mucus-secreting goblet cells are characteristic of Barrett's esophagus. Since all metaplasia are reversible, Barrett's esophagus is also reversible (option D). Only 0.2 to 1% of Barrett's esophagus leads to dysplasia and adenocarcinoma.

Alician blue is used in the staining of the biopsy specimen, as it stains the goblet cells (option C). Mucicarmine is the specific stain.

Seattle protocol is used for the management of Barrett's esophagus.
questions.learning: Mucus secreting foveolar cells are characteristic Mucus-secreting goblet cells (not foveolar cells) are characteristic of Barrett's esophagus, as there is intestinal metaplasia of the esophagus.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: An Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP) image of the child is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ureterocele

The image shown above depicts the "cobra head" sign on excretion urography in a patient with a bilateral ureterocele.

A ureterocele is the cystic enlargement of the intramural ureter. It is common in females. Clinical presentation: Children with a ureterocele usually present with infection. Adults present with renal stones.

Diagnosis: IVU shows a classical cobra head sign or ‘adder head’ sign or 'spring onion sign'. It refers to a dilated, contrast-filled distal ureter, surrounded by a thin rim of ureteric wall and bladder mucosa. On ultrasonography, it can be seen as a fluid-filled cystic mass in the bladder. Cystoscopy shows a bulging, translucent swelling involving the ureteric orifice where there is urinary stasis.

Treatment: Surgical excision with re-implantation of the ureter is the treatment of choice for a simple ureterocele.

Other Options:

Option B: Due abnormal ascent of the metanephros during embryological development leads to an ectopic kidney, increasing the risk of infection, hydronephrosis, etc.

Option C: Duplication of Ureter: Also known as Duplex Kidney, this is due to the incomplete fusion of the upper and lower poles of the kidney. The drooping lily sign is seen on Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP).

Option D: Posterior urethral valves are the most common cause of severe obstructive uropathy in children. Diagnosis is most commonly made antenatally with ultrasound (Keyhole sign is seen). Clinically, a poor urinary stream, dribbling, and palpable bladder (due to diverticula) can be present. The investigation of choice is micturating cystourethrography.

Pearl PF1667: IVU signs and associated conditions

Medullary sponge kidney

* Bouquet of flowers/ paintbrush appearance

* It refers to the cystic dilatation of the distal collecting tubules

Duplex kidney

* Drooping lily sign

* It refers to the inferolateral displacement of the lower pole due to an obstructed upper pole in a duplicated collecting system

Horseshoe kidney

* Handshake sign - due to the position of the lower poles closer to the spine, and the lower calyces closer to each other

* Flower vase sign - due to medially rotated calyces

Retroperitoneal fibrosis

* Maiden waist deformity

* It refers to the medially drawn ureters caused by fibrosis at the lumbosacral junction

Retrocaval ureter

* Fish hook / Reverse J deformity

* Right ureter hooks behind the IVC as it passes posterior to it

Ureterocele

* Cobra/ Adder head appearance

* It refers to the dilation of the distal ureter

Transitional cell carcinoma of the ureter

* Goblet sign

* It is due to the focal dilation of the ureter by an intraluminal mass
questions.learning: Ureterocele — The image shown above depicts the "cobra head" sign on excretion urography in a patient with a bilateral ureterocele. A ureterocele is the cystic enlargement of the intramural ureter.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with severe dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia and infertility. A diagnosis of endometriosis was made and she was posted for laparoscopy surgery. During the procedure, dense pelvic adhesions were seen with the bowel stuck to the fundus and cystic ovaries stuck to each other. What is the next step in managing this patient?
options: Gestrinone to decrease the LH surge
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cystectomy and adhesiolysis

The clinical scenario is suggestive of endometriosis and the next step in the management of this patient is cystectomy and adhesiolysis.

After the surgery the patient is advised to start infertility treatment too.

Medical management of endometriosis:

* Gestrinone is an anti-estrogenic, anti-progestational, and mildly anabolic drug that reduces sex-hormone-binding globulin to release free testosterone. It also decreases the LH surge. It causes regression of lesions and amenorrhea. It is a 19-nortestosterone derivative similar to danazol, but with fewer side effects.

* Combined oral contraceptives are used for symptom control and alleviate disease. These also cause menstrual cycle regulation and delay pregnancy.

* Oral progestogens exert an anti-estrogenic effect and cause decidualization and endometrial atrophy. This causes disease regression. It doesn't prevent ovulation, thus is suitable for women who are trying to conceive.

* Mirena IUCDs reduce dysmenorrhea and menorrhagia. It is a single-sitting treatment with minimal side effects.

* Aromatase inhibitors like letrozole are anti-estrogens given for disease regression.

* Anti-inflammatory drugs like mefenamic acid and naproxen relieve dysmenorrhea.

Therapeutic procedures:

* Aspiration of Peritoneal fluid from the cul-de-sac removes PGE2, relieves dysmenorrhea, pelvic pain, and improves fertility

* Destruction of endometriotic lesions <3cm with diathermy, Nd-YAG laser or CO2 vaporization can be attempted.

* Larger lesions and chocolate cysts can be excised.

* Cystectomy can be done for pelvic pain but can reduce fertility potential.

* Laparoscopic breaking of adhesions relieves dysmenorrhea and chronic pelvic pain. It also restores tubal patency and improves ovulation. Pre-sacral neurectomy can be done simultaneously..

* Laser uterosacral nerve ablation (LUNA) is done for pelvic pain.

Pearl PF1294: Endometriosis

Sites of Endometriosis:

* Pelvic endometriosis: Pelvic peritoneum, the pouch of Douglas, uterosacral ligament.

* Rectovaginal endometriosis.

* Ovarian endometriosis.

* Chocolate cyst of the ovary.

* Other sites—appendix, pelvic lymph nodes.

* Metastatic— lungs, umbilicus, scar endometriosis.

One pathology review revealed that endometriosis has been identified on all organs except the spleen.

Examination findings in endometriosis:

* Abdomen: Cystic swelling, fixed and tender.

* Pelvis: Cystic tender mass.

* Vaginal examination: Fixed, tender, retroverted uterus. Tenderness in the lateral fornices (indicative of endometriosis even if no mass).

* Speculum inspection of the Posterior fornix: Bluish/blackish puckered spots on speculum, tender to touch. The presence of puckered spots is pathognomonic of endometriosis.

* Posterior Fornix Palpation: Uterosacral ligaments & pouch of Douglas feel thickened and shotty with multiple small palpable nodules. This is called the cobblestone feel of uterosacral ligaments.
questions.learning: Cystectomy and adhesiolysis — The clinical scenario is suggestive of endometriosis and the next step in the management of this patient is cystectomy and adhesiolysis.
